    Design engineer primer · Book 1

    Design Field Guide

    How to design interfaces, and why the good ones work, live on the page. Start here defines design and design engineering. Part 1 is about judgment: what makes a design good and how to train your eye. Part 2 covers the patterns that solve problems people keep running into. Part 3 covers the building blocks: what each component is for, how it breaks, and what to use instead. Part 4 is about taking a problem to a shipped solution with agents and tools. Play with the demos as you read, and tick “Learned” when something clicks.

    Your progress stays in this browser

    Preface

    How to read this book

    This book is for anyone who decides how an interface should work, and most of all for design engineers, who make those calls in code. It teaches by showing: every idea comes with a demo you can try on the page.

    Three ways to read it

    Read it from the start. Each part builds on the one before, and Part 4 puts the first three to work on one problem. Or start from a question: When you hear this, try that goes from what people say to a pattern, and Before you pick one, ask three questions goes from what people need to a component. Or keep it open while you work: Before you ship, ask these and Effective design, step by step turn the book into questions for your next change.

    How an entry works

    An entry starts with what the idea is and a demo, with a short “Try it” line that says what to look for. Many entries then show the forms or ways it comes in. Then come the rules, each with its own demo and a switch between two sides: what goes wrong, and “Do this instead”. The first side is called “Common mistake” in Parts 1 and 4, “When it backfires” for patterns, because every pattern has a cost, and “When it breaks” for components. Last, “In real products” shows the idea in products you may know.

    Tick “Learned” when an idea clicks. The contents show how many you’ve ticked, and your progress stays in this browser.

    What the examples are

    The product examples are this book’s summaries of how those products worked when it was written, not the companies’ own descriptions, so check the product before you cite how it behaves. Part 4 names the tools of 2026, such as Claude Code, Figma, Linear and Playwright. Each rule says what to do first, so it still holds when a tool changes.

    How to cite it

    Every entry, section and rule has its own link: press the # next to its title. To cite one, give the version and the link’s anchor, such as “Design Field Guide v35, #good-problem-framing-rule-2”. Agents can read the same book as plain text, starting from llms.txt.

    Start here

    Design and design engineering

    Two short definitions before the rest of the book: what design is, and what a design engineer does.

    What design is

    Design is deciding how something should work for the people who use it. How it looks is part of that, but it’s the last part.

    It helps to think of three layers. The problem comes first, and each layer after it rests on the one before.

    The problem

    Who is this for, and what are they trying to get done? If this is wrong, nothing built on it can save the design.

    The behavior

    What happens when people act: what they see, what they can undo, and what happens when something fails.

    The surface

    Layout, type, color and motion. It makes the behavior easy to read, but it can’t fix the wrong behavior.

    Most of what people call bad design is a wrong call about the problem or the behavior, not the surface. The demo shows one parking app, changed at each layer, and in every version you park for what turns out to be 1 hour 20 minutes.

    Only the new problem removes the ticket altogether, because it answers the real question. That is why this book starts with judgment about problems and gets to components last.

    What design engineering is

    A design engineer designs in the material the product is made of: code. Instead of handing over pictures, they build the thing, try it, and change it until it works.

    The role exists because many design decisions only show up when something runs. How long should a spinner wait before it appears? What happens to a 40-character name? Where does focus go when a dialog closes? A mockup rarely answers these, but a prototype in code answers them in minutes.

    Prototypes

    Quick working versions that answer a design question, so the team decides on evidence instead of opinions.

    The details

    States, timing, motion, edge cases and the keyboard path. Mockups skip them, but people notice all of them.

    What ships

    Keeping what was designed and what ships the same, through components, tokens and review of the built thing.

    It sits between two roles that already exist. The three differ mostly in where each one starts and what each one is judged on.

    DesignerDesign engineerFrontend engineer
    Starts fromA problem and the people who have itA design question, or a design that has to work for realA spec and a codebase
    ProducesFlows, mockups, the design systemWorking prototypes, interface details, componentsFeatures that ship, are tested and can be maintained
    Judged onWhether it solves the right problem clearlyWhether the built thing feels as intended, in every stateWhether it works, is fast and lasts

    The rest of the book follows that work, from judging the problem to shipping the solution.

    Part 1

    Good design

    What makes a design good, how to tell, and how to train your eye. The patterns and components later in the book are tools, and this part is about knowing when and how to use them.

    Before you start

    Good design is mostly invisible

    When design is good, people get what they came for and don’t think about the interface at all. That makes good design hard to see, and easy to mistake for good looks. Polish matters, but it comes last.

    This part breaks “good” into habits you can practice.

    Right problemIt solves something real, for someone specific, and you know how you’d tell.
    Clear and consistentThe important thing is obvious, and the same thing always looks and works the same way.
    Considered to the edgesThe words, the timing, the messy data and the keyboard path were all designed on purpose.

    How each entry reads

    Each entry is a short article. It states the idea and lets you try it in a demo. Then come the common mistakes, each with a demo you can switch between the mistake and the fix. Last, real products that get it right. Several demos are small games (spot the problem, spot the difference), because judgment is trained by looking closely.

    ChapterThe habit
    Start from the problemFrame the problem and define “good” before drawing anything.
    Make it clearUse hierarchy, grouping, rhythm and contrast so the important thing is obvious.
    ConsistencySame thing, same look, same place, and break the rule only on purpose.
    WordsWrite labels, errors and help as part of the interface.
    CraftDesign the timing, the messy data and the keyboard path.
    Judge the workCritique against the goal, with heuristics and principles as lenses.
    Practice & your edgeTrain your eye, prototype in code, and write the reasoning down.

    Chapter 1

    Get the problem right first

    Most bad design is a good answer to the wrong question: the layout is tidy and the button works, yet it solves something nobody had, or skips what people needed first. The three entries below are the work that comes before any pixels: know what has to hold, frame the problem, and decide how you’ll tell it worked.

    Hierarchy of needs

    The hierarchy of needs is an order for building a feature. First it has to work, then work every time, then be easy to use. Only after that does delight count, like a small animation or a friendly line of text.

    Each layer rests on the ones below it, so a pleasant touch on a feature that sometimes fails doesn’t feel pleasant: it feels like nobody checked. Easy to use includes people who use a keyboard or a screen reader, so accessibility belongs in that layer and can’t wait for the polish.

    PleasurableHolds
    UsableHolds
    ReliableHolds
    FunctionalHolds
    Trip notes Not saved yet
    FlightsHotelDay tripsPacking

    Saved versions: 0

    Try it: press Save and enjoy the little check. Then break Reliable and save twice: the celebration plays, then the save fails. Break Usable to hide Save in a menu, or Functional to see everything above it go shaky.

    Rules

    Four rules keep the layers in order.

    1Make it work before you polish it

    When the animation is done before the feature, people get the nice moment and then find nothing behind it. The polish makes the failure feel worse, because it promised something. Build from the bottom up, and add the polish last.

    Try: save a recipe, then open Saved.

    A polished heart animation, but saving doesn’t work yet.

    No animation yet, but saving works.

    2Check more than the happy path

    A feature can work when everything goes right and still fail people often, because networks are slow, lists are empty and servers return errors. If those cases show a blank screen, people can’t tell whether to wait or leave. Try each case before you call the feature done, and give each one a clear state.

    Try: switch between the four cases under the inbox.

    A slow, empty or failed load shows a blank inbox.

    Each case gets its own state, and Error offers Retry.

    3Make room for delight once it holds

    There is always another bug, so delight can wait forever. The product then works but feels flat: finishing something feels the same as nothing happening. Once the base holds, plan small moments of care, like a friendly confirmation or a smooth transition, as part of the work.

    Try: tick off the last two tasks.

    Ticking off the last task looks like any other tick.

    Finishing the list shows a short “All done for today.”

    4Don’t cover a failure with a joke

    A cheerful message on a failed payment leaves people with no idea what went wrong, and it can feel like the product doesn’t take their money seriously. Say plainly what failed and what they can do about it. Keep the playful touches for moments that went well.

    A joke covers the failed payment. Try: press Pay. Do you know what to do next?

    The message says why the card was declined and offers another card. Try: press Pay, then Use another card, then Pay again.

    In real products

    Notice that each product shows its base is dependable before it adds anything playful.

    Frame the problem

    Framing the problem means writing down who has it, what they’re trying to do and what stops them, before anyone draws a screen. It also says how you’ll know the problem got smaller, which success criteria then spell out.

    When a request arrives as a solution, the frame turns it back into the problem behind it, so the team can compare more than one answer. Name the person closely enough to include how they work, for example with a keyboard only or on a small phone.

    Feature requestTicket

    Add a “Duplicate event” button to the toolbar

    People keep asking for a way to duplicate events. Add a Duplicate button next to Delete in the top toolbar.

    The only answer on the table Find Delete Duplicate

    The ticket already picked the answer. All that’s left to decide is where the button goes.

    Problem statement

    Duplicate from the event

    Copy an event with all its details from its own menu or a shortcut, right where people are working.

    Copy and paste details

    Copy the details of one event and paste them onto another day.

    Make it repeat

    Turn the event into a repeating one, so people don’t need a copy at all.

    Try it: read the ticket, then switch to After. Edit the answers and watch the problem statement update. Type “everyone” into the first box to see a framing that’s too broad. Then open the solutions: the toolbar button is still an option, now one of several.

    Rules

    Five rules keep a problem frame useful.

    1Restate the request as a problem

    A ticket often names its own answer, like “add an Export to PDF button”, and if the work starts there, the only question left is where the button goes. The request is a hint about what hurts, not a spec, so write down the problem behind it first, then look for answers.

    The work starts from the button the ticket asks for. Try: pick a spot for the button. Is anything else left to decide?

    The same ticket, with a button to restate it as a problem. Try: press Restate as a problem, then read the answers it opens up.

    2Name the person, the moment and the obstacle

    A frame like “make settings easier to use” fits almost any design: two people can read it, picture different screens, and both feel right. Say who it is, when it happens and what gets in their way. If two readers still picture different things, narrow it again. A who that’s only a group, like “users” or “everyone”, is always too broad. The brief check lists the words to watch for.

    Try: press Ask two people.

    The frame says only “Make settings easier to use.”

    The frame names who, when and what stops them.

    3Show where you saw it

    A problem nobody has seen is a guess: the team can’t tell how often it happens or how much it hurts, so the talk turns into opinions. Point to where it came from: a support message, a session you watched, a count. One real example is worth more than a paragraph of reasons.

    Try: press Share with the team.

    The only evidence is “I think this happens a lot.”

    The evidence is a support count, a session count and a quote.

    4Keep the answer out of the frame

    “People can’t find the Sort button” already holds its answer: only one design fits it, so the frame just repeats the request. Any control name in the problem, like a button, a dialog or a toggle, is the sign to look for. Describe what people are trying to get done, without naming a control. Then sketch at least two different answers.

    Try: press Check the answers.

    The frame names a Sort button.

    The frame describes the goal without naming a control.

    5Leave what you don’t know empty

    A frame filled with guesses reads like fact, so nobody checks it, and the team builds for a problem that may not exist. Say where each part came from: something people told you, something you read or saw, or your own guess. Look before you guess, in the support threads, tickets and notes that already exist. When nobody knows yet, leave the part empty and add it to a list of things to check. Label any guess with how you’ll check it, and when two sources disagree, show both.

    Every part is filled in, and nothing says where it came from. Try: press Share with the team.

    Each part says where it came from, and the unknowns are a list. Try: press Share with the team.

    In real products

    Notice how narrow each problem is: who, what they want, and what stops them. The frames are this book’s summary, not the companies’ own notes.

    Define “good” before building

    Success criteria say what you would see or count if a change worked. Where the problem frame says what to solve, they say what “done” looks like.

    Good criteria describe what people do, not how the design feels. “People find Export without help” can be checked, but “Export is more intuitive” can’t. Include the other ways people work too, for example “people using only a keyboard can finish checkout”.

    Try an example:

      Sample numbers

      Try it: read the starting line. The vague words get marked, with a rewrite you could check. Try the examples, then write your own. Below, switch between the two measures and ask which one could go up while people struggle.

      Rules

      Four rules keep success criteria useful.

      1Count people who got it done

      Views, clicks and time on page can all go up when a design gets worse, because a confusing page makes people click around and stay longer. Count what people came to do instead: how many finished the task, how long it took and how many errors they hit.

      Try: press Release the redesign.

      The help center counts views, clicks and time on page.

      The same help center counts who found an answer.

      2Watch people, not only numbers

      A number tells you that something changed, not why: a drop in sign-ups could come from any field on the form. Watch a few people use it. Five short sessions often show the exact place where people stop, which no dashboard will.

      The dashboard shows that sign-ups dropped. Try: press Why?

      The same number, with five sessions you watched. Try: open each session.

      3Write them down before you build

      Without criteria, a change is done when it ships: nobody can say whether it helped, and the review only checks that it looks fine. Write the criteria in the ticket or the brief before work starts, so the review can test the change against them.

      Try: press Review the change.

      The ticket has no criteria.

      The ticket lists three criteria.

      4Turn feelings into things you can see

      Words like easier, cleaner and more intuitive sound like goals, but nobody can check them, so after a test people argue about whether it felt easier. Turn each feeling into something you can watch: found without help, finished on the first try, fewer questions to support.

      The demo at the top of this entry marks these words, and the brief check in Part 4 flags the same ones. Fill the slots with your own task and numbers.

      Vague wordWrite instead, for example
      easy, easier, simple, simpler, intuitive, user-friendlyPeople find X without help, in under N clicks.
      good, better, improve, improved, improves, improvement, nice, nicerFewer support questions about Y, or fewer retries when people do it.
      clean, cleaner, clearer, modernPeople spot the main action in a five-second look at X.
      seamless, smooth, smootherNobody gets stuck or asks for help between X and Y.
      somehow, etcList what you mean: X, Y and Z.

      Try: press Run the test.

      The goal is “Booking a table feels easier.”

      The goal is “People book a table without help, on the first try.”

      In real products

      Chapter 2

      Make the important thing obvious

      People scan a screen before they read it: in the first moment they see a few shapes, guess what the screen is for, and look for the thing they came to do. Clarity comes from hierarchy, grouping, rhythm and contrast, long before color or style. The four entries below cover what stands out, what belongs together, what lines up, and what can be read at all.

      Visual hierarchy

      Visual hierarchy is the order in which people notice things on a screen. Size, weight, color, position and space set that order. In each region, one thing should clearly lead and the rest should step down from it.

      When the order is clear, people find what matters in one glance and read the rest only if they need it. Build the same order into the markup, with real headings and lists, so people using a screen reader can move through the page the same way.

      Rules

      Four rules keep visual hierarchy clear.

      1Let one thing lead

      When everything is bold, big or bright, nothing stands out, and people have to read every line to find the one they need. Pick one focal point per region, usually the outcome or the next step, and make everything else quieter.

      Try: press Glance. The pass shows for one second. Which gate was it?

      Everything on the boarding pass is big and bold.

      The gate and the boarding time lead, and the rest steps down.

      2Don’t rely on color alone

      Like any meaning carried by color alone, a title set apart only by its color blends into the text around it in grayscale, in bright sun or for people who see color differently. Set the order with size, weight, position and space, and let color add to it.

      Try: turn on Grayscale. Where does each section start?

      Section titles stand out only by their color.

      Titles are also bigger and bolder, with space above them.

      3Keep to three or four levels

      Eight sizes and four weights, each a little different, don’t read as an order: people can’t tell which level a line is on, so the page looks uneven instead of organized. Three or four levels are enough, for example a title, key facts, body text and small print. Make each step big enough to see at a glance.

      Try: turn on Show styles and count the levels.

      Eight text styles, each a small step from the next.

      Four levels: title, key facts, body and small print.

      4Keep one primary button

      Two filled buttons side by side ask for the same attention, so people stop to work out which one is the next step, and some press the wrong one. Keep one primary action per view and make the others secondary, as in Button hierarchy.

      Try: find the button that takes you to payment, and press it.

      Continue shopping and Check out are both filled.

      Check out is filled, and Continue shopping is secondary.

      Proximity

      Proximity means that things close together look like they belong together. People read the space between items before they read the words, so the gaps on a screen tell them what goes with what.

      Space only groups things for people who can see it, so give assistive tech the same groups: a real label for every field, and a named group around each set of fields.

      Export settings

      Spacing

      14 px
      14 px

      Between ÷ inside: 1.0×

      Try it: each label and its field form a group. Both gaps start at 14 px, so every label floats halfway between two fields. Drag “Space between groups” up until the hint shows a check. Then make the space inside bigger than the space between, and watch each label seem to name the field above it.

      Rules

      Four rules keep spacing honest.

      1Use more space between groups than inside them

      When every gap is the same, people can’t tell where one group ends and the next begins, so a caption between two photos could belong to either. Make the space between groups clearly bigger than the space inside them. About twice as much is a good start.

      Try: click the photo that “Lake, June” describes.

      Every gap is the same, so each caption sits halfway between two photos.

      Each caption sits close under its photo, with more space before the next one.

      2Try space before boxes and lines

      Borders and divider lines around every group give people a lot of lines to read past: the page looks busy, and the lines compete with the content. Group with space first, and add a line or a box only when space alone isn’t enough, like in a long, dense list.

      Try: turn on Show lines and count them.

      Every row and every group has its own border.

      The same groups, made with space alone.

      3Put a control next to what it changes

      When a setting sits at the top and the button that applies it sits far below, people don’t see that they belong together: they change the setting and nothing happens, or they hunt for the button. Keep a control next to the thing it changes, and its action next to the control.

      Try: make the photo brighter.

      Apply brightness sits below four other options, far from its slider.

      Apply brightness sits right under its slider.

      4Keep help text tight under its field

      A message that sits closer to the next field than to its own seems to be about the next field, so people fix the wrong thing or miss the message. Keep help and error text close under their field, with the bigger gap after them, as in Text field.

      Try: press Create account. Which field is the message about?

      The error sits closer to the next field than to its own.

      The error sits tight under its field, with the bigger gap after it.

      In real products

      Notice where the bigger gaps fall: between groups, never inside them.

      Spacing rhythm

      Spacing rhythm means every gap on a screen comes from a short scale of sizes, such as 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32 pixels, and the edges of things line up. People never measure the gaps, but they notice when gaps vary for no reason: the screen looks untidy, and it takes longer to see what belongs together.

      It works together with Proximity: Proximity decides which gaps should be small and which large, and rhythm decides which sizes those gaps can be. Set the steps in rem, so the gaps grow when people make their text larger.

      Try it: turn on the grid. In Ad-hoc, the left edges miss the 16 px line by a few pixels each, and the readout counts every different value the panel uses. Switch to the 8px scale: a few values from one scale, and one left edge.

      Rules

      Three rules keep spacing steady.

      1Take every gap from one scale

      When each gap is picked by eye, a screen ends up with many sizes that are almost the same. People can’t tell 11 from 13, so the small differences only look like mistakes. Give the team a short scale and use only its steps, so a review can ask “which step?” instead of “why 13?”.

      Try: turn on Show gaps and count the different sizes.

      Every gap was picked by eye: 13 here, 7 there, 19 above the button.

      Every gap is a step from one scale: 4, 8, 16 or 24.

      2Line edges up, or offset them clearly

      Edges that sit a few pixels apart look like an error, so people see a ragged column and trust the screen a little less. Put shared edges on the same line. When something should stand apart, like a note under a price, indent it by a full step or more so it reads as a choice.

      Try: turn on Show edges.

      The left edges sit a few pixels apart.

      The edges share one line, and the cancellation note is indented by a full step.

      3Choose density on purpose

      When each panel gets its own padding, one list is cramped and the next one is roomy, so people have to adjust at every panel and the cramped rows are harder to tap. Pick a density for each kind of screen, such as compact for a busy settings page and roomy for a welcome dialog, and build both from the same steps.

      Try: turn on Show row heights, then scroll from one list to the other.

      On the same screen, Your playlists is cramped and Recently played is roomy.

      Both lists use one compact density, built from the same steps.

      In real products

      Notice the few gap sizes that repeat, and the edges that line up. Dashed lines mark the shared edges.

      Contrast, and never color alone

      Contrast is how clearly text and controls stand apart from what’s behind them. With too little, people squint, miss things, or can’t read the screen at all in sunlight. WCAG asks for at least 4.5 : 1 for body text, and 3 : 1 for large text and for the edges and icons people need to see.

      The second half of the idea is about meaning. Color can make a status quicker to spot, but it can’t be the only clue, because some people can’t tell certain colors apart and some screens show everything in gray. Pair every color with a shape, an icon or a word.

      Rules

      Four rules keep text readable and meaning clear.

      1Give text enough contrast

      Pale gray text looks calm in a mockup on a good monitor, but on a phone in sunlight, or for someone with weaker eyes, it fades away. Give body text at least 4.5 : 1 against its background, and large text at least 3 : 1. Check the quiet text too: captions, placeholders and hints.

      Try: turn on Bright sunlight and read the delivery address.

      The order details are pale gray, far below 4.5 : 1.

      Body text uses the main text color, and the caption a gray that still passes 4.5 : 1.

      2Don’t carry meaning with color alone

      A green or red amount only tells something to people who see the color. For everyone else, money in and money out look the same. Add a sign, an arrow or a word, such as “+” and “Received”, so color still helps people scan and the meaning stays when the color is gone.

      Try: turn on Remove color. Which payments came in?

      Money in and money out differ only by green and red.

      Each amount also has a sign, an arrow and a word.

      3Pick colors that differ in lightness

      Many people can’t tell red from green, especially when the two are equally light, so a seat map in those colors becomes one muddy shade. Choose colors that are also clearly lighter and darker than each other, and add a mark and a word to each state.

      Try: turn on Red-green color blindness, then pick a free seat.

      Free and taken seats are a green and a red of the same lightness.

      Free seats are light, and taken seats are dark with a cross.

      4Check both themes

      A gray that passes on white can fail on dark gray. This happens when colors are picked in the light theme and copied into the dark one, which leaves dim text on a dim background. Measure every text and background pair in each theme, and give the dark theme its own values.

      Try: switch the card to Dark and read the caption.

      The caption gray was picked in the light theme and reused in the dark one.

      Each theme has its own caption gray, and both pass.

      Chapter 3

      Same thing, same look, same place

      People learn a product one screen at a time, and they bring habits from every other product they use. The entries below cover spotting drift, keeping shared values in one place, and breaking the rule only on purpose.

      Internal and external consistency

      Consistency means one action has one look, one concept has one name, and the same buttons sit in the same order everywhere. People learn a product by noticing patterns, so when the patterns hold, what they learned on one screen works on the next. When they don’t, people slow down and wonder whether two things that look different do different things.

      There are two kinds. Internal consistency is about your own product: the same thing looks and works the same on every screen. External consistency is about everything else people use, the platform and other common products, as in Jakob’s law. Keyboard and screen-reader users lean on both, because they can’t take in a whole screen at a glance.

      Settings
      Warm
      Black and white

      0 of 5 found

      Click anything that doesn’t match the rest.

        Try it: this settings screen has five inconsistencies. Click or tab to anything that looks off. Each find is numbered on the screen and explained in the list below it. Stuck? Press Reveal all.

        Rules

        Three rules keep a product consistent.

        1Give one action one look

        When Add to cart is a filled button on one page and a plain link on another, people wonder whether the two do different things: a link usually opens a page, so some expect to see the item rather than add it. Build the action once as a component and use it everywhere. If two places really need different styles, they probably need different names too.

        Try: add the lamp, then add the mug from your wishlist.

        Add to cart is a filled button on the product and a plain link in the wishlist.

        Add to cart is the same button in both places.

        2Give one thing one name

        When one thing has two names, people assume there are two things, so they look in the wrong place or doubt that their action worked. Pick one word for each concept and keep a short glossary. Use the same word in buttons, menus, messages and help.

        Try: add the hotel, then find it.

        The button says “bookings”, the message says “reservations” and the tab says “Trips”.

        The button, the message and the tab all say “Trips”.

        3Follow the platform’s conventions

        People bring habits from every other app they use. Most dialogs put the main button at the right end, with Cancel just before it, so when a product flips that order, people press by position and hit the wrong button. Follow the convention unless you can show a clear win for a real task, and if you do break it, break it the same way everywhere.

        Try: press Delete, then press the left button in the dialog, where Cancel usually sits.

        The dialog puts Delete where most apps put Cancel.

        The dialog keeps the usual order: Cancel, then Delete at the right end.

        In real products

        Notice what stays the same from screen to screen, and which habits people bring from other products.

        Design tokens

        A design token is a shared value with a name, such as a corner radius, a spacing step, a color or a text size. Components point at the name instead of holding their own number, so when the token changes, every component that uses it changes with it.

        Tokens are how Spacing rhythm and consistency hold up in a large team. They can carry contrast too: give every background token a matching text token, like “accent” and “on-accent”, and check each pair once, so no component can pick a pair that fails.

        8px
        4px
        15px
        Accent
        Trip to LisbonNew

        48 photos · 3 people

        Album sharedUndo

        Try it: drag Radius to 0, then to 16. The card, input, buttons, badge and toast all change at once, because none of them holds its own value. Then try a bigger spacing unit or another accent, and watch the token block change with it.

        Kinds of tokens

        Most systems have three layers of tokens: base, role and component. Each layer points at the one before it, so a change happens in one place.

        Rules

        Three rules keep tokens useful.

        1Point components at tokens

        When each component holds its own numbers, a change has to be made in every component. Someone always misses one, and the product drifts: a 6 px corner here, an 8 px corner there. Point every component at a token instead, so a change in one place reaches all of them.

        Try: turn on Rounder corners, then pick Green.

        The card uses the radius and accent tokens, but the input, button, badge and link hold their own values.

        Every part points at the tokens.

        2Name tokens by their job

        A token named after its value, like blue-500, can’t change without becoming wrong: to rebrand, you either edit every component, or make blue-500 green and turn everything else that used it green too. Name tokens by their job, such as accent or rain. Only the job token knows which blue it is, so a rebrand changes one line.

        Try: press Make the brand green.

        The button and the rain chart both use blue-500.

        The button uses accent, and the chart uses rain.

        3Keep the set small

        Tokens that are close, like radius-7, radius-8 and radius-9, look the same on screen. People can’t choose between them, so they pick one at random, and the product drifts anyway. Keep a few clear steps, each with a job. When two tokens are close and used for the same job, merge them.

        Try: pick a radius for the new card.

        Eleven radius tokens, from radius-2 to radius-12.

        Three radius tokens, each with a job.

        In real products

        Break it on purpose

        Consistency doesn’t mean everything looks the same. When one thing really is different, such as an action that destroys work, it should look different, and it should be the only thing that does. People notice the one element that breaks a pattern, but only while the pattern holds everywhere else.

        This is the other half of Internal and external consistency. Like any meaning carried by color, an exception needs a second cue: an icon, a divider, a place at the end of the list, or the word itself, like “Delete”.

        Document “Budget 2026”

        Try it: switch between the three versions and notice where your eye lands first. Then find “Delete document” in each one, and note how long it takes.

        Rules

        Three rules keep exceptions meaningful.

        1Keep exceptions rare

        When every action gets its own color, weight or badge, nothing stands out, and people have to read every item to find the one they need, as on a screen where everything is bold. Keep about one exception per screen, for the one thing that really differs, and give everything else the normal style.

        Try: press Start, then find and press Pay.

        Every action has its own color or badge, Pay included.

        Only Pay stands out.

        2Write down the reason

        An exception without a reason looks like any other style choice, so the next person copies it to places where it doesn’t belong, and soon it means nothing. Write the reason next to the rule, like “red only for actions that destroy data”. If you can’t write a reason, follow the rule.

        Try: press Build the next screen.

        The guide makes red an exception for “Delete account” and “Upgrade”, with no reason.

        The guide keeps red for actions that destroy data, and says why.

        3Audit for drift

        Not every difference is a choice: someone copies an old screen or picks a value that’s close enough, and small variants pile up release after release. Check the product now and then. Fold drift back into the system, and if a variant has a real job, give it a name and add it.

        Copied and close-enough buttons pile up with each release, and nobody checks. Try: press Next release twice.

        The same drift, with an audit that folds it back and names the one real variant. Try: press Next release twice, then Run audit.

        In real products

        Chapter 4

        Treat the words as the interface

        Most of an interface is words. People read the label on a button, the title of a dialog and the first line of an error long before they notice the layout. Each of those words sets what people expect to happen next, so writing them is design work. The entries below share one test: can someone act on the words alone?

        Labels that say what happens

        A button label should say what happens when people press it: a verb, and the thing it acts on. “Save draft” and “Delete 3 photos” do that, and “OK” and “Yes” don’t.

        Labels are the smallest case of plain language, and they matter more on a button, because pressing it changes something.

        Round 1 of 4
        0 best picks

        • Verb + object. “Save playlist”, not “OK”.
        • People’s words. “Invite”, not “Execute”.
        • One case style. Sentence case on every button.

        Try it: in each round, pick the label you’d ship. Your pick replaces the dashed label in the mock, so you can judge it in place. Your score comes after round 4.

        Rules

        Four rules keep labels clear.

        1Name the action, not the answer

        “OK”, “Submit” and “Yes” only make sense next to the question above them. People who skim read the buttons first, and so do screen-reader users who jump between buttons, so they have to go back to the text to learn what a button does, or guess. Use a verb and an object, like “Delete draft”, so the button makes sense on its own.

        Try: the question is blurred, the way people skim. Press the button that keeps your email.

        The buttons say “No” and “Yes”.

        The buttons say “Keep draft” and “Delete draft”.

        2Use people’s words

        Words like “Execute query” describe what the code does, not what people want to do, so people stop to translate them and some give up. Use the words people use for their own tasks, like “Search” and “Add contact”. Labels in people’s words covers how to find those words.

        Try: find Maria, then add a new contact.

        The buttons say “Execute query” and “Instantiate contact”.

        The buttons say “Search” and “Add contact”.

        3Pick one capital style

        When “Add To Cart” sits next to “Save for later”, the page looks like it was put together from different apps, and people notice the mismatch before they read the words. Pick one style and use it on every button, menu item and title. Sentence case is a common choice: only the first word and names get a capital.

        Try: read the labels from top to bottom. Do any look out of place?

        The labels mix Title Case and sentence case.

        Every label uses sentence case.

        4Keep one verb per action

        If the menu says “Remove” and the dialog it opens says “Delete”, people can’t tell whether it’s the same action, and often it isn’t: removing a photo from an album keeps it, deleting it doesn’t. Give each action one name everywhere, so the confirm button repeats the verb from the menu item that opened it.

        The menu says “Remove”, but the dialog it opens says “Delete”. Try: you want this photo out of the album. Open its menu and press Remove.

        The menu and the dialog both say “Remove”. Try: you want this photo out of the album. Open its menu and press Remove from album.

        In real products

        Read only the buttons in each sketch: they still tell you what will happen.

        Error messages that help

        A good error message says what happened, why if you know, and what to do next, in plain words that don’t blame anyone. People read it at a bad moment, when something they wanted didn’t work, and the message decides whether they fix it in a few seconds or give up.

        This entry is about the words. Where the message goes, next to a field or across the page, is covered in Inline message and Error state.

        Write the message

        Preview

        Checks

          Try it: the bad example is loaded. Rewrite it until every check passes, then press the button in the preview. Load the good example to compare. Wavy underlines mark the words the checker flags.

          Rules

          Four rules keep error messages helpful.

          1Describe the problem, not the person

          “You entered an invalid value” tells people they did something wrong, but not what, so they feel blamed and still have to guess the rule. Describe the thing in neutral words and include the rule, like “Quantity needs a number from 1 to 99”, so people can fix it in one try.

          Try: change Quantity to 150 and press Update. Then fix it.

          The message says “You entered an invalid value.”

          The message says “Quantity needs a number from 1 to 99.”

          2Lead with plain words

          A code like “Error 0x80070002” means nothing to most people, who can’t tell whether the problem is theirs, the app’s or the network’s, and screen readers read it out one character at a time. Say what happened in plain words first. Keep the code small, or behind “Show details”, for support and developers.

          The message is only a code. Try: press Send. Can you tell what went wrong?

          The message says the attachment is over the size limit, and the code is behind “Show details”. Try: press Send, then Show details.

          3Offer the next step

          A message that explains the problem and offers only “OK” leaves people where they started: once it closes, they have to find the fix on their own. Put the action that fixes it on the message, on a button that names it, like “Give Sam access” or “Try again”.

          Try: press Send to Sam, then get the link to Sam. Count the clicks.

          The message only offers “OK”.

          The message offers “Give Sam access”.

          4Match the tone to the stakes

          Red capitals and words like “fatal” make people think their work is lost. Most errors aren’t like that: the problem can be fixed, or the app will try again on its own. Use calm words that fit what happened, and say what still works: “Your changes are saved on this device.”

          Try: type a few words, then turn Wi-Fi off.

          The message shouts “FATAL ERROR” when the connection drops.

          A calm message says the note is saved on this device.

          In real products

          Plain words, one term per concept

          Plain language means the words people already use, in short sentences, with the main point first and one name for each concept. People read fast and often read only part of the text, so plain words let them understand it the first time.

          It helps everyone, and most of all people reading in a second language, people with cognitive or learning disabilities, and anyone tired or stressed. Labels apply the same rules to buttons.

          JargonMixed names

          Plain words

            One term per concept

            Try it: press Replace next to a jargon word, or edit the text yourself. Fix the mixed names, then watch the sentence length. Compare with the plain rewrite: it leads with what to do.

            Rules

            Four rules keep writing plain.

            1Use everyday words

            Words like “utilize” and “initiate” make people slow down and translate. Some stop reading, and people reading in a second language may not know them at all. Use the words people use, like “use” and “start”. If a technical term can’t be avoided, explain it the first time it appears, including where to find it.

            Try: start a return for the running shoes.

            The form uses jargon: “Utilize the form to initiate a return”, “RMA”, “SKU”.

            The form uses everyday words and says where to find each number.

            2Put the point first

            When a message opens with background and conditions, people have to read to the end to learn what it means for them, and many stop before they get there. A notification preview may show only the first line. Lead with what people need to know or do, and put the reason and the details after it.

            Try: read the preview on the lock screen. Then press it to open the whole message.

            The notification opens with the background, and the preview ends before the point.

            The notification opens with the point.

            3One idea per sentence

            A long sentence makes people hold several ideas at once, so they lose track, read it again, or miss the part that mattered to them. Give each idea its own sentence, and split any sentence that needs “and” twice.

            Try: find how many days you have to collect the parcel.

            One long sentence carries five ideas.

            Each idea has its own short sentence.

            4Give each thing one name

            If a shop says “bag” in one place, “basket” in another and “cart” in a third, people wonder whether these are different places and look for their items in the wrong one. Pick one term, keep it in a short glossary, and use it everywhere, help pages included, as one thing, one name explains.

            Try: add the scarf, then find where it went.

            The shop calls one thing a bag, a basket and a cart.

            The shop calls it a cart everywhere.

            In real products

            Chapter 5

            Sweat the states and the edges

            Craft is what happens in the last 10% of a design: the timing, the messy data and the keyboard path. Mockups rarely show any of it, and people notice all of it. It lives in code, which is why it’s where a design engineer earns their keep. The entries below take those three edges one at a time. The looks a single control takes, from hover to loading, have their own entry: Interaction states.

            Motion with a purpose

            Motion should explain a change, like where a panel came from or where a deleted item went, and then get out of the way fast. Motion that explains nothing only makes people wait.

            Two settings shape every animation: how long it takes, and its easing, which is how its speed changes along the way. The demo below lets you change both on the same panel.

            250 ms
            Feels snappy

            Your device is set to reduce motion, so the panel below appears without sliding. That’s the behavior to build: the change still happens, only the movement goes.

            PhotosInfo panel
            Beach.jpgHarbor.jpgMarket.jpg

            Harbor.jpg

            Try it: press Play at 250 ms with Ease-out. Then drag Duration to 800 ms and play again, and imagine opening that panel fifty times a day. Last, try each easing at the same duration.

            Rules

            Four rules keep motion useful.

            1Keep it short

            An animation that takes 600 ms looks smooth the first time, but by the tenth time people are waiting for it, and if it blocks clicks while it plays, the app feels broken. Keep most interface motion around 150–300 ms: small moves get less, big ones a little more, and nothing should block the next click.

            Try: move all four emails to Archive as fast as you can.

            The sheet takes 600 ms to open and close, and blocks clicks while it moves.

            The sheet takes 180 ms and never blocks a click.

            2Animate to explain, not to decorate

            When everything bounces, fades and slides, motion stops meaning anything, because people can’t tell which movement is about the thing they just did. Use motion to show a change, such as where something came from, where it went or what was added, and cut any animation that explains nothing.

            Try: add Milk to the list. Where did it go?

            Everything bounces each time the list changes.

            Only the new item moves.

            3Respect reduced motion

            Large movement on screen can make some people dizzy or sick, so they turn on the reduce motion setting on their device, and an app that ignores it keeps sliding and zooming anyway. Check prefers-reduced-motion and test with the setting on. Swap slides and zooms for an instant change or a short fade: the change still happens, only the movement goes.

            Try: open a hotel, then go back.

            The hotel zooms up to fill the screen.

            The hotel appears with a short fade.

            4Match the easing to the direction

            Linear motion looks mechanical. Ease-in starts slow, so something that arrives with it feels late, and something that leaves with ease-out seems to linger. Ease out for things that enter, so they arrive fast and settle, and ease in for things that leave. Keep overshoot for rare, playful moments.

            Try: open and close the queue a few times.

            The queue enters with ease-in and leaves with ease-out.

            The queue enters with ease-out and leaves with ease-in.

            In real products

            Design with real, messy data

            Real data is long, missing, huge and empty. Names run past the edge, images fail to load, counts reach the millions, and fields come back blank. A design made only with tidy sample data breaks on the first day of real use, and people see those cases every day after that.

            For every field, decide what happens when it is very long, missing, very large, empty, or squeezed into a narrow space. Checking more than the happy path covers slow, empty and failed loads. This entry is about the data itself.

            Make the data messy

            Try it: in Before, turn on all five and count what breaks. Switch to After and look at how each one is handled. Then press Reload card in both versions and watch whether the text jumps.

            Rules

            Four rules keep a design working with real data.

            1Test with the extremes from the start

            A mockup filled with a short name, a perfect image and a tidy number always looks finished, so the problems show up only after launch, when real people bring real data. Put the extremes in the mockups, the stories and the test data from the start, so they get designed instead of discovered.

            Try: press Load real events.

            The calendar was designed with tidy sample events only.

            The calendar was designed with a long title, a missing place and a big guest list from the start.

            2Keep the part that tells items apart

            When long names are cut at the end, items that differ only at the end look the same: three files all read “Quarterly report dra…”, and people pick the wrong one. Cut the middle to keep the end, or let the text wrap to two lines. Keep the full text in the page so screen readers read it, and show it on hover and on focus.

            Try: attach the April report.

            The names are cut at the end, and the three reports look the same.

            The middle is cut, so the month stays visible, and the full name shows on hover and focus.

            3Reserve space for what loads later

            When something loads late, it pushes everything below it down, and a click aimed at a button lands on the wrong thing. Reserve the space before the content arrives: give images a fixed aspect ratio, and make skeletons the same size as the content they stand in for.

            Try: press Reload, then press Book on Casa Azul right away.

            A sponsored hotel loads late and pushes the list down.

            The sponsored hotel’s space is reserved, so nothing moves.

            4Format values for people

            Raw values like “1234567”, “null” and “undefined” show that nobody planned for this case: a long number is hard to read at a glance, and “null” looks like a bug. Format numbers and dates for reading, like “1.2M followers”, with the exact value one step away, and write a fallback for every field that can be empty.

            Raw values reach the screen: “1234567”, “null”, “undefined”. Try: read the artist page.

            The count reads “1.2M followers”, and empty fields say so in words. Try: read the artist page, then press the follower count.

            In real products

            Keyboard paths are craft

            Every control should work from the keyboard alone, focus should move in the order people read, and a visible ring should always show where it is. People who can’t use a mouse depend on this, and so do screen reader users and people who type fast.

            Focus is the keyboard’s pointer. Tab moves it, and Enter or Space act on what it points at. If people can’t see focus, or it jumps around, they can’t tell what the next key will do.

            Focus path

              Try it: choose Before, then press Tab to move through the form and watch the focus path. Can you tell where you are? Try to reach Book. Then choose After and do it again. Shift+Tab goes back.

              Ways to move with the keyboard

              There are four main ways to move with the keyboard. Most apps need Tab and arrow keys, a skip link helps on long pages, and shortcuts help in apps people use all day.

              Rules

              Four rules keep the keyboard path usable.

              1Keep the focus ring visible

              Focus rings are often removed because they look out of place, so keyboard users press Tab, see nothing change, and can’t tell which button Enter will press until it’s too late. Restyle the ring to fit the design instead of removing it. :focus-visible shows it for keyboard use and hides it on most mouse clicks.

              Try: click Reply, then press Tab twice and Enter. Which button did you press?

              The focus ring is removed.

              The ring is restyled to fit the design, and :focus-visible shows it for the keyboard only.

              2Make focus order match reading order

              People expect Tab to follow the layout: left to right, top to bottom. When CSS moves things around, or a positive tabindex sets its own order, focus jumps to a field they haven’t reached yet, so they type into the wrong field or skip one. Put elements in the DOM in reading order, and use only tabindex="0" and tabindex="-1".

              Try: click Card number, then press Tab three times and watch the path.

              CSS moves the fields around, so Tab follows a different order from the one on screen.

              The fields are in the DOM in reading order, so Tab follows the layout.

              3Use real buttons and links

              A div or span with a click handler works with a mouse and nothing else: Tab skips it, Enter does nothing, and a screen reader doesn’t call it a button. Use a button for actions and a link for going somewhere, because they get focus, the keys and a role for free. See Link vs button.

              Try: click Size, then press Tab until you reach Add to cart, and press Enter.

              Add to cart is a div with a click handler.

              Add to cart is a real button.

              4Move focus with what opens and closes

              When a dialog opens and focus stays behind it, keyboard users keep tabbing through a page they can’t see. When it closes and focus goes back to the top, they have to find their place again. Move focus into the dialog when it opens, and when it closes, put focus back on the control that opened it.

              Focus stays behind the dialog when it opens, and jumps to the top of the page when it closes. Try: click Share, press Tab and Enter to open the dialog, then press Tab. Where is focus?

              Focus moves into the dialog when it opens, and back to Delete photo when it closes. Try: click Share, press Tab and Enter to open the dialog, then press Tab, Enter or Escape.

              Chapter 6

              Judge work against its goal

              Taste grows by judging work out loud. Each time you say why something works or doesn’t, measured against what it’s for, your eye gets sharper. The three entries below are lenses for that judgment: a critique format that ties every comment to the goal, Nielsen’s ten heuristics for finding usability problems, and Dieter Rams’ ten principles for asking what good means. Try each one on your own work first.

              Critique against the goal

              A critique judges work against what it is for. It starts from the goal, says what serves the goal and what doesn’t, and only then suggests a fix, so the designer gets something to act on and still chooses the fix.

              That is what separates it from a reaction: “I don’t like it” says how you feel, not what to change. Put needs like access into the goal too, such as “works with a keyboard alone”, so a missing focus ring counts against the goal and nobody can wave it off as polish.

              Vague“I don’t like it.”

              Goal
              We want a traveller to book a room in under a minute.
              What works
              The photo shows the real room, so people can judge it before they open anything.
              What doesn’t serve the goal
              “book →” is a small grey link in the corner. The one action this card exists for is the hardest part to see.
              Suggestion
              Could “Book” be the card’s main button, right under the title?

              Vague“Make it pop.”

              Goal
              We want a traveller to book a room in under a minute.
              What works
              The card is calm, so a list of twenty of them will still be easy to scan.
              What doesn’t serve the goal
              Four badges carry as much weight as the title. People can’t tell which ones matter, so the eye has nowhere to land.
              Suggestion
              Keep the one badge that helps people choose, like “Free cancellation”. Stars and the pool can move to the detail page.

              Vague“It feels off.”

              Goal
              We want a traveller to book a room in under a minute.
              What works
              The layout matches the other cards, so people scan it the same way.
              What doesn’t serve the goal
              The title is cut off. “Harbour View Hotel and Sp…” could be any of three hotels with similar names, so people can’t tell them apart.
              Suggestion
              Let titles wrap to two lines, so the part that tells them apart stays visible.
              What is it for, and who is it for?
              Something specific worth keeping.
              Name the problem. Save the fix for the next field.
              One idea. A question is fine.

              Your critique

                Try it: pick a vague comment and read the rewrite. The card marks what each comment was really about. Then switch to Write your own, critique the same card, and press Assemble. Try leaving a field empty, or writing “I love the colors”.

                Kinds of critique

                Work at different stages needs different feedback, so there is one kind of critique for each stage. Each kind wastes time when it comes at the wrong stage, so ask which one is wanted. If you can’t ask, go by how finished the work is.

                KindWhenLook at
                DirectionEarly sketches, while the idea can still changeWhether it solves the right problem
                FlowThe steps exist as rough screensWhether people can get from start to finish without getting stuck
                PolishThe flow is settled and the screens are close to doneContrast, alignment and wording

                Rules

                Four rules keep critique useful.

                1Tie each comment to the goal

                “I don’t like it” leaves the designer guessing, so they either defend the design or change something at random. Say what the design does, or fails to do, for the people it’s for. A reaction is still useful as a clue: look closer at what caused it, then name that.

                Try: read the thread. What should the designer change, and why?

                The comments are likes and dislikes.

                Ana’s comment names the goal, what works, what doesn’t and one suggestion.

                2Name the problem before the fix

                “Make the button bigger” is a fix without a problem. The designer can only do it or argue, and the fix may not solve anything. Name the problem first, such as “people can’t find Checkout”, so the designer can judge your fix and may find a better one.

                The comment only asks for a bigger Checkout button. Try: press Apply the suggestion. Can people find Checkout now?

                The comment names the problem: Checkout sits below six suggested items. Try: try both fixes. Which one solves the problem Ana named?

                3Ask what feedback is wanted first

                Notes on spacing and colors don’t help an early sketch, because the idea may still change and take the details with it. Ask first whether the designer wants feedback on direction, flow or polish. For early work, ask about the idea and leave the details for later.

                Reviewers give pixel notes on an early sketch. Try: read the notes. Do any of them help decide whether the idea works?

                The designer says what feedback is wanted, and reviewers ask about the idea. Try: read the request first, then the notes.

                4Hear their read first

                When the reviewer speaks first, the designer’s view bends toward theirs: they defend the design or take every note, and the doubt they already had never comes up. Ask the designer what works for them and what worries them, then give your critique, and say where the two agree and where they don’t. The same goes for an agent’s review: get the designer’s read before you show it.

                The reviewer opens with her notes. Try: press Two weeks later.

                The reviewer asks for the designer’s read first. Try: press Write down the next steps.

                In real products

                Notice that each one ties feedback to a goal or to one spot, and leaves the fix to the owner.

                Heuristic review

                A heuristic review checks a design against a short list of rules of thumb. The best-known list is Jakob Nielsen’s ten usability heuristics. One person can run it in an hour, before anyone outside the team sees the design.

                It finds likely problems, not proven ones, which separates it from a usability test, where you watch real people use the design. The ten heuristics also leave out accessibility, so add a separate pass for keyboard, focus, contrast and screen readers.

                Spot the problems

                Every part of this mock dialog is a button. Some parts are fine.

                0 of 6 found

                Click anything in the dialog that looks wrong.

                1. 1 · Visibility of system statusSeverity 3 · major

                  A spinner and “Preparing…” don’t say what’s happening or how long it will take. People can’t tell slow from stuck.

                  Fix: name the step and show progress, like “Adding photos, 3 of 12”. A progress bar fits here.

                2. 2 · Match between the system and the real worldSeverity 2 · minor

                  “Re-encode w/ EXIF strip (q=0.8)” is the system’s language. People can’t tell what ticking it does to their photos.

                  Fix: use their words and name the trade-off: “Make photos smaller (lower quality, removes location)”.

                3. 3 · User control and freedomSeverity 3 · major

                  Cancel is greyed out while it prepares, and there’s no close button. Once the dialog opens, people can’t back out.

                  Fix: keep Cancel and a close button working at every moment, and let Escape close it. See Dialog.

                4. 4 · Consistency and standardsSeverity 2 · minor

                  “OK” doesn’t say what will happen, and it sits on the left, where other dialogs put Cancel. People press the wrong one out of habit.

                  Fix: name the button for its action, “Export”, and keep the button order every other dialog uses.

                5. 5 · Error preventionSeverity 4 · catastrophe

                  The name field takes characters files can’t use, like “/” and “?”. Nothing warns before Export overwrites a file with the same name.

                  Fix: catch bad characters as people type, and offer “final-2” when the name is taken. See Constraints.

                6. 10 · Help and documentationSeverity 2 · minor

                  The only help is a tiny “?” with no label, far from the options that need explaining.

                  Fix: put one line of help right under the option that needs it, and link to the full docs from there.

                Rules

                Four rules keep a heuristic review useful.

                1Pair it with watching people

                A review finds what reviewers expect to go wrong, but real people trip over things no list predicts and breeze past some problems the review rated high. If the review is the only test, the team fixes guesses. Watch a few people try the same flow, and let what they do decide which findings matter.

                The review is the only test. Try: press Fix and ship. What happens after launch?

                The team also watches five people try the flow. Try: press Watch 5 people, then Fix and ship.

                2Ask three to five reviewers

                One reviewer finds only part of the problems, because each person notices different things. Ask three to five people to review on their own, then merge the lists. Past five, each new reviewer adds little. An agent’s review counts as another reviewer only if it looks through a different lens or runs on a different model, because one model asked twice repeats its own blind spots.

                One person reviews alone. Try: count what the reviewer found, then press Show what was missed.

                Several people review on their own, and the lists are merged. Try: press Add a reviewer three times and watch the count.

                3Rate each problem by severity

                A flat list of problems gives the team no order, so they fix the quick ones first and the problem that stops people from paying waits. Rate each problem from 0 to 4 and fix from the top. The rating weighs how many people hit the problem, how much it hurts and whether it gets in their way every time.

                SeverityMeansExample
                0 · Not a problemNot a usability problem after all. Drop it and write down why.“I’d make it blue”, with no problem behind it
                1 · CosmeticFix it if there’s time left.A typo: “Delivey fee”
                2 · MinorLow priority: people notice it but get past it.Prices are low contrast
                3 · MajorHigh priority: people struggle or lose work.The basket empties when you switch restaurant
                4 · CatastropheFix it before release: people can’t finish the task.Card payment fails if the address has an accent
