                In real products

                Each one gets a different heuristic right. Naming the heuristic when you see it done well makes it easier to spot when it’s missing.

                Rams’ ten principles

                Dieter Rams designed radios, record players and shelves for Braun and Vitsœ. His ten principles of good design are still among the most quoted in design. He summed them up as “Less, but better.”

                He wrote them about physical products, and in software they work best as questions to ask of a screen. The readings in the cards below are one translation, so argue with them and write your own.

                1. Ask: Does it make something newly possible, or newly easy?

                  In software, this means new technology earns its place by removing friction people already feel.

                  Example: a photo editor shows the result while you drag a slider, so people stop guessing and undoing.

                2. Ask: Does it help someone finish a real task?

                  In software, this means each feature serves a job people actually have, and the screen puts that job first.

                  Example: a delivery app opens on where your order is, not on offers.

                3. Ask: Is it pleasant to work in for hours?

                  In software, this means calm, well-made visuals, because people who spend all day in a tool feel its quality.

                  Example: a photo app keeps its own colors quiet, so people’s photos are the most colorful thing on screen.

                4. Ask: Can people tell what it does without help?

                  In software, this means labels, structure and feedback explain each part, so the interface teaches itself.

                  Example: a date field says what it expects, like “Day / Month / Year”, before people type.

                5. Ask: Does it step back so people’s own work can lead?

                  In software, this means few interruptions, and controls that stay quiet until people need them.

                  Example: a reading app hides its toolbars while people read, and shows no pop-ups in the middle of a chapter.

                6. Ask: Does it promise only what it delivers?

                  In software, this means no dark patterns: no fake urgency, no hidden costs, and no tricks that push people toward choices they wouldn’t make.

                  Example: a booking site shows the full price, fees included, before people press Book.

                7. Ask: Will this still make sense in a few years?

                  In software, this means patterns and formats that age well, so people’s work and habits survive each update.

                  Example: documents saved years ago still open after an update, and shortcuts keep their meaning.

                8. Ask: Did anyone design the edge cases?

                  In software, this means empty states, errors, long names, slow networks and the keyboard path are all designed on purpose.

                  Example: a very long file name is shortened in the middle and shown in full on hover.

                9. Ask: Does it waste energy, compute or attention?

                  In software, this means treating compute, bandwidth and people’s attention as limited resources.

                  Example: a photo backup uploads only new photos, and waits for Wi-Fi before it sends videos.

                10. Ask: What can we remove without hurting the goal?

                  In software, this means cutting what doesn’t serve the goal until only the essential is left. A clear label can be the essential part.

                  Example: one Send button that always works the same way, in place of three ways to send a message.

                Pick three to keep in mind this week.

                Try it: open a few cards to read the question each principle asks and what it means in software. Then pick three to hold your work against this week. Your picks stay in this browser.

                Rules

                Three rules keep the principles useful.

                1Ask them as questions, not rules

                Read as rules, some of the ten pull against each other. “Unobtrusive” says hide the toolbar, “understandable” says label every tool, and a checklist can’t say which one wins. Ask each one as a question about the goal, and the tension leads you to a design that serves both.

                Two principles are rules on a checklist. Try: tick both rules. What does the toolbar look like?

                The principles are asked as questions about the goal: the tools are labeled and hide when you tap the photo. Try: tap the photo, then tap it again.

                2Cut what doesn’t serve the goal

                “As little design as possible” is often read as minimal styling: gray, flat, no labels. The screen looks simple, but people have to hunt for what they need. Remove what doesn’t serve the goal instead, and keep a visible label or a clear button, because it is often the essential part.

                Try: turn off notifications.

                “Less design” is read as gray icons with the labels hidden.

                The icons keep their labels.

                3Treat “honest” as a design rule

                “Honest” sounds like a rule for advertising, so teams skip it, and a sign-up gets a fake countdown, a pre-ticked add-on and a price that grows later. People find out after they pay and stop trusting the product. Show the full cost before people commit, and leave add-ons unticked. See Smart defaults.

                A countdown, a pre-ticked add-on, and the later price in small print. Try: press Subscribe. Is that what you expected to pay?

                No countdown, nothing pre-ticked, and the full price shows before Subscribe. Try: tick the add-on, watch the button, then press Subscribe.

                In real products

                Each one serves a principle by leaving something out, or by caring about a detail most people never notice.

                Chapter 7

                Train your eye, design in the real material

                Taste is a skill you train. You build it by looking closely at real products, rebuilding the details that work, and naming why they work. As a design engineer, you also have an edge: you can design in the real material, where timing, real data and every state are real from the first minute. The entries below turn both into habits: look closely, try the risky part in code, and write down why you chose what you chose.

                Copywork and close looking

                You train taste by looking closely at good work. Rebuild a screen you admire, detail by detail, and name why each detail is there. Copying makes you notice spacing, weight and color that you would otherwise skim past.

                Looking closely is not the same as collecting: a folder of screenshots trains nothing until you compare, rebuild and explain what you saved.

                Original

                Lisbon trip 48 photos · Edited today Three days by the sea, with Sam. AlbumOpen

                Copy: find 5 differences

                Found 0 of 50 misses

                Click anything on the copy that looks different.

                  Try it: compare the two cards, then click each detail on the copy that looks different. Tab and Enter work too. Stuck? Compare one property at a time: spacing, then type, then color, then alignment, then corners.

                  Rules

                  Four rules make close looking pay off.

                  1Tag what you save by problem

                  Screenshots saved under their default names are hard to find again, so when you design an empty state next month, you can’t search for one. Tag each shot by the problem it solves, like “empty state”, “bulk delete” or “long names”, so your collection answers the question you have.

                  Try: type “empty” in the search box.

                  Screenshots keep their default names.

                  Each screenshot is tagged by the problem it solves.

                  2Write down why it works

                  A copy without a reason only fits the case you copied, so when the next case is different, you don’t know which part to keep. Write one line next to each copy on why it works, because the reason still helps when the picture doesn’t match.

                  Try: rows now need a price. Pick a color for it.

                  The note on the saved list says only “nice list, copy this”.

                  The note says why the list works: only the title is dark.

                  3Study whole flows, not showcase shots

                  Showcase shots show only the happy path with perfect data, and much of the design work goes into the other states. Sign up, make mistakes on purpose, and capture every state you see. Tab through the flow and turn on a screen reader for a minute too.

                  Try: open each state.

                  Only the polished showcase shot was captured.

                  The whole flow was captured: empty, loading, error and the keyboard path too.

                  4Compare one property at a time

                  Looking at two whole screens, you only notice that one “feels nicer”, and you can’t use what you can’t name. Compare one property at a time: spacing, then weight, then color, then corners. Small differences are easy to see once you look for one thing.

                  Two whole cards, and the question of which feels nicer. Try: name one difference, then press Show the differences.

                  A button for each property shows one difference at a time. Try: pick each property in turn.

                  In real products

                  Prototype in the real material

                  Prototyping in the real material means building the risky parts of a design in code, early. A mockup shows one still moment with tidy text, while code shows what happens when the message is long, the response is slow or the window is narrow. It also lets you test what a picture can’t: keyboard use, focus, screen readers and reduced motion.

                  A prototype is not the feature. It answers one question, like “Can people read the toast before it goes?”, and then it’s thrown away. Keep mockups for what they answer faster, such as layout ideas and wording.

                  Tweak

                  Preview

                  Generated CSS
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: drag the sliders and press Save album. Turn on the long message and set the duration to 2 s: can you read it before it goes? Point at the toast to pause it. When it feels right, copy the CSS.
                  
    
                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep prototypes useful.
                  

                  

                  1Try the risky part in code early
                  A mockup uses short names and answers at once. The real build gets long names and slow responses, and nobody sees that until weeks later, when the design is signed off and changing it costs more. Build the risky part in code first, with real data and real timing, so problems show up while the design can still change.
                  

                  The approved mockup uses short names and instant results. Try: press Open the first build, then type “lamp”.
                  A week-1 prototype in code uses real names and a real 1.2 s delay. Try: type “lamp” in the prototype.
                  

                  2Mark throwaway code as throwaway
                  Prototype code is written fast, with fake delays, hard-coded colors and no tests. If nobody says so, it gets merged and ships, and months later someone has to work out which parts were real. Say it’s a prototype in the branch name and at the top of the file, then rebuild the idea properly.
                  

                  Try: press Merge.
                  The prototype looks like any other branch.
                  The branch name and the top of the file say it’s a prototype.
                  

                  3Decide what “good” means before you tune
                  Tuning without a goal never ends: each value looks a little off, so you keep nudging it and stop when you’re tired rather than when it works. Write down what has to be true first, like “people can read the caption before the slide changes”, then tune until it passes and stop.
                  

                  There’s no goal, only a slider and a count of tweaks. Try: move the slider a few times. When is it done?
                  A “Done when” line says the caption needs about 4 s. Try: move the slider until the check passes.
                  

                  4Try the messy cases on purpose
                  On your own laptop, with tidy sample data, everything looks fine, and people find the messy cases for you after launch: long names, empty lists, slow connections and small screens. Go through each one before you ship, and design what people see in it.

                  Write down the reasoning
                  

                  

                  Design rationale is the reasoning behind a design decision, written down. It says what the problem was, which options you considered, which one you chose and why. The next person reads it before they change the design. Without it, they guess, and may undo a choice that was made for a good reason.
                  

                  Rationale is not a description of how the design works, which the design itself shows. It records why it works that way, including the options you turned down. Record accessibility decisions too, like the keyboard path, because they are the first thing lost in a later rewrite.

Press Start blank to write your own: the draft stays in this browser, and Copy gives you a PR description to paste.
                  
    
                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep design rationale useful.
                  

                  

                  1Keep it where people will look
                  Decisions are often made in a chat thread or on a call, and a month later nobody can find them, so a new teammate has to ask again or guess. Put the decision in the pull request description or a short doc, and link it from the issue so it’s one click from the question.
                  

                  Try: press Find the reason.
                  The decision was made on a call and lives only in chat.
                  The decision is in the pull request, linked from the issue.
                  

                  2Include what you rejected
                  A record that only names the winner answers “what”, not “why not”, so the next person suggests an option you already tried and the team argues it again. List each option you turned down, with one line on why, and the second discussion ends before it starts.
                  

                  Try: press Ben’s proposal.
                  The record names only the chosen option.
                  The record lists each rejected option with one line on why.
                  

                  3Write it while you decide
                  Written weeks later, a record comes from memory. The reasons have faded, so it says “it seemed best”, which helps nobody. Write it while you’re still choosing, because spelling out each option’s trade-off often turns up a better option you hadn’t seen.
                  

                  The record is written weeks later, from memory, to close the ticket. Try: press Write it up.
                  The record is written while deciding, and a third option turns up. Try: press Write the next trade-off until all are written.
                  

                  4Lead with what changes for people
                  Reviewers read the top of a pull request description and skim the rest. If it opens with refactors and file names, they can’t tell what people will notice, and the change people will feel gets the least review. Start with what changes for people, then why, then how it’s built.
                  

                  Try: read the first lines only. What will people notice?
                  The description opens with refactors and file changes.
                  The description starts with what changes for people, then why, then how.

                  Part 2
                  
  
                  Patterns
                  
  
                  Named solutions to problems that keep coming back. Each one is built from the components in Part 3.
                  

                  


                  
  
                  
    
                  Before you start
                  
    
                  Name the problem before the fix
                  
  
                  
  
                  
    
                  Interface problems repeat across products, and so do their solutions. A pattern is a solution shape that has worked many times before: undo instead of a confirm, a command palette when menus get too deep, a template instead of a blank screen.
                  
    
                  Patterns give you a head start and a shared name, but they’re risky when you reach for one before you understand the problem. So read each pattern as a problem, a pattern and its trade-off.
                  
  
                  
  
                  
    
                  ProblemWhat people struggle with, in their own words. “There’s too much here.”
                  
    
                  PatternA known shape that has solved it before. Progressive disclosure: show the basics, reveal the rest.
                  
    
                  Trade-offWhat the pattern costs. Hidden things get forgotten, and experts pay an extra click.
                  
  
                  
  
                  
    
                  How each entry reads
                  
    
                  Each pattern is a short article. It starts with the problem it solves and a demo. Then the main ways to do it. Then the rules: every pattern has a cost, and each rule shows how it backfires and how to soften it, with a demo you can switch between the two. Last, real products that use it.

                  Chapter 8
                  Too much at once
                  
  
                  
    
                  A panel with twenty settings asks people to judge all twenty before they can do anything, so they freeze, skim, or miss the one setting that mattered. The patterns in this chapter show the basics first and keep the rest one step away, so the screen starts simple and nothing is out of reach.
                  
  
                  

  
                  
    
                  Progressive disclosure
                  

                  

                  Progressive disclosure shows the settings most people need first and keeps the rest one step away, so people can start without judging every option on the screen. Nothing is removed: the rest is there for the people who look for it.
                  

                  It works together with smart defaults, but where a default fills in a value for people, progressive disclosure decides what they see at all. Hidden settings should start on good defaults, so most people never need to open them.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  Print
                  
        
                  
          
                  
          
                  
          
                  
        
                  
        
        
                  
        
                  
          
                  
            
                  
          
                  
            
                  
          
                  
          
                  
          
                  
            
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: open the advanced settings, set Margins to 5, then hide them again: the summary keeps that change in view. Reload the page, and the section stays open or closed the way you left it. Switch to Before to see all eight at once.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  There are four common ways to keep the rest one step away. They differ in where the hidden part waits.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep progressive disclosure useful.
                  

                  

                  1Say what’s hidden
                  A button that says only “More options” gives no hint of what’s behind it, so people who need one of those settings don’t know it exists, and they give up or ask someone. Name what’s inside on the button and say how many, so people can tell whether it’s worth opening before they open it.
                  

                  Try: without opening anything, can this email be sent tomorrow at 8:00? Then open More options.
                  The button says only “More options”.
                  The button names the three settings inside.
                  

                  2Let experts skip the extra click
                  People who use the hidden settings every time pay for the split every time, and if the section closes again after each use, they open it over and over. Remember whether each person left it open, and give frequent users a keyboard shortcut or a setting to always show everything.
                  

                  Try: export three photos, checking Advanced each time.
                  Advanced closes again after every export.
                  Advanced stays the way you left it, and a setting or Alt+A keeps it open.
                  

                  3Split by what people change
                  The line between basic and advanced is often a guess made before launch. If most people open the hidden part every time, the guess was wrong, and the split only adds a click. Look at what people actually change, and move anything most people need up into the basics.
                  

                  Try: create an event with a video call.
                  The video call is hidden in More options, and 82% of people open it for that.
                  The video call moved up into the basics, and More options holds what few people change.
                  

                  4Show what the hidden settings changed
                  A hidden setting can still change the result, and people can’t fix a cause they can’t see. While the section is closed, show a short summary of every value that isn’t the default, and let people clear it from there. The most common case, a filter left on from an earlier visit, is covered in search with filters.
                  

                  A price filter set last week is hidden behind Filters. Try: press Search. Why only one lamp?
                  While Filters is closed, it shows each filter that’s on, and one click clears it. Try: press Search, then clear the filter.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

  
                  
    
                  Smart defaults
                  

                  

                  A smart default is a value filled in for people because it fits most of them, so they can accept it and move on, or change it. Each good default removes one decision, and on a long form that adds up.
                  

                  A default is a real value that will be used, shown in a field people can change. That separates it from a placeholder, which disappears when people type and is never used, and from a preset, which sets several linked values at once.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  New export
                  
        
                  
          
                  
            
            
          
                  
          
                  
            
            
          
                  
          
                  
            
            
          
                  
          
                  
            
            
          
                  
          
                  
            
            
          
                  
        
                  
        
                  
          
          
          
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: in Before, press Export with the form still blank. In After, change the format and watch it get marked, then export: the next export starts from what you just used.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  Defaults differ in where the value comes from.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep smart defaults useful.
                  

                  

                  1Base defaults on what people pick
                  A default that’s wrong for many people is worse than none, because they have to notice it and change it on every visit. Look at what people actually choose and start there, then remember what each person used last, so someone with a different habit stops fixing it too.
                  

                  Try: order 13 × 18 cm prints twice.
                  Size starts on Passport, which few people order.
                  Size starts on 10 × 15 cm, which most people order, then on your last size.
                  

                  2Keep defaults in view
                  Some defaults are applied where people can’t see them, so the result surprises people and they have no idea which setting caused it. Show every default in the form, in a field people can change. Mark values that differ from the default in words, not only with color, so people see what will happen before they press the button.
                  

                  Photos are reduced to 2048 px out of sight. Try: press Upload.
                  The size shows in the form, and a change is marked in words. Try: change the size, then press Upload.
                  

                  3Start risky options off
                  A default can quietly serve the business instead of the person, like a pre-ticked “public” box, and because most people never change defaults, they end up sharing what they meant to keep. Pick the safe, reversible option: anything that publishes, deletes, costs money or overwrites files should start off.
                  

                  Try: press Create album.
                  “Anyone with the link” starts on.
                  The album starts private.
                  

                  4Use real values, not placeholders
                  Gray text in an empty field looks like an answer, so people skip the field, and the form fails because it was empty all along. The gray text also vanishes as soon as they type. Put a real value in the field, or write the hint as a label or help text.
                  

                  “2 people” is only a placeholder. Try: press Book, then type in the field.
                  “2 people” is a real value. Try: press Book.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  Notice where each default comes from: the spot you clicked, the most common choice, where you are, or what you already wrote.
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

  
                  
    
                  Presets
                  

                  

                  A preset sets several linked values at once, under a name that says what you get, like “Fast” or “Best quality”. People pick the outcome they want instead of tuning each value, and the values stay in view, so people can still adjust one.
                  

                  Unlike a smart default, which fills in one field, a preset fills in a group of fields that only make sense together. Build the picker as a radio group, so arrow keys move between presets.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  What “Balanced” sets
                  
        
                  
          
            
                   Edited
                  
            
                   Edited
                  
            
                   Edited
                  
                            
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  About 14 s to export
                  
      
                  Try it: pick each preset and watch the values it sets. Then change Bitrate by hand: the picker switches to Custom and marks the edit. Pick a preset again to leave Custom, then press Undo on the toast to get your edits back.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  Presets come in four common forms. They differ in how people choose one, and in whether it stays linked after it’s picked.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep presets useful.
                  

                  

                  1Show what each preset sets
                  A preset name alone doesn’t say what will change, so people pick one and find out what it did only when the result arrives, and careful people avoid presets. Show the values each preset sets next to the picker, and let people edit them.
                  

                  Try: pick Eco, then Comfort.
                  The heating modes don’t say what they set.
                  Each mode shows the temperatures it sets, which can be edited.
                  

                  2Switch to “Custom” after an edit
                  Once someone changes a value, the settings no longer match the preset, so a label that still shows the preset’s name is wrong, and people trust it. Switch the label to “Custom” as soon as a value changes, and mark what was edited. Picking the preset again brings its values back.
                  

                  Try: set Calls from to Everyone, then pick Sleep again.
                  After an edit, the label still says “Sleep”.
                  After an edit, the label says “Custom” and marks the change.
                  

                  3Offer a few, named by outcome
                  A long list of presets is a new decision on top of the old one, and internal names make it worse, because people can’t tell what “JPG-80-2048” is for. Keep three to five presets, and name each one by what people want to do, like “Email” or “Print”.
                  

                  Try: pick a preset for emailing three photos to Grandma.
                  Twelve presets with internal names.
                  Four presets, named for what people will do with the photos.
                  

                  4Let people save their own
                  Some people need the same mix of settings every time, and no built-in preset matches it, so without a way to save it they set each value again on every visit. Let them save their mix as a preset with their own name, next to the built-in ones.
                  

                  Every new search starts without filters, so they have to be set again. Try: turn on Nonstop and Under €150, then press New search.
                  Save as preset adds “My usual” next to the built-in presets. Try: turn on the same filters, press Save as preset, then New search, then pick your preset.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

                  

                  
  
                  
    
                  Chapter 9
                  
    
                  Scared to click
                  
  
                  
  
                  
    
                  When an action feels risky, people hesitate: they try fewer settings, explore less and learn the tool more slowly, because any click might cost them work. The patterns in this chapter all make actions safe to try. Undo takes the cost away after the fact, preview shows the result before it happens, and version history keeps a way back to any earlier point.
                  
  
                  

  
                  
    
                  Undo instead of “Are you sure?”
                  

                  

                  Undo lets people act at once and take the action back afterwards. The app deletes, moves or sends right away and keeps a way back open, so a wrong click costs a second instead of lost work.
                  

                  A confirm dialog asks “Are you sure?” before the action, when people haven’t seen the result yet, and after a few of them people click through without reading. Undo works after the action, when people can see what they did.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  
          Notes
          
                  Deleted: 0Interruptions: 0
                  
        
                  
        
                    
          
                  • Grocery listEdited today
                    • 
          
                  • Trip to LisbonEdited yesterday
                    • 
          
                  • Book club picksEdited 3 days ago
                    • 
          
                  • Gift ideasEdited last week
                    • 
        
                  
        
                  No notes left.
                  
      
                  
      
        
                  
          
                  
            
                  Delete this note?
                  
            
                  Are you sure? This can’t be undone.
                  
          
                  
          
                  
            
            
          
                  
        
                  
                        
      
                  Try it: in Confirm dialog mode, delete three notes and watch the interruptions add up. Switch to Undo and do the same, then press Undo on a toast or Ctrl+Z (⌘Z on Mac). Each note comes back in its old place.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  Undo comes in four common forms. They differ in how long the way back stays open and where people find it.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep undo useful.
                  

                  

                  1Plan where deleted things go
                  Undo only works if the deleted thing still exists somewhere. If the app removes it for real and Undo is added later, Undo can only rebuild a rough copy, and people get back a name without the details they cared about. Plan for it in the data model from the start: mark items as deleted and keep them until the way back closes. Version history uses the same idea.
                  

                  Try: delete Maya Chen, then press Undo.
                  Undo was added late, so it rebuilds a blank copy of the contact.
                  Contacts are only marked as deleted, so Undo brings back the real one.
                  

                  2Keep Undo open long enough
                  People often notice a mistake a few seconds late, after they look back at the screen, so an Undo that leaves after two seconds is already gone. Keep it until the next action, or for several seconds after people return to the page. Pause any timer while the pointer or focus is on the toast.
                  

                  Try: delete a photo, finish reading this line, then reach for Undo.
                  Undo leaves after two seconds.
                  Undo stays until your next delete.
                  

                  3Keep a confirm for what can’t be undone
                  Some actions can’t be reversed, such as emptying the trash, sending money or sharing with other people, and without a question one slip loses things for good. Ask first for these actions, and only these. Name the consequence in the question and put the action on the button, such as “Delete 12 files”. See Dialog.
                  

                  Try: press Empty Trash.
                  Empty Trash acts at once, with no way back.
                  Empty Trash asks first and names what will be lost.
                  

                  4Give more than one way back
                  A toast is easy to miss and leaves after a while, so if Undo lives only there, people who missed it have no way back. Also support Ctrl+Z (⌘Z on Mac) and an Undo item in a menu that names what it will undo. After Undo, put focus on the restored item so keyboard users can carry on.
                  

                  Undo is only on the toast. Once it’s gone, Ctrl+Z does nothing. Try: archive an email, wait for the toast to leave, then press Ctrl+Z or ⌘Z.
                  Ctrl+Z and the Edit menu still undo after the toast is gone. Try: archive an email, wait for the toast to leave, then press Ctrl+Z or ⌘Z, or open Edit.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  Notice where each way back lives: on screen, on the keyboard or in a menu.
                  
      
                  
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

  
                  
    
                  Preview before commit
                  

                  

                  A preview shows what a change will do before it’s applied. People try a setting on their own content, see the result, and then apply it or go back, and nothing changes until they say so.
                  

                  It suits changes that are slow, costly or hard to reverse. For quick changes that are easy to take back, undo is lighter: the change happens at once, and people step back if they don’t like it.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
                  Resize imagePreview · not applied
                  
        
                  
          
                  
          
                  
        
                  
        
                  1024 × 768 · no changes
                  
        
                  
          
                  
            
            
            
            
          
                  
          
                  1024 px
                  
        
                  
        
                  
          
          
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: pick 3:4 and drag Long side. The dashed outline is the image now and the filled box is the preview. Then press Apply, or Cancel to go back.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  Previews come in three common forms, which differ in where the result shows.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep previews useful.
                  

                  

                  1Make the preview match the result
                  A preview is only useful if people can trust it. When it’s drawn differently from the real result, small differences slip in, like text that fits in the preview and is cut off in the result, and people stop trusting it. Draw the preview with the same code as the final output, and if it can’t match, label it “Approximate preview”.
                  

                  Try: type a long name, such as Alexandria Montgomery, then press Print.
                  The preview uses a smaller font than the printer.
                  The preview uses the same layout as the printed badge, and warns when a name won’t fit.
                  

                  2Keep the preview fast
                  People adjust a setting by watching the result, so if the preview trails behind the control, they overshoot, wait and adjust again, and the control feels sticky. Show a quick rough version right away and finish it when the full one is ready, and hold back slow work while a slider is still moving.
                  

                  Try: drag Text size from one end to the other and watch the page.
                  Each change redraws the whole page before the next one starts.
                  A rough version follows the slider at once, and the sharp page follows when you let go.
                  

                  3Show that it’s a preview
                  People forget they’re in a preview, leave, and believe the change was applied, then find out later that it never happened. Mark the preview with a label and an outline, and keep Apply and Cancel in view the whole time. Put the label in text so screen readers announce it too, and ask before people leave with changes that aren’t applied.
                  

                  Try: pick Dark, then press Back.
                  Nothing marks the preview, and Back leaves without a word.
                  A label and an outline mark the preview, Apply and Cancel stay in view, and Back asks before dropping it.
                  

                  4Skip it for small changes
                  A preview step on every setting turns each change into two clicks, so people get slower and stop reading the previews. Apply cheap, reversible changes at once and offer undo, and keep preview-then-apply for changes that are slow, costly or hard to reverse.
                  

                  Try: turn off all three notifications and count the clicks.
                  Each switch opens a preview with its own Apply button.
                  Each switch applies at once, and Undo takes it back.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

  
                  
    
                  Version history & soft delete
                  

                  

                  Version history keeps earlier versions of a document so people can go back to one. A trash does the same for deleted items, which wait there for a while before they’re gone. Both let people make big changes without fear of losing what worked.
                  

                  Where undo covers the last few seconds, version history covers days and weeks, and it still works after the app was closed.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
                  Lisbon tripVersion history
                  
        
                  
          Saved versions, newest first
          
                  
        
                  
        
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  
          Trash (2)
          
                  
            
                  Deleted documents stay here for 30 days, then they’re removed for good.
                  
            
                  
          
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: pick v2 and read what restoring will do, then restore it: it comes back as v5 on top, and v3 and v4 are still there. Then open Trash and bring a deleted document back.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  There are four common forms, which differ in what they cover: a whole document, one value or deleted items.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep version history useful.
                  

                  

                  1Name versions by what changed
                  A list of times says when something changed, not what changed, so people open one version after another to find the one they want. Describe each version by its change, such as “Added the menu”. Write that line automatically, and let people rename the versions that matter.
                  

                  Try: find the last version before the photos were added.
                  Versions are listed by time only.
                  Each version says what changed.
                  

                  2Restore as a new version
                  If restoring an old version deletes everything newer, one wrong restore loses days of work, and people avoid restoring at all. Add the restored version on top as the newest one, so everything newer stays in the history and the restore itself can be undone.
                  

                  Try: restore v1, then try to get v3 back.
                  Restoring an old version deletes every newer one.
                  Restoring adds the old version on top, and the newer ones stay.
                  

                  3Say what restoring will change
                  A time doesn’t say what will happen to the current document, so people restore and then find parts missing that they wanted to keep. Show a short summary of the difference next to the Restore button, such as “Removes 2 slides and brings back the old title”. Put it in text, so screen readers read it too.
                  

                  Try: restore Monday’s version, then look at the slides.
                  Restore shows only a time.
                  A summary next to Restore lists what will change.
                  

                  4Say when the trash empties
                  A trash that empties without warning removes things people still expect to find, and one that never empties grows until nobody can find anything in it. Empty it after a set time, such as 30 days, say so in the trash itself, and show how long each item has left.
                  

                  Try: press Skip a week three times, then look for the flight booking.
                  The trash empties without warning.
                  The trash says when it empties and shows the days left on each email.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

                  


                  
  
                  Chapter 10
                  Did it work?
                  
  
                  
    
                  You press a button and nothing seems to happen, so you press it again, or you decide it’s broken and give up. Jakob Nielsen put this first in his ten usability heuristics, as visibility of system status: people should always know what the system is doing, and hear back quickly. The patterns below answer “did it work?” at the right moment and in the right place, with Part 3 components like the spinner, the progress bar and the toast.
                  
  
                  

  

  
                  
    
                  Instant feedback
                  

                  

                  Instant feedback means the screen answers an action right away: a pressed button changes, a ticked box shows a tick, a save says “Saving…”. People know their action registered, so they don’t click again or give up.
                  

                  The work itself may take seconds, but the sign that it started should take less than a tenth of a second. Put the new state in text as well, so screen readers announce it too.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
                  
          
                  No feedback
                  
          
          
                  
          
                  Not tried yet
                  
        
                  
        
                  
          
                  Instant feedback
                  
          
          
                  
          
                  Not tried yet
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: press each Save once, the way you normally would. Both take 1.2 seconds. “No feedback” stays silent the whole time, and every extra click sends another save. “Instant feedback” answers at once and ignores repeat clicks while it works.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  Feedback comes in four common strengths. The bigger or slower the action, the stronger the answer.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep feedback useful.
                  

                  

                  1Leave the confirmation up long enough
                  A confirmation that flashes by is gone before people look at it, so they’re left unsure and do the action again. Keep a short confirmation on screen for one to two seconds, or better, switch to a state that lasts, like “Saved just now”, until the next change.
                  

                  Try: press Copy link and check whether it worked.
                  “Copied” shows for a quarter of a second.
                  “Copied” stays on the button for two seconds.
                  

                  2Show it where the action happened
                  People look at the thing they just clicked, so a change in a far corner of the screen goes unseen and they click again. Show the answer on the button, row or card that was used. A counter elsewhere can update too, as a second sign.
                  

                  Try: add the headphones to your cart.
                  Add to cart only changes the small count at the top.
                  The button itself says “Added”, and the count at the top changes too.
                  

                  3Match the strength to the action
                  When every small action gets a toast, the toasts pile up and people stop reading them, so they miss the one that matters too. A changed control is enough for most clicks. Keep toasts and other strong signals for actions that matter or take a while.
                  

                  Try: tick three tasks, then press Share with Sam.
                  Every tick shows a toast.
                  A tick only changes the box, and a toast appears only when the list is shared.
                  

                  4Ignore repeat clicks while it works
                  When a button gives no sign during a slow action, people click again, and each click can run the action again: two comments, two orders. While it works, say so on the button and ignore further clicks. Use aria-disabled instead of disabled, so keyboard focus stays on the button.
                  

                  Try: press Post, then press it again before anything changes.
                  Post shows nothing while it works.
                  Post says “Posting…” at once and ignores more clicks until it’s done.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

  
                  
    
                  Optimistic UI
                  

                  

                  Optimistic UI shows the result of an action before the server confirms it. The app assumes the action will work, updates the screen at once, and sends the request in the background. If the request fails, it puts things back and says so.
                  

                  It goes one step further than instant feedback, which only shows that the action has started: here the result itself shows at once. That suits small actions that almost always succeed, such as a like, a star or a status change.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
                  
          
          
        
                  
        
      
                  
      
                  
        
                  Recipes1 favorite
                  
        
                    
          
                  • Lemon pastaReady in 20 minutes
                    • 
          
                  • Chickpea curryFeeds four
                    • 
          
                  • Banana breadOne bowl, no mixer
                    • 
          
                  • Greek saladNo cooking needed
                    • 
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: star a few recipes in each mode. Waiting makes every star take almost a second, while Optimistic flips at once. Then tick “Simulate a failure” and star one in Optimistic mode: the star rolls back, the row flashes, and an error explains what happened, with Retry.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  Four kinds of actions often use it, and each needs its own way to show a failure. Tick “Make the next request fail” to see it.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Three rules keep optimistic UI honest.
                  

                  

                  1Show failures where they happened
                  Sometimes the request fails after the screen has changed. If nothing says so, the change quietly vanishes later or looks saved when it isn’t, and people find out much later, when it matters. Roll the change back where people can see it, say what failed, and offer Retry. Announce the rollback in text too, because a heart that empties again is invisible to a screen reader.
                  

                  The save fails, but the heart stays filled. Try: tap the heart on the lamp, wait a moment, then press Reload.
                  When the save fails, the heart empties again, and a toast says why and offers Retry. Try: tap the heart on the lamp and wait a moment.
                  

                  2Wait when it matters
                  Some actions often fail or carry a real cost, like payments or deletes. Showing success at once and taking it back a moment later is worse than waiting, because people may already have closed the app, sure it worked. For these, wait for the server’s answer and show progress. Keep optimism for small, reversible actions that almost always succeed.
                  

                  Try: press Pay and watch the screen for two seconds.
                  Pay shows “Paid” at once, then takes it back when the card is declined.
                  Pay shows “Paying…” and only says “Paid” or “Declined” once the bank answers.
                  

                  3Let the latest request decide
                  Two quick clicks send two requests, and the answers can come back in the wrong order. If the screen follows whichever answer arrives last, it can show a state the person didn’t choose. Treat the server’s answer as the truth, but let only the latest request decide what’s shown.
                  

                  Try: click the switch twice quickly, then wait two seconds.
                  The screen follows whichever answer arrives last, so it can show On after you chose Off.
                  Only the latest request decides what’s shown, so the screen matches your choice.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  
      
                  
        
        
        
      
                  
      
                  
      
                  
      
      
    
                  

                  

                  

  
                  
    
                  Background work with notification
                  

                  

                  Some work takes longer than people want to wait, such as an upload, an export or a backup. Background work lets it run while people keep doing other things. A small indicator shows that it’s still going, a toast says when it’s done, and finished results wait in a list until people look at them.
                  

                  That is what separates it from a progress bar in a dialog, which makes people sit and watch: here people keep working while the progress stays on screen. Tell screen readers when the work starts and when it ends, not at every step of progress.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
                  
          Holiday album
          
            
            0
          
        
                  
        
                  
          
                  
          
                  
            
            
          
                  
          
                  BeachHarbour
                  
          
                  Nothing running.
                  
          
                  Finished
                  
        
                  
      
                  
      
                  Try it: start an export, then keep typing the caption or add a few photos. The corner shows progress the whole time. When it’s done, a toast offers View and the Exports badge clears. Start two in a row to see the count go up.
                  
    
                  

                  Ways to do it
                  

                  There are four common ways to keep background work in view. They differ in how much room the work takes and in how people hear that it’s done. Many products combine two, like an indicator while it runs and a toast at the end.
                  

                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  Rules
                  

                  Four rules keep background work useful.
                  

                  

                  1Keep progress on screen
                  People rarely stay on the screen where they started a long job, and once they move on, progress that lived on that screen is gone. They can’t tell if the work is still running, stuck or done, so they go back to check or start it again. Put a small indicator in a bar that stays on every screen.
                  

                  Try: start the download, then open Trips and Saved.
                  Progress shows only on the screen where the download started.
                  A small indicator stays in the top bar on every screen.
                  

                  2Keep finished work in a list
                  A toast that says “ready” is easy to miss, because people look away or it fades before they finish what they’re doing. If that toast was the only way to the result, the result is lost to them. Keep finished work in a list they can open later, and mark new items until they’ve been opened.
                  

                  Try: export the statement and let the toast go. Now open the file.
                  The “ready” toast fades, and the file has no other home.
                  Finished files stay in Downloads, marked New until they’re opened.
                  

                  3Group notices that come together
                  When many items finish close together, one toast per item piles up. The toasts cover the screen and all say nearly the same thing, and people have to read or close each one. Send one toast for the whole batch, with a link to the items.
                  

                  Try: press Download all.
                  Each finished song gets its own toast.
                  One toast covers the whole batch, and View shows the songs.
                  

                  4Make failures louder than success
                  A failure that looks like a success goes unnoticed until someone needs the file, and by then it may be too late to redo the work. Keep a failure on screen until it’s dealt with: mark it clearly, say what went wrong, and offer a way to fix it.
                  

                  A file that failed looks almost the same as one that worked. Try: press Back up now. Did every file back up?
                  The failure stays in red, says what went wrong and offers Retry. Try: press Back up now, then Retry.
                  


                  

                  In real products
                  

                  Notice where progress lives while the work runs, and where the result waits once it’s done.
                  
  
                  
    
    
    
    
  
                  
  
                  
  
                  
  
  

                  

                  

                  

                  


                  
  
                  Chapter 11
                  Can’t find it
                  
  
                  
    
                  A small product can be learned by browsing: open a menu, scan it, click. As it grows to hundreds of pages, commands and settings, browsing stops working, and people look for things with words instead: they type into a search box, or scan the labels for the word already in their head. The patterns below make sure those words lead somewhere: a palette that runs any command by name, a search that says what it’s hiding, and labels written in the words people actually use.
                  
  
                  

  
                  
    
                  Command palette
                  

                  

                  A command palette is a search box for actions. People press a shortcut, usually Ctrl+K (⌘K on Mac), type what they want to do and press Enter. They don’t need to know which menu holds the command, only a word for it.
                  

                  That is what separates it from search: search finds things, like a file or an email, and a palette runs commands, like “Export to PDF”. It adds a fast path for people who know what they want, and it doesn’t replace the menus.
                  

                  
      
                  
        
                  
          Trip notes
          
        
                  
        
                  
          
                  HeadingParagraph
                  
          
                  
          
                  
            
                  
            
                    
            
                    ↑↓ move · Enter run · Esc close
                    
          
                    
        
                    
      
                    
      
                    
        Matching
        
                    
          
          
        
                    
      
                    
      
                    
      
                    Try it: open the palette, or click the page and press Ctrl+K or ⌘K. Type “send”, “zoom” or “xpdf”, then pick with the arrow keys and Enter. Now switch matching to Exact and type “send” again.
                    
    
                    

                    Ways to do it
                    

                    Palettes differ in what they search and when they open.
                    

                    
  
                    
    
    
    
    
  
                    
  
                    
  
                    
  
  

                    

                    Rules
                    

                    Four rules keep a command palette useful.
                    

                    

                    1Give it a visible way in
                    A palette that opens only with a shortcut is hidden from anyone who doesn’t know the shortcut, so newcomers never find it and keep hunting through menus. Give the palette a button people can see, with the shortcut written on it. Keep the menus too, and show each command’s shortcut there, so people learn the keys over time.
                    

                    The palette opens only with a shortcut, and nothing on screen says it exists. Try: turn on week numbers.
                    A button in the top bar opens it and shows the shortcut. Try: turn on week numbers with the button, then click the calendar and press Ctrl+K or ⌘K.
                    

                    2Match the words people type
                    People type the word in their head, not the command’s official name. With strict matching, “dark mode” finds nothing when the command is called “Change theme”, and people decide the app can’t do it. Match loosely: letters in order, plus a few synonyms for each command. Show why a result matched, so people learn the real name.
                    

                    Try: type “dark mode”, then “thm”.
                    Only the command’s exact name finds it.
                    Synonyms and letters in order find it too, and each result says why it matched.
                    

                    3Name commands as a verb and an object
                    A palette full of one-word entries is hard to scan: “PDF” and “Export” could each mean several things, so people try them one by one. Name every command as a verb and an object, like “Export to PDF”. Group them, and show recent commands first when the box is empty.
                    

                    Try: without typing, find the command that saves the slides as a PDF.
                    The empty box shows a flat list of one-word entries.
                    Recent commands come first, then groups of names with a verb and an object.
                    

                    4Use one well-known shortcut
                    A shortcut that is also a normal key gets in the way of typing: if “/” opens the palette everywhere, people can’t type “and/or” in a note. Use the shortcut most apps share, Ctrl+K (⌘K on Mac), listen for it only where it applies, and never take keys people need for typing.
                    

                    The “/” key opens the palette, even while people type a note. Try: type “and/or” in the note.
                    Only Ctrl+K or ⌘K opens it, and every other key types. Try: type “and/or” in the note, then press Ctrl+K or ⌘K.
                    


                    

                    In real products
                    

                    Notice what each palette teaches on the side: a shortcut, the current selection, or where the command lives in the menus.
                    
  
                    
    
    
    
    
  
                    
  
                    
  
                    
  
  

                    

                    

                    

  
                    
    
                    Search with filters and recents
                    

                    

                    Search with filters helps people narrow a long list fast, such as products, emails or files. The search box takes words, and filters narrow by kind, like size, date or type. Recent items cover the common case of coming back for something used before.
                    

                    Unlike a command palette, which runs actions, search finds things. It works only when people can see what the search and the filters leave out. Tell screen readers the result count once typing pauses, not on every key.
                    

                    
      
                    
        
                    
          
          
                    
        
                    
        
                    
          
          
          
        
                    
        
                    
        
                    
      
                    
      
                    
      
                    Try it: turn on Photos, then type “portrait”: one match is hidden by the filter, and the panel says so. Then type “detial”. Clear the box to see recents, and pick a file to move it to the top.
                    
    
                    

                    Ways to do it
                    

                    There are four common shapes. Chips and a panel narrow the results, a scope picks where to search, and recents help before anyone types.
                    

                    
  
                    
    
    
    
    
  
                    
  
                    
  
                    
  
  

                    

                    Rules
                    

                    Four rules keep search with filters useful.
                    

                    

                    1Show what the filters hide
                    Filters often stay on from an earlier visit, and if people can’t see them, they search, find nothing and decide the item doesn’t exist. Keep active filters in view and show the result count. Say how many matches sit outside the filters, and offer one click to see them.
                    

                    A size filter from an earlier visit hides behind a button. Try: search for “rain jacket”.
                    Active filters stay in view, and the count says what they leave out. Try: search for “rain jacket”, then show the other sizes.
                    

                    2Don’t stop at “No results”
                    An empty page with only “No results” leaves people stuck, because they can’t tell if they misspelled a word, used the wrong term or filtered too much. Repeat what they searched for, offer a close spelling, and offer to clear filters. Empty state covers how “no results” differs from “nothing yet”.
                    

                    Try: search for “lasagne”.
                    The page says “No results” and nothing else.
                    The page repeats the search, offers a close spelling and offers to clear the filter.
                    

                    3Start with a few filters
                    Each filter is one more thing to read, so with fifteen, the filter panel turns into a form and the results drop out of view. Start with three to five filters that match how people already choose, like price and breakfast for a hotel. Put the rest behind “More filters”, and add new ones when people ask for them.
                    

                    Try: find a hotel with breakfast for under €120.
                    Fifteen filters push the hotels out of view.
                    Four chips match how people choose a hotel, and the rest wait behind More filters.
                    

                    4Show recent items before anyone types
                    People often search for something they used a short while ago, and an empty box makes them type the name again and remember how it’s spelled. Show recent items as soon as the box gets focus. When filters are on, show only the recent items that fit them.
                    

                    Try: find “Golden hour”, the song you played this morning.
                    The empty search box shows nothing until people type.
                    Recent songs and searches show as soon as the box gets focus.
                    


                    

                    In real products
                    

                    
  
                    
    
    
    
    
  
                    
  
                    
  
                    
  
  

                    

                    

                    

  
                    
    
                    Labels in people’s words
                    

                    

                    People scan menus and links for the word already in their head. When a label matches it, they click with confidence, and when it doesn’t, they guess, go back and try again, or give up. This pull of matching words is called information scent.
                    

                    Labels in people’s words carry that scent: they name things the way customers do, not the way the team does inside the company. Each label should also make sense on its own, because many people, screen reader users among them, jump from label to label without seeing the layout around it.
                    

                    
      
                    
        
        
      
                    
      
                    
        
                    Task: change where photos are saved.
                    
        
                    
        
                      
        
                      
        
                      Clicks: 0
                      
      
                      
      
                      Before: not found yet · After: not found yet
                      
      
                      Try it: on Before, find where photos are saved and watch the click count. Then switch to After and do it again. Both menus have the same shape and the same shortest path of 3 clicks, so the words are the only difference.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      A label can carry more or less scent, and the more alike the options are, the more each label needs to say.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep labels in people’s words.
                      

                      

                      1Use people’s words, not the team’s
                      Teams name things after how the system works: “entities”, “remittance”, a database field. People don’t know those words, so they read every option and guess. Collect the words people use in support questions, reviews and searches before you name things, and use those.
                      

                      Try: click the field where you’d write “March rent”.
                      The payment form uses the bank’s internal terms.
                      The form uses the words people use for their own money.
                      

                      2Name what’s inside, not the brand
                      Clever or branded names are fun to write, but they don’t say what’s behind them, so people open each one to find out and remember none of them. Use plain names that say what each section holds, and keep personality for empty states and onboarding, where it doesn’t cost a click.
                      

                      Try: find the songs you downloaded to play offline.
                      Clever names say nothing about what’s inside.
                      Plain names say what each section holds.
                      

                      3Use one name for one thing
                      When one thing has two names, people assume they are two things and wonder whether the cart and the bag hold the same items. As with consistent naming anywhere in a product, pick one term for each concept, use it everywhere and keep a short glossary.
                      

                      Try: add the lamp, then open what you’ve added.
                      The same basket is called “basket”, “cart” and “bag”.
                      It’s called “basket” everywhere.
                      

                      4Test the whole path with a task
                      A label can be right and still go unfound, because it sits under a parent nobody opens. People pick a top-level section first, and if that name doesn’t match their goal, they never see what’s inside. Give people a task, like “Where would you add your passport number?”, and watch where they click first, which is called tree testing. Move items to where people look.
                      

                      Try: add your passport number.
                      “Passport details” sits under Payments, where few people look.
                      A tree test showed that people look under Account, so it moved there.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

                      


                      
  
                      
    
                      Chapter 12
                      
    
                      Blank screen
                      
  
                      
  
                      
    
                      The first minutes decide whether people stay. An empty page gives no clue where to start, what a finished result looks like or how the tools work. The empty state in Part 3 covers the message on an empty screen. This chapter is about getting people moving: hand them something that already works, and teach the next step at the moment they need it.
