                      Templates and starter content
                      

                      

                      Templates and starter content give people a working example to start from, instead of an empty page. People see what a finished result looks like and change it into their own, so they reach a first result faster and see what the product can do.
                      

                      Where a preset fills in settings, a template gives a whole starting document, with content people are meant to replace. After a template opens, move focus to the first thing to change.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
                      
          Untitled video
          
            
            
          
        
                      
        
                      
          
                      
            
                      Start from a template
                      
            
                      
              
              
              
            
                      
            
          
                      
          
                      
        
                      
      
                      
      
                      
      
                      Try it: pick a template: the video already plays, the parts meant for you are marked “edit me”, and one line says what to do first. Then press Start over and choose Start blank to go straight to an empty timeline.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      There are four common ways to give people a start. They differ in where the start comes from: a gallery of templates, a filled-in example in a new account, people’s own past work, or a few one-click starts on an empty page.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep templates useful.
                      

                      

                      1Offer a few different starts
                      If every template works the same way, people take it as the only way and fit their content into it, even when it doesn’t suit them. Offer a few starts that differ in kind, and say in one line what each is good for, so people pick by goal and see the range of what the product can do.
                      

                      Try: pick a start for a photo slideshow of your trip.
                      All four templates are the same bullet-list deck in different colors.
                      Four different starts, each saying what it’s good for.
                      

                      2Keep templates up to date
                      Templates go stale: an old year, renamed features, a chart type that no longer works. A broken template is often someone’s first experience of the product, so own templates like features: give each one an owner, check it with every release, and update or retire it.
                      

                      Try: open the Monthly budget template.
                      The budget template still says 2023, and its chart no longer works.
                      The template names its owner and last check, and opens as Budget 2026 with a working chart.
                      

                      3Mark what to change
                      A good example looks finished, so people can’t tell which parts are theirs to change, and the example text they miss ends up in what they send. Mark the parts meant to be edited with words and a border, not color alone, and add one line that names the first thing to do.
                      

                      Try: click the parts you’d change, then press Check.
                      The résumé looks finished, and nothing marks the parts to change.
                      Parts to change are marked “edit”, and one line says what to do first.
                      

                      4Keep a blank start one click away
                      People who know what they want don’t need a template, and if every new file opens a gallery first, they click past it each time. Keep “Blank” as an equal choice next to the templates, one click away.
                      

                      Try: make three blank forms and watch the click count.
                      Every new form opens the template gallery, and Blank hides under More options.
                      “Blank form” sits next to “From a template”, one click away.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      Notice that a blank start stays one click away, and each template already works before you change anything.
                      
  
                      
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

  
                      
    
                      Contextual hints over tours
                      

                      

                      A contextual hint teaches one thing at the moment people need it, next to the thing it explains. It appears after a related action, such as a first click on an empty whiteboard, and stays away once people know the thing, so people who already know it never see it.
                      

                      A product tour works the other way round: it explains everything up front, before people have a reason to care. Most people skip it, and the rest forget it by the time they get stuck.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
        
      
                      
      
                      
        
                      
          Kitchen ideas
          
        
                      
        
                      
          
          
                      
        
                      
        
                      
          
                      
            
                      Step 1 of 5
                      
            
                      Welcome
                      
            
                      
            
                      
              
              
            
                      
          
                      
        
                      
      
                      
      
                      
        
        
      
                      
      
                      
      
                      Try it: click through the tour, then try to remember step 3 when you need it. Switch to Contextual hint and click the empty board once: a hint on adding a note appears beside that spot, and after “Got it” it stays gone, even after a reload. Double-click instead and you never see it, because you already know how to add a note.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      Hints range from quiet to loud. Placeholder text sits inside an empty field. A help icon waits until people ask. A callout points at one control, once. A nudge appears after people do something the long way and offers the short way. Pick the quietest one that still reaches people at the right moment.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep contextual hints useful.
                      

                      

                      1Show one hint at a time
                      When every feature gets its own hint, they all show up at once. People can’t tell which one matters, the bubbles sit on top of the things they wanted to use, and they close them all without reading. Show one hint, right after people do the related thing, and skip hints for things they already use.
                      

                      Four hints open at once and cover the photo and the tools. Try: count the hints, then try to press Crop.
                      One hint appears when Adjust opens, and Crop, used before, gets none. Try: press Adjust, then press Crop.
                      

                      2Remember when people close a hint
                      A closed hint that comes back tells people their choice didn’t count, and after the second time they close hints without reading them, new ones included. Remember every closed hint, ideally with the account so it holds on every device, and give people one place to see the tips again.
                      

                      The hint comes back every time the app opens. Try: press Got it, then Open the app again.
                      A closed hint stays closed, and Show tips again brings it back. Try: press Got it, then Open the app again. Then press Show tips again.
                      

                      3Keep the target in view
                      A hint is about one control. If it sits on top of that control, people have to close the hint before they can try what it explains, and by then they have half forgotten it. Place the hint beside the control and point at it. Keep the control usable, and don’t move keyboard focus into the hint.
                      

                      Try: press Filters while the hint is open.
                      The hint covers the button it explains.
                      The hint sits below Filters and points up at it, and the button still works.
                      

                      4Keep key help somewhere else too
                      Once a hint is closed, it’s gone, so if it was the only place that explained something, people who need it later have nowhere to look. Write the same help in the help pages or a help panel, and link there from the hint so people know where to find it again.
                      

                      Try: press Got it, then open Help and look for how to change an event’s length.
                      How to change an event’s length is only in the hint.
                      The help covers it too, and Learn more in the hint opens it.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

                      


                      
  
                      Chapter 13
                      Prevent, explain, recover
                      
  
                      
    
                      An error is most frustrating when the product could have prevented it. The best error is the one that can’t happen, and the next best explains itself in plain words and loses nothing. Part 3 covers the parts that show errors, the inline message and the error state; the patterns below work around them, so fewer errors happen and the ones that do cost less.
                      
  
                      

  
                      
    
                      Constraints that prevent errors
                      

                      

                      A constraint makes a wrong value impossible to enter. Instead of a free text field and an error afterwards, people pick from options that all work, or set a number that stops at its limits. There is nothing to refuse, because every choice is valid.
                      

                      Validation works the other way round: it lets people type anything, then checks it and explains the mistake. Use a constraint when the valid values are few or follow a clear rule, and keep validation for values too varied to offer as choices.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
        
      
                      
      
                      
        
                      Video size
                      
        
                      
          
                      
            
            
            
                      
          
                      
          
                      
            
            
            
                      
          
                      
        
                      
      
                      
      
                      
        
                      Video size
                      
        
                      Sizes are multiples of 8. Every option below already is one.
                      
        
                      
          
                      
            
            
          
                      
          
                      
            
            
          
                      
        
                      
        
                      
          
          
        
                      
        
                      
          
          
          
                      Any multiple of 8 from 256 to 4096. Other numbers snap to the nearest one.
                      
          
                      
        
                      
      
                      
      
                      
        
      
                      
      
                      
      
                      Try it: in Free text, the height 750 is refused, and you only learn the rule from the error. Switch to Constrained, where every choice is already valid. Then pick Custom… for the width, type 1001 and press Tab: it rounds to 1000 and says so.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      Constraints come in a few shapes. A list offers only the values that work. A number with limits stops at its smallest and largest value. Options that don’t apply right now stay visible but turned off. Split fields take one part of a value at a time, so its shape can’t go wrong.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep constraints useful.
                      

                      

                      1Leave a way out for odd cases
                      A short list covers most people, but not everyone. Someone with an odd-sized window has no way to enter the width they really need, so they give up or pick something wrong. Add a “Custom…” choice for those cases, check what people type there, and say so when you round it.
                      

                      The list has four set widths, and none fits a 105 cm window. Try: order a blind for a window 105 cm wide.
                      Custom… takes any width from 40 to 300 cm and says when it rounds. Try: pick Custom…, type 104.6 and press Tab. Then try 400.
                      

                      2Say why an option is off
                      A grayed-out option with no reason looks broken: people click it, nothing happens, and they don’t know whether to upgrade, free up space or give up. Put the reason next to the option, in plain text: what it needs and how to get it. Leave out options that can never apply to this person.
                      

                      Two options are grayed out, and nothing says why. Try: try to pick Lossless.
                      Lossless says it needs Premium and links to the plans. Dolby Atmos, which can never apply, is left out. Try: read why Lossless is off, then press See plans.
                      

                      3Show the rule before people need it
                      Some values follow a rule that can’t be built into the control, like which characters a username may use. If people only learn the rule from an error, they have to guess again. Write the rule in the label or the help text under the field, so people get it right on the first try.
                      

                      People learn the username rule only from the error. Try: type Ana Silva and press Save.
                      The rule sits in the help text under the field. Try: read the help text, type a username and press Save.
                      

                      4Keep the rule in one place
                      The list, the help text and the final check often get written at different times. When they disagree, people pick a value the list allows and get refused at the end. Write the rule once and build the list, the help text and the check from it, so they can’t drift apart.
                      

                      The list goes to 30 nights, the help text says 31, and the final check allows 28. Try: pick 30 nights and press Book.
                      The list, the help text and the check all come from one rule: up to 28 nights. Try: open the list of nights, then press Book.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      Notice that choices that can’t work are either never offered or visibly off.
                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

  
                      
    
                      Forgiving input
                      

                      

                      Forgiving input accepts a value in the ways people actually write it. “1024 x 768”, “1024×768” and “1024 by 768” all mean the same size, so the field reads all of them. It cleans up spaces, symbols and units on its own, and it shows how it read the input.
                      

                      Where a constraint limits what people can enter, forgiving input lets them enter a value their way and does the translating. Both prevent the same thing: an error about formatting that any person would have understood.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
                      
          
          
        
                      
        
                      
          
                      Width
                      
          
                      Height
                      
          
                      
        
                      
        
                      
          
        
                      
      
                      
      
                      
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
      
                      
      
                      Try it: press the examples, or type your own: every one that makes sense is read, and the readout says how. Only a single number, the one truly ambiguous case, makes it ask.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      A field can forgive in a few ways. It can accept several formats for the same value. It can clean up formatting, such as spaces and dashes. It can notice a likely typo and offer the fix. It can read plain words, like “tomorrow 9am”. Each way shows the result, so people can check it.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep forgiving input useful.
                      

                      

                      1Show how you read it
                      A field that guesses can guess wrong, and if it says nothing, people find out later, when the parcel costs seven times as much or the wrong thing arrives. Show the reading next to the field, in words, before the value is used, so a wrong guess is caught on sight.
                      

                      Try: type 5,5 and look at the price.
                      It reads “5,5” as 55 kg and says nothing.
                      A line under the field says how it read the weight, so 5,5 shows as 5.5 kg.
                      

                      2Ask only when it could mean two things
                      Most input has one obvious reading, and asking about it only slows people down. Some input really could mean two things, like “7” for a time, and a field that quietly picks one is sometimes wrong without anyone noticing. Take the obvious reading when there is one, and ask only in the real two-way cases, with each answer one click away.
                      

                      Try: type 7 and press Add. Then try 7pm.
                      It reads “7” as 7:00 am, though it could mean either.
                      “7” gets a choice of 7:00 am or 7:00 pm, and “7pm” is taken as it is.
                      

                      3Forgive the same way everywhere
                      When one field accepts “12m 30s” and the next one rejects it, people can’t learn what works, so they fall back to the strictest format everywhere or give up on the shortcuts. Put the reading of times, sizes and amounts in one shared function and use it in every field, so a format that works once works everywhere.
                      

                      Try: type 12m 30s in Skip to, and 1h in Sleep timer.
                      Skip to takes only mm:ss, and Sleep timer only minutes.
                      Both fields read the same formats, such as 12:30, 12m 30s or 1h.
                      

                      4Say when the value itself changes
                      Cleaning up spaces or a “cm” is harmless, so do it without comment. Changing the number is different, because people get something they didn’t ask for. When you round to the nearest valid value, say so, and when the value is far outside what’s possible, refuse it and give the limit instead of picking one.
                      

                      Try: type 10 x 14 and press Tab. Then try 100 x 150, and 10x15cm.
                      It changes the size to the nearest print size without a word.
                      It says when the size changes, refuses 100 x 150 and tidies 10x15cm without comment.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

  
                      
    
                      Autosave and draft recovery
                      

                      

                      Autosave keeps people’s work without them asking. Each change is saved a moment after it’s made, and a small status says so. If the app crashes or the tab closes, the work is waiting when people come back.
                      

                      Autosave keeps only the latest state, so it belongs together with version history, which keeps the earlier ones.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
                      Notes · Weekend
                      
        
                      
          
          
          
            
            
          
        
                      
        
                      
          
                      
            
            
          
                      
        
                      
      
                      
      
                      
        
      
                      
      
                      Try it: type a few words and pause until it says Saved. Then simulate a crash: the field comes back empty, and the banner offers your draft. You can also reload this page, because the draft lives in this browser.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      Autosave takes a few forms. A document saves as people type and shows the save state. A settings page saves each change the moment it’s made. A message box keeps unsent text when people move somewhere else. After a crash, the app offers the work it kept on the device.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep autosave useful.
                      

                      

                      1Show that work is saved
                      If people can’t see that their work is saved, they don’t trust it: they keep saving by hand, or they lose work when a save fails without a word. Show a save status where they already look. If a save fails, say so plainly, keep the work on the device and send it once the connection is back.
                      

                      Try: turn Wi-Fi off, add a line, then press Close and reopen. Then turn Wi-Fi on.
                      No status shows, and a save made offline fails without a word.
                      The status says “Saved”, or “Offline · kept on this device” until Wi-Fi is back.
                      

                      2Keep earlier versions
                      Autosave saves mistakes too: if someone deletes a paragraph by accident, the save goes through a second later and the old text is gone. Pair autosave with version history, so any earlier version is one step back. A recovered draft should also wait until people choose Restore or Discard.
                      

                      Try: press Delete paragraph, wait for Saved, then try to get it back.
                      An accidental delete gets saved, and there’s no way back.
                      History lists each saved version, with Restore.
                      

                      3Catch edits from another tab
                      The same document can be open in two tabs or on two devices. Each copy saves its own text, so the last save replaces the other without a word, and people notice much later that what they added in the other place is gone. Detect the clash and ask before one copy replaces the other.
                      

                      Try: add an item in Tab 1, then one in Tab 2. Read the saved list.
                      Each tab saves its own copy, and the last save wins without a word.
                      Tab 2 says the list changed and offers Reload or Keep mine as a copy.
                      

                      4Offer recovery only when something was lost
                      A recovery prompt that shows up every time teaches people to dismiss it, so the one time it matters, they press Discard without reading. Offer recovery only when the draft differs from what was saved. Clear old drafts after a while, and let Discard be undone for a moment.
                      

                      Try: press Close and reopen. Then type something, press Crash and press Discard.
                      The prompt shows on every reopen, even when nothing was lost.
                      The prompt shows only when the draft differs from what was saved, and Discard offers Undo.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      Notice how each product shows that work is safe, and what comes back after a close or a crash.
                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

                      

                      
  
  
                      Chapter 14
                      Newcomers & experts
                      
  
                      The same product serves someone on day one and someone on day five hundred. Newcomers need few choices and an obvious next step, while experts want speed and control. Serve both with a calm surface first and faster paths underneath for the people who look for them, kept out of each other’s way. Nielsen’s heuristic calls this “flexibility and efficiency of use”.
                      

  
                      
    
                      Layered interface
                      

                      

                      A layered interface shows a simple set of controls first and keeps the full set one step away. New and occasional users get the few choices that matter, and experts open the advanced layer to change the rest. Both layers change the same settings, so switching between them loses nothing.
                      

                      Where progressive disclosure tucks away the settings few people change, a layered interface gives newcomers and experts each a named layer of the same controls, and people pick the one they work in.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
        
      
                      
      
                      
        
                      
          
          
        
                      
        
                      
          
          
        
                      
        
                      
          
                      
            
                      
              
              
            
                      
            
                      
              
              
            
                      
            
                      
              
              
            
                      
            
                      
              
              
            
                      
          
                      
          
                      
            
                      What happens to your order
                      
            
                        
              
                      1. Upload
                      2. Crop
                      3. Print
                      4. Pack
                      5. Ship
                        6. 
            
                      
          
                      
        
                      
        
                      
          
          
          
          
        
                      
        
      
                      
      
                      Try it: switch to Advanced and change the paper or the copies. Switch back to Simple: your values stay, and a note says what’s different. Add to cart in either mode and the toast shows the same settings.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      There are a few ways to layer. Show more and a separate page work as in progressive disclosure. The other two split the work into two versions: a mode switch flips the whole screen between a basic and a full version, and a quick form handles the common case and opens the full form for the rest.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep a layered interface useful.
                      

                      

                      1Build both layers on one set of settings
                      If Simple and Advanced are two separate forms, they drift apart: a value typed in one is missing in the other, and some settings work in only one mode. Build Simple on top of the same settings as Advanced, so it only hides fields and keeps their values.
                      

                      Try: type a city in To, switch to Advanced, then back to Simple.
                      Simple and Advanced are separate forms, and Advanced starts empty.
                      One form, where Advanced adds fields below the same From and To.
                      

                      2Keep the way to more in sight
                      If the way to the full controls is hard to find, people assume the simple layer is all there is, and they scroll through everything or leave. Put the way in a fixed, visible place, as a named button or a segmented control, and say what’s behind it, such as “Filters: size, color, price”.
                      

                      Try: find shirts in size M.
                      The filters hide behind an unlabeled icon in a corner.
                      A button reads “Filters: size, color, price”.
                      

                      3Show what changed out of sight
                      Settings changed in the advanced layer still apply after people go back to the simple one, and a change nobody can see makes results look wrong for no clear reason. Show a short summary in the simple layer, such as “1 advanced setting changed”, with a way to show it and a way to reset it.
                      

                      Try: switch to Advanced, raise Warmth, then switch back to Simple.
                      Simple shows no sign of the Warmth change made in Advanced.
                      Simple says “1 advanced setting changed: warmth”, with Show and Reset.
                      

                      4Decide where each new option goes
                      When nobody decides where a new option goes, it lands in Advanced, which over time becomes a long, unsorted list where settings many people need get buried. For each option, choose the simple layer, the advanced layer, or a better default that makes it unnecessary. Keep Advanced for real expert choices, grouped in a sensible order.
                      

                      Try: find where to set an out-of-office reply.
                      Advanced is one long list, with Out-of-office reply near the bottom.
                      Out-of-office reply sits in Simple, Advanced is short and grouped, and link conversion became a default.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

  
                      
    
                      Keyboard shortcuts and accelerators
                      

                      

                      A keyboard shortcut runs a command from the keyboard, without the mouse. People who repeat the same commands all day save a second or two each time, and that adds up. Shortcuts are for people who already know the command, while new people find it in a button or a menu and learn the key from there.
                      

                      Where a command palette lets people search for a command by name, a shortcut runs one they already know with a single key press.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
                      Lisbon tripYou used 0 shortcuts
                      
        
                      
          
                      
            
            
            
            
          
                      
          
          
                      
            Tram 28HarbourOld townSunset
          
                      
        
                      
      
                      
      
        
                      
          
                      
            
                      Keyboard shortcuts
                      
            
                      Rotate photoR
                      
            
                      Save albumS
                      
            
                      Fit viewF
                      
            
                      Show this list?
                      
            
                      They work while focus is inside this demo, and never while you type in a field.
                      
          
                      
          
                      
        
                      
                            
      
                      Try it: click the photo board, then press R, S and F. Type “fire” in the search box: no shortcut fires while you type. Press ? for the list. Click Save twice to get a hint.
                      
    
                      

                      Ways to do it
                      

                      Shortcuts come in four shapes. A single key is the fastest, but it only works where people aren’t typing. A key with Ctrl or ⌘ works anywhere. A sequence of two keys gives room for more commands. A command palette lets people type the name of any command and shows its key on the way.
                      

                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      Rules
                      

                      Four rules keep shortcuts useful.
                      

                      

                      1Show the keys where people look
                      A shortcut nobody knows about saves nobody any time, and people don’t read help pages, so they never learn the key and keep clicking. Show each key next to its command, in buttons, menus and tooltips, and keep the full list behind “?”.
                      

                      The keys work, but nothing on screen shows them. Try: skip three songs. Is there a faster way?
                      Each button shows its key, and “?” opens the full list. Try: skip a song with the button, then click the player and press N. Press ? for the list.
                      

                      2Don’t take keys the browser already uses
                      People rely on keys like copy, paste, undo, find and close tab in every app. If your app uses one of them, either the browser wins and your command never runs, or your app wins and people lose a key they rely on. Pick keys that are free, and let people see and change all of them in one place.
                      

                      The app uses Ctrl+W to close a note, but the browser uses it to close the tab. Try: press the keys under the window to close the note.
                      Close note uses Esc, and Shortcuts lists every key, each one changeable. Try: press the keys to close the note. Then open Shortcuts and change a key.
                      

                      3Ignore single keys while people type
                      A single-letter shortcut is fast in a list, but in a text field the same letter is part of a word. As with a palette that opens on “/”, a shortcut that still fires there runs commands people didn’t ask for. Turn single keys off while focus is in a text field, and give each shortcut a clear area where it works.
                      

                      A archives the chat, even while people type a reply. Try: click the reply box and type “Thanks, see you at 6”.
                      A does nothing in the reply box and archives from the message list. Try: click the reply box and type “Thanks, see you at 6”. Then press Esc to leave the box, and press A.
                      

                      4Keep a visible way to do it
                      Some people never use the keyboard: they use a mouse, a touch screen or voice. Others haven’t learned the key yet, and if a command only has a shortcut, none of them can use it. Give every command a button or a menu item, and treat the shortcut as the faster path to it.
                      

                      Try: copy the yoga class to Tuesday using only the mouse.
                      Only the D key duplicates an event, and the menu doesn’t offer it.
                      The ⋯ menu has Duplicate too, with its key shown next to it.
                      


                      

                      In real products
                      

                      Notice how each product teaches its shortcuts on the slow path, and keeps single keys out of the way while people type.
                      
  
                      
    
    
    
    
  
                      
  
                      
  
                      
  
  

                      

                      

                      

  
                      
    
                      Customization: favorites and pinning
                      

                      

                      Customization lets people shape a product around the few things they use most, such as starring a contact, pinning a chat or adding a button to a toolbar. The full list stays as it was, and their own picks sit on top of it, one step away.
                      

                      It differs from personalization, where the product guesses, like a “Recently used” list that changes by itself. With customization people choose, so it only changes when they change it.
                      

                      
      
                      
        
                      Insert a block
                      
        
                      Pinned
                      
        
                      Nothing pinned yet. Press the star on a block you use often.
                      
        
                        
        
                        All blocks
                        
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: add “Checklist” three times and accept the offer, or press a star. Reload the page: your pins stay. Reset puts the list back to the default.
                          
    
                          

                          Ways to do it
                          

                          There are four common ways, which differ in what people pick: an item to star, an item to pin at the top of a list sorted by date, the buttons a toolbar shows, or the sections of a home screen.
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep customization useful.
                          

                          

                          1Fix the defaults first
                          It’s tempting to leave a weak screen as it is, because “people can set it up themselves”, but most people never do: they keep the screen they were given and work around it. Make the default right for most people first, and offer customization on top for the rest.
                          

                          Try: find your balance and the Pay button.
                          The default home leads with offers and puts the balance and Pay last.
                          The balance and Pay come first, and Customize is still there.
                          

                          2Offer it when it helps
                          A setting nobody finds doesn’t help anybody, and few people go looking in Settings. The best moment to offer customization is when someone keeps doing the same thing: after they share with the same person a few times, offer to make that person a favorite, right there.
                          

                          Favorites exist, but only under Settings. Try: share with Mum three times. Where would you make her a favorite?
                          After three shares with the same person, the app offers to make them a favorite. Try: share with Mum three times, then accept the offer.
                          

                          3Add on top, don’t reorder
                          Help articles and support staff say things like “open the third item”. If customizing moves items around in the main list, those directions no longer match what people see. Keep pins in a separate place at the top and leave the full list in its usual order, with “Reset to default” in one obvious place.
                          

                          Try: pin Display. Then follow the help note and open the third item.
                          Pinning moves Display up the main list, so the third item is no longer Privacy.
                          Pins get their own row at the top, the main list keeps its order, and Reset to default clears the pins.
                          

                          4Keep the pinned list short
                          Pins are added in a second but often removed only from a settings page, so the pinned section keeps growing until it is as long as the list it was meant to shorten. Let people unpin right where the pin appears, and when nothing is pinned, show an empty state that explains how pinning works.
                          

                          Unpinning takes three steps per chat. Try: unpin two chats you no longer need.
                          Each pin has its own unpin button, and an empty state explains pins once none are left. Try: unpin all of them. What shows when none are left?
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          

                          

                          

                          
  
                          Chapter 15
                          Lean on how people already behave
                          
  
                          
    
                          Some designs feel right before anyone can say why. Often it’s because they lean on a few well-known observations about people: what they expect, how they point, how they choose. Jon Yablonski collected many of them at lawsofux.com. Treat them as rules of thumb: they explain a lot and help you spot problems, but they still need checking with real people.
                          
  
                          

  
                          
    
                          Jakob’s law
                          

                          

                          Jakob’s law says that people spend most of their time in other products, so they expect yours to work the same way. A search box has a magnifying glass, a link is underlined, and the cart sits in the top right corner. People use these without thinking and bring those habits to every new product they open.
                          

                          The law isn’t a ban on new ideas, but it tells you what one costs: every break from a convention is something people have to stop and learn. Sometimes that cost is worth paying, but it should be a choice.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
        
                          Templates
                          
        
                          
          
                          
            
            
          
                          
          
                          No template fits? Start from a blank document
                          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: in Before, find where to search and how to start from scratch. Then switch to After, where nothing new was added and each part looks the way it does everywhere else.
                          
    
                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Three rules help you work with people’s habits.
                          

                          

                          1Use the control people already know
                          A new kind of control can look fresh in a design review, but in use people try what works everywhere else, and it doesn’t work here. Some never find out how it works. Use the familiar control, which assistive tech understands too, and change it only when testing shows a clear win for a real task.
                          

                          Try: set the quantity back to 1.
                          The quantity is a new kind of control: a tap adds one, and only a long press takes one away.
                          The quantity uses the − and + stepper that people know from other shops.
                          

                          2Adapt a convention to the task
                          A convention that is right in one kind of product can be wrong in another. In a document, Enter starts a new line, but in a table people expect Enter to save the cell and move down. Find out how people do this work in the tools they already use, and test the result with them.
                          

                          Try: type 900 for Rent, press Enter, then type 450 for Food.
                          The budget table copies a document habit: Enter adds a new line inside the cell.
                          Enter saves the cell and moves to the one below, as in other spreadsheets.
                          

                          3Teach a break where it happens
                          Sometimes a product has a good reason to break a convention. If nothing explains the change, people try the usual way, nothing happens, and they don’t know why. Show a short hint at the moment they try the usual way, and keep the familiar path working where you can.
                          

                          Try: change the note and save it.
                          The notes app saves on its own and has no Save button, but nothing says so.
                          A “Saved” status shows it’s done, and Ctrl+S (⌘S on Mac) still works and says notes save on their own.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice what each product kept familiar.
                          
  
                          
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Fitts’s law
                          

                          

                          Fitts’s law says that the time it takes to hit a target depends on its size and its distance. A big target close to the pointer or the thumb is fast to hit. A small target far away is slow, and people miss it more often.
                          

                          It applies to every click and tap: buttons, links, menu items, close icons. The screen edges help too, because the pointer stops there and can’t overshoot. People with a tremor, on a touch screen or using zoom feel the difference most.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
                          Click the lit target to start.
                          
      
                          Tiny, far: –Big, near: –
                          
      
                          Try it: in “Tiny, far”, click the lit dot until it says done. Then switch to “Big, near”, go again, and compare the averages and the misses. Tab and Enter work too, but this law is about pointing.
                          
    
                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Three rules put Fitts’s law to work.
                          

                          

                          1Make the hit area bigger than the icon
                          Small icons look tidy, but a 12-pixel target is hard to hit, especially with a finger or a shaky hand, so people miss, try again, and sometimes hit the thing next to it. The icon can stay small if the clickable area around it is large, at least 24 by 24 pixels. See Icon button.
                          

                          Try: remove the three blurry photos. Count your misses.
                          The remove buttons are as small as their 12-pixel icons.
                          The icons stay small, but each button’s hit area is 32 pixels.
                          

                          2Put the action near what it acts on
                          When the button sits far from where people are working, every use costs a long move across the screen. On a wide screen that adds up, and on a phone it can mean a stretch of the thumb. Put the action next to the field, at the end of the form, or in a menu that opens at the pointer.
                          

                          Try: fill in the postcode, then press Save. Check how far the pointer moved.
                          Save sits in the top corner, far from the last field.
                          Save sits right under the last field, where the pointer already is.
                          

                          3Keep risky actions away from common ones
                          If Delete sits right next to Reply and both are the same size, a fast move lands on either one, and a small slip deletes something. Make the common action the big, easy target, move the risky one away or into a menu, and let people undo it.
                          

                          Reply and Delete are small buttons side by side, and Delete can’t be undone. Try: press Reply, then look how close Delete is. Press it once.
                          Reply is the big button under the email. Delete sits apart, and it can be undone. Try: press Reply, then delete the email and undo it.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice how each one makes the target bigger, or puts it where the pointer or thumb already is.
                          
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Hick’s law
                          

                          

                          Hick’s law says that the more choices people see, the longer it takes them to pick one, because each extra option is one more thing to read and compare. The effect is strongest when people don’t know the list yet and have to scan it.
                          

                          It doesn’t mean a product should offer less, but that it should show the likely choices first and keep the rest easy to reach. When people already know what they want, a search box beats any list. A screen reader reads options one at a time, so a long list costs even more there.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
      
                          
      
                          Pick the “Receipts” folder as fast as you can.
                          
      
                          4 options: –16 options: –
                          
      
                          Try it: pick “Receipts” three times with 4 options, then three times with 16. The order shuffles each time, so you have to look. Compare the averages.
                          
    
                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Three rules put Hick’s law to work.
                          

                          

                          1Group long lists, or let people search
                          In a long flat list, people read item after item until they find theirs, because nothing tells them where to look. Put recent choices first, group the rest, or add search that narrows the list as they type. See Combobox.
                          

                          The destinations are one long, unsorted list. Try: open the list and pick Lisbon. Note the time.
                          Recent destinations come first, and a search box narrows the list as people type. Try: pick Lisbon again, from Recent or by typing “lis”.
                          

                          2Make the likely choice stand out
                          When every option looks the same, people have to read and weigh all of them, even when one is the usual answer, which slows them down and leads to wrong picks. Make the likely choice stand out: a sensible default, one primary button, the most used item at the top.
                          

                          Try: close the document and keep your changes.
                          All four buttons look the same.
                          Save is the one primary button and has focus. The other three are quieter.
                          

                          3Tuck rare options away, don’t delete them
                          Cutting options makes a menu shorter, but someone needed each one, and those people now can’t do their task at all. Keep the common options in view, and put the rare ones behind “More” or in an advanced section.
                          

                          Try: download the photo at full size.
                          The menu was cut to three options, and full-size download was one of the cuts.
                          The common options stay in view. The rare ones sit behind More options.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice how each one cuts a long list down to a few likely choices before people have to pick.
                          
  
                          
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Tesler’s law
                          

                          

                          Tesler’s law says every task holds some complexity that can’t be removed, only moved. When a photo app imports pictures, it still has to save them to a folder. Either people type the full folder path, or the app offers the folders they used recently. The design question is who carries that work: the system or the person.
                          

                          Usually the system should carry it, because the team solves the hard part once instead of every person solving it every time. But moved complexity always lands somewhere, such as an error message, the help pages or the next screen, so when you simplify a step, check where the work went.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
        
                          
          
          
          
                          Type the full folder path, for example /Users/you/Pictures/Lisbon trip
                          
          
                          
        
                          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          
        
                          
          Save imported photos to
          
          
          
        
                          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: in “On the person”, save to a Lisbon trip folder. Then switch to “On the system”: a folder still has to be chosen, but now the app offers recent ones and nobody types a path.
                          
    
                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Three rules help you put complexity in the right place.
                          

                          

                          1Keep control within reach
                          Some complexity exists because people need the choice. One fixed export size works for sharing a photo but not for a print shop that needs the full size, and if the app hides that choice, people can’t finish the task at all. Keep the simple path as the default, and put the full controls in an advanced layer one click away.
                          

                          Try: export the photo for the print shop, which needs at least 3,000 px.
                          Export has one fixed size, 1080 px wide.
                          Export still takes one click, and Full size waits under More options.
                          

                          2Solve it once in the product
                          Some complexity lands on people only because the team didn’t handle it. A phone field that accepts one exact format makes every person reformat their number, often after an error. Accept the formats people type and tidy them up in the product, so the team does the work once.
                          

                          Try: type 07700 900 123 and press Save.
                          The field accepts only one format: +447700900123, with no spaces.
                          The field takes the number as typed and saves it as +44 7700 900123.
                          

                          3Test the simple version with real data
                          A simple flow often works only for the sample data it was built with. Real photos have odd names, other file types and huge sizes, and when those fail, the complexity comes back as error messages people can’t act on. Before you call a flow simple, try the messy cases: large files, unusual names, hundreds of items.
                          

                          Try: press Upload 4 files.
                          Upload was tested with one small sample photo, and three real files fail.
                          Upload was tested with real phone files: the HEIC photo becomes a JPG, the odd name works and the big video uploads in parts.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice which hard part each product carries for people, and where it still lets them take over.
                          
  
                          
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          

                          

                          


                          
  
                          
    
                          Cheat sheet
                          
    
                          When you hear this, try that
                          
  
                          
  
                          Start from what people say or do, pick the pattern, then check its trade-off before you build. Each pattern links to its entry.
                          
  
                          
    
                          
      
                          If people say…TryWatch for
                          
      
        
                          “There’s too much here.”Progressive disclosureHidden settings get forgotten
                          
        
                          “I don’t know what to pick.”Smart defaultsDefaults that are wrong for many
                          
        
                          “I just want it fast. Or good.”PresetsPresets that hide what they change
                          
        
                          “I’m scared to delete this.”UndoNeeds real history in the data model
                          
        
                          “What will this do?”PreviewA preview that differs from the result
                          
        
                          “I broke it. How do I go back?”Version historyHistory nobody can read
                          
        
                          “Did that click work?”Instant feedbackFeedback too fast to notice
                          
        
                          “Why is this so slow?”Optimistic UIFailures that roll back silently
                          
        
                          “Can I do something else meanwhile?”Background workPeople forgetting it’s still running
                          
        
                          “Where’s that command again?”Command paletteInvisible to newcomers
                          
        
                          “I know it’s in here somewhere.”Search with filtersFilters hiding results
                          
        
                          “I looked there and didn’t see it.”Labels in people’s wordsInternal names leaking into the UI
                          
        
                          “Where do I even start?”TemplatesAnchoring everyone to one way of working
                          
        
                          “How does this part work?”Contextual hintsHints piling up
                          
        
                          “Why won’t it accept that?”Constraints or forgiving inputBlocking valid edge cases, or guessing wrong
                          
        
                          “I lost my work.”AutosavePeople not trusting it
                          
        
                          “This is overwhelming.” / “This is too slow for me.”Layered interfaceTwo layers drifting apart
                          
        
                          “I do this a hundred times a day.”Keyboard shortcuts or customizationUndiscoverable shortcuts
                          
                                
    
                          
  
                          

                          


                          
  
                          Part 3
                          
  
                          Components
                          
  
                          The building blocks: what each one is for, where it breaks, and what to use instead.
                          

                          


                          
  
                          
    
                          Before you start
                          
    
                          Read every component as a promise
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          Every component makes a promise to the person using it, about three things.
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          Attention
                          How much it interrupts. A badge waits to be noticed. A dialog stops everything until it gets an answer.
                          
    
                          Lifetime
                          How long it stays. A toast is gone in seconds. A banner stays until the state behind it changes.
                          
    
                          Control
                          What people can do with it. A tooltip can only be read. A popover can hold buttons and fields.
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          How each entry reads
                          
    
                          Each component is a short article. It says what the component is for, with a demo. Then its forms, and the rules: each shows how the component breaks and what to do instead, with a demo you can switch between the two. Last, real products that use it.
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          The interruption ladder
                          
    
                          For anything the product needs to tell people, use the lowest step that still does the job. Each step up costs more attention, so it has to be worth more. Click a step to jump to it.
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          
      Inline messageNext to the thing
      BadgeWaits to be seen
      ToastSays it, then goes
      BannerStays while true
      DialogStops everything
    
                          
    
                          QuieterLouder
                          
  
                          

                          


                          
  
                          
    
                          Chapter 16
                          
    
                          Feedback & status
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          Feedback tells people whether an action worked. Match how noticeable it is to how much it matters: small confirmations stay quiet, problems stay until they’re fixed, and lasting states stay visible while they’re true.
                          
  
                          

  
                          
    
                          Inline message
                          

                          

                          An inline message is a short line of text right next to the thing it’s about. Most often it sits under a form field and says what’s wrong and how to fix it. It can also give a hint before people type, or point out a value that looks like a mistake.
                          

                          Where a banner is about the whole page or app, an inline message is about one field or one item, and it sits right beside it.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
                          Must be between 1 and 12.
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: type 4 and press Tab, then type 0. The message waits until you leave the field.
                          
    
                          
    


                          Forms
                          

                          Inline messages come in four kinds: a hint, an error, a warning and a success note. A hint is there before people type. The other three respond to what they typed, and only an error stops them from going on.
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep inline messages useful.
                          

                          

                          1Bring the problem to where people look
                          After a failed submit, the message often sits next to a field that has scrolled out of view, so people see nothing change near the button and press again or give up. Add a short summary at the top of the form that lists each problem, links to its field and gets focus when the form is sent.
                          

                          Try: press Place order and find out what went wrong.
                          The Email error appears out of view, above the button.
                          A summary at the top names the problem, links to Email and gets focus.
                          

                          2Give each field one next step
                          When every check adds its own red line, the form turns into a wall of errors: people can’t tell what to fix first, and several lines say the same thing. Show only the most useful message for each field. If something is still wrong after they fix it, the next message appears then.
                          

                          Try: press Create account, then fix the fields and try again.
                          Every failed check adds its own line, seven in all.
                          Each field shows one message: the next thing to fix.
                          

                          3Wait until people leave the field
                          An error that appears on the first key press tells people they’re wrong before they’ve finished, when they’re only not done yet. Check the value when they leave the field or send the form, and if a message is already showing, clear it as soon as the value is right.
                          

                          Try: type a few digits and press Tab, then finish the 10-digit number.
                          The error shows from the first digit.
                          The check runs when you leave the field, and the error clears as soon as the number is right.
                          

                          4Say what to do instead
                          “Invalid date” says that something is wrong, but not which date or why, so people guess and often change the wrong field. A good message names the field and the rule in plain words, and offers the fix as a button when it’s obvious.
                          

                          Try: press Search stays, then fix the dates.
                          The message says only “Invalid date.”
                          The message says “Check-out must be after check-in” and offers a button that sets a valid date.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Toast
                          

                          

                          A toast is a short message that appears near the edge of the screen after people do something. It confirms that the action worked, such as “Email archived”, and often offers Undo. It leaves on its own after a few seconds, and people can keep working while it’s there.
                          

                          Where a banner describes a state that lasts, like being offline, and stays until the state ends, a toast reports one moment and fades. So it can’t carry anything people must see.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
        Morning LightSlow RiverPaper Boats
      
                          
      
                          Try it: remove a song, then press Undo. Then show the error toast and look away for a few seconds.
                          
    
                          

                          Forms
                          

                          Toasts come in three common forms: a plain toast only confirms, a toast with Undo lets people reverse what they just did, and a progress toast reports a short task while it runs. All three leave on their own.
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Five rules keep toasts useful.
                          

                          

                          1Don’t put errors in a toast
                          A toast leaves after a few seconds, whether anyone read it or not, so people who looked away never learn that the photo didn’t upload. Put the error next to the file it’s about, or in a banner that lasts until the problem is solved, where it has room to explain the limit and offer a way forward.
                          

                          Try: press Upload photo.heic, then look away for three seconds.
                          The upload error is a toast that leaves after three seconds.
                          The error stays on photo.heic, with the size limit and a way to compress it.
                          

                          2Don’t make it the only way to act
                          When a toast holds the only Restart button, the button leaves with it, and people who miss it have no way left to finish the update. Put requests like this in a banner or a notification that stays until people choose, so “Later” is a real choice and not a missed chance.
                          

                          Try: press Check for updates, then wait.
                          The only Restart button is on a toast that leaves after four seconds.
                          A banner offers Restart and Later, and stays until you pick one.
                          

                          3Combine messages into one
                          When several things finish at once, each can fire its own toast, and they pile up, cover the page and repeat the same news. Use one toast that updates as things finish, such as “3 photos uploaded”, so people get one clear result and the page stays usable.
                          

                          Try: press Upload 3 photos.
                          Each photo gets its own toast, and three stack up.
                          One toast counts the uploads, then says “3 photos uploaded”.
                          

                          4Leave a trace that lasts
                          A toast only helps if people are looking when it appears. If the export finishes while they’re in another part of the app, they come back to no sign that it’s done. Also mark the result somewhere that waits, such as a badge on Files or an entry in a notifications list, where people find it whenever they look.
                          

                          Try: start the export, switch to Messages, and come back after 4 seconds.
                          A toast on Files is the only sign that the export is done.
                          A badge on Files and a Ready row in the list wait for you.
                          

                          5Offer Undo instead of asking first
