                          A confirm dialog on every delete gets clicked through without reading, as the Undo pattern explains. For actions that can be reversed, act right away and show a toast with Undo: it takes fewer clicks, and a mistake is one press to fix.
                          

                          Each delete asks “Delete this email?” first. Try: delete two emails.
                          Each delete happens at once, and a toast offers Undo. Try: delete two emails, then press Undo.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Banner
                          

                          

                          A banner is a strip across the top of an app or page. It describes a state that lasts and changes what people can do: they’re offline, the file is read-only, the trial is ending. It stays while the state lasts and leaves when it ends, where a toast reports one moment and fades.
                          


                          
      
                          
        
                          Packing list
                          
        
                          You’re offline. Changes are saved here and will sync when you reconnect.
                          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: turn “Online” off, then back on.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Banners come in three tones, set by how serious the state is: info, warning and error. The tone also decides whether people can close it. A fourth, smaller form covers only one part of a page.
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep banners useful.
                          

                          

                          1Use it only for what’s happening now
                          People learn fast what the top of the screen means. If a banner there always means “something is going on right now”, they read it. If it also carries news and offers, they learn to skip it, and then they skip the offline notice too. Put news somewhere people can open when they want, such as a “What’s new” entry.
                          

                          A Family plan offer takes the banner spot. Try: turn Online off. Which banner do you read first?
                          The offer waits behind What’s new, and the banner is kept for being offline. Try: open What’s new, then turn Online off.
                          

                          2Let information be closed
                          Some banners are only information, such as a tip or a note that this is a shared copy, and once read they’ve done their job. If they can’t be closed, they keep taking space and turn into a stripe people look past. Let people close them, and remember that they did.
                          

                          The tip can’t be closed. Try: press Open the next day a few times.
                          The tip can be closed, and it stays closed. Try: close the tip, then press Open the next day.
                          

                          3Show one at a time
                          Several states can be true at once: offline, read-only, a tip. Each banner is short, but stacked they push the page down, and people rarely read past the first. Show the most serious one and put the rest in a notifications list.
                          

                          Several banners stack up. Try: turn Online off. How much of the budget can you still see?
                          Only the most serious banner shows. The rest wait in a list behind it. Try: turn Online off, then press 2 more.
                          

                          4Don’t move the page
                          Like content that loads late, a banner that appears or leaves pushes everything below it, and a click aimed at a button lands on the wrong thing. Lay the banner over the top edge, or keep its space reserved, so nothing under the pointer moves.
                          

                          Try: press Send a few times while the banner comes and goes.
                          The banner pushes the chat down.
                          The banner lies over the top of the chat, so nothing moves.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Badge
                          

                          

                          A badge is a small mark on another item: a dot or a number on an icon, a tab or a button. It tells people at a glance that something there is new or needs them, like 3 unread messages or 1 update. It goes away once they’ve looked.
                          

                          Where a toast interrupts to say something just happened, then fades, a badge doesn’t interrupt. It waits on the item until people are ready to look.
                          

                          
      
                          
        3
      
                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          Try it: add 120 items and watch the badge cap at 99+, then empty the cart.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Badges come in four forms, set by what people need to know. A dot says only that something is new. A count says how many. A label names the kind of thing, like “New” or “Beta”. A status mark shows a live state, like who is online.
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep badges useful.
                          

                          

                          1Clear it once people look
                          A badge that still says 3 after someone has seen all 3 is out of date, so people stop trusting it and miss the next one that matters. Remove it as soon as they view what it points to, so a badge always means there’s something they haven’t seen yet.
                          

                          Try: open Shared, look at the photos, then go back to Library.
                          The badge on Shared stays after you’ve seen the photos.
                          The badge on Shared clears once you open it.
                          

                          2Badge only what needs attention
                          When every row has a bright number, none of them stands out, and people open folders one by one to find what changed. Keep badges for what’s new or needs action, and show totals as plain text next to the item, where they don’t compete.
                          

                          Try: find the folder with something new for you.
                          Every folder has a badge with its total.
                          Only Shared, which has something new, has a badge. The other totals are plain text.
                          

                          3Cap the number
                          A big number makes the badge wider than the icon it sits on and crowds the icons next to it. Past a point, nobody reads the exact number anyway: it just means “a lot”. Show “99+” instead, and put the exact count at the top of the list it opens.
                          

                          Try: press Get new mail a few times and watch the badge.
                          The badge shows the full count, 486 and climbing.
                          The badge stops at 99+, and the inbox shows the exact count.
                          

                          4Say what the number means
                          A red 3 on a gear could mean errors, warnings or updates, and red also reads as danger, so people either worry or ignore it. Put what it counts in the button’s label and a tooltip, like “3 updates available”, so people can decide whether to look now without opening anything.
                          

                          Try: guess what the 3 means, then point at the button or Tab to it.
                          A red 3 sits on an unlabeled gear.
                          The button says Settings, and its tooltip says “3 updates available”.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice that each badge stays small, and only shows a number when the number matters.
                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

                          


                          
  
                          
    
                          Chapter 17
                          
    
                          Loading & progress
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          Pick the indicator by how long the wait is: under 400 ms, show nothing; up to about ten seconds, a spinner; longer, real progress.
                          
  
                          

  
                          
    
                          Spinner
                          

                          

                          A spinner is a small turning circle that says “working on it”. It’s for short waits, up to about ten seconds: sending a message, loading search results, saving a change. It sits on the thing that’s busy.
                          

                          Where a spinner says only that work is happening, a progress bar also shows how much is done, so it’s the better choice for longer waits.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
                          Ready
                          
      
                          Try it: press both buttons. Only the slow load shows a spinner.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Spinners come in four forms, set by how much is waiting: in a button, inline next to a field, in one section, and over the full page. Use the smallest one that covers what’s loading, so the rest of the page stays usable.
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep spinners useful.
                          

                          

                          1Wait before showing it
                          When results come back in a fraction of a second, the spinner only blinks, which looks like a glitch and makes the app feel slower than it is. Hold it back for about 400 ms, so fast results just appear and a spinner means there’s a real wait.
                          

                          Try: press Lamps, Chairs and Mugs. Then turn on Slow network and try again.
                          The spinner shows at once, even when results take 0.3 s.
                          The spinner is held back, so 0.3 s results just appear.
                          

                          2Use a progress bar for long waits
                          A spinner can’t say how much is done or how long is left, so after a while people wonder if it’s stuck, and they cancel or reload. Once a wait can run past about ten seconds, show a progress bar and what’s happening, so people can choose to wait or go do something else.
                          

                          Try: press Upload video and wait. The clock runs 5× fast.
                          The 6.5 GB upload shows only a spinner for a whole minute.
                          A progress bar shows the percent, the GB sent and the time left.
                          

                          3Keep the rest of the app working
                          A spinner over the whole screen locks everything, even the parts that aren’t loading, so someone writing a reply has to stop and wait for a folder list. Put the spinner on the part that’s loading, so it shows what’s busy and everything else stays usable.
                          

                          Try: press Refresh, then try to keep typing your reply.
                          A spinner covers the whole mail app for four seconds.
                          Only the folder list spins, and the reply stays editable.
                          

                          4Hold the content’s space
                          A spinner is usually smaller than the content that replaces it, so the page jumps when the content arrives, like any content that loads late. Show a skeleton in the shape of the coming content instead, so nothing below it moves.
                          

                          Try: press Refresh and watch the Upload file button.
                          A small spinner stands in for the list, so Upload file jumps when the files arrive.
                          Skeleton rows hold the list’s space, so Upload file stays put.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Progress bar
                          

                          

                          A progress bar is a line that fills as long work gets done: an upload, a download, an export, a backup. It shows how far along the work is, and often what it’s doing and how much is left. Unlike a spinner, it lets people decide whether to wait or do something else.
                          


                          
      
                          
        
                          Beach day.mov to MP4
                          
        
                          
        
                          Not started0 of 30 seconds
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: press Start. The bar slides while the video is read, then fills as it converts. You can cancel at any point.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Progress bars come in four forms. A bar of known length fills as work gets done, and a bar of unknown length moves without filling. A small ring sits on one item in a list, and a background strip tracks long work while people do something else.
                          

                          
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep progress bars useful.
                          

                          

                          1Show stages when you can’t measure
                          Some work has nothing to count, so the bar sits at 0% and then jumps to done, and until then people can’t tell if it’s working or stuck. Use a moving bar to show it’s alive, with a label that names each stage as it starts, so people see it’s getting somewhere.
                          

                          Try: press Restore and wait.
                          The bar sits at 0% until the restore is done.
                          The bar moves, and a label names each stage: Checking files, Copying, Verifying.
                          

                          2Count real work
                          A bar that isn’t tied to real work often races ahead, then sits at 99% for most of the wait, so people think it froze and stop believing it. Move it by real units, like photos exported, and if one part can’t be counted, say so with a label like “Finishing up…”.
                          

                          Try: press Export album and watch the bar.
                          The bar races to 99%, then sits there.
                          The bar counts photos up to 30 of 30, then says “Finishing up…”.
                          

                          3Let people keep working
                          When an export locks the whole app, people can only sit and watch the bar, and if they change their mind, there’s no way to stop it. Run long work in a small strip, as background work, let people carry on, always offer Cancel, and tell them when it’s done.
                          

                          Try: press Export, then rename the video or pick a clip.
                          The export covers the editor until it’s done.
                          The export runs in a strip with Cancel, and the editor stays usable.
                          

                          4Put it on the item
                          A new file can look ready in the list while it’s still uploading, and a tiny bar in a corner goes unseen. Show progress on the item itself, where people are already looking, and add a summary, like an uploads count in the top bar.
                          

                          Try: press Upload trip-video.mov, then find out how far along it is.
                          The only progress is a tiny bar in the corner.
                          Progress shows on the file itself, and the top bar says “1 uploading”.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Skeleton
                          

                          

                          A skeleton is a gray outline of content that is still loading, with the same boxes and lines as the content that will replace it: a box for each photo, a bar for each line of text. When the content arrives, it drops into place and nothing moves. Unlike a spinner, which only says “wait”, it shows what is coming and where it will go.
                          


                          
      
                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
                          Try it: press Reload and watch whether the layout moves when the cards arrive. Then press Reload and fail.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Skeletons take the shape of what they stand in for. The common forms are a grid of tiles, a list of rows and a block of text. A fourth, smaller form holds the place of one value on a page that has already loaded.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep skeletons useful.
                          

                          

                          1Match the real layout
                          A skeleton is there to hold the space of content that loads late, so if its shape is wrong, the page still jumps when the content arrives. Give each placeholder the size and place of what will fill it, and if you can’t know the shape in advance, use a spinner instead.
                          

                          Try: press Reload and watch the Share album button when the photos arrive.
                          Three text lines stand in for a grid of photos.
                          A tile for each photo holds the grid’s space.
                          

                          2Skip it when loading is quick
                          When content arrives almost at once, a skeleton shows for only a split second, too short to read as loading, so people see a flicker and the app feels jumpy instead of fast. As with a spinner, wait about 400 ms before showing it, so fast content just appears.
                          

                          Try: switch between Playlists and Albums a few times.
                          The list loads in 0.15 s, and placeholders flash each time.
                          The list loads in 0.15 s and appears with no skeleton.
                          

                          3Replace it if loading fails
                          A skeleton tells people that content is on its way, so if loading fails and it stays, they keep waiting for something that will never come, then reload or give up without knowing why. As soon as loading fails, replace it with what went wrong and a way to try again.
                          

                          Try: wait a few seconds for the inbox.
                          Loading fails after two seconds, and the skeleton stays.
                          The skeleton gives way to an error that says what happened, with Retry.
                          

                          4Keep the motion calm
                          Fast shimmer on every part of the screen is tiring to look at, and it covers parts that are already known, like the account name, so nothing can be read until everything arrives. Show what you have at once and load the most important part next. Give only the parts still loading a slow, soft pulse, and stop it for people who turn off motion.
                          

                          Try: press Reload and notice what you can read first.
                          Everything shimmers fast, even the account name, until it all arrives.
                          The account name shows at once and the balance comes next. Only the rows still loading pulse, slowly, and not at all with reduced motion.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

                          


                          
  
                          
    
                          Chapter 18
                          
    
                          Overlays
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          Overlays sit on top of the page and close when you click away, so keep them small and never let them hold work people could lose.
                          
  
                          

  
                          
    
                          Tooltip
                          

                          

                          A tooltip is a small label that appears when people point at something or move to it with the keyboard. It answers a quick question, like what an icon button does. It goes away as soon as the pointer or focus moves on.
                          

                          Where a tooltip only adds a name or a short note, with nothing in it to click, a popover opens on a click, stays open and can hold buttons and links.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          Try it: hover the buttons, then press Tab to move through them with the keyboard.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Most tooltips name an icon button, and some also show its keyboard shortcut. Others explain a word in one short sentence, or show the full text of a name that is cut off. All of them hold a few words of plain text and nothing else.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep tooltips useful.
                          

                          

                          1Don’t rely on hover
                          Phones and tablets have no hover, so a tooltip there never appears, and people decide without the information, such as what an extra fee pays for. Put the text on the page where people can see it. If there isn’t room, add an info button that opens a popover when tapped, which works the same with a finger, a mouse or a keyboard.
                          

                          Try: tap (click) the info button next to Flexible ticket, then tap it again.
                          On a phone, tapping the info button shows nothing.
                          Tapping the info button opens a popover that explains the ticket.
                          

                          2Don’t hide what people must know
                          Most people never point at a small info icon, so if a warning hides there, they find out what the setting does only when their old messages are already gone. Put anything people need for a decision on the page, as helper text right under the choice.
                          

                          Try: set Disappearing messages to After 24 hours.
                          The warning hides in a tooltip on the info icon.
                          The warning sits under the setting as helper text.
                          

                          3Don’t put links or buttons in it
                          A tooltip closes as soon as the pointer moves off the icon, and the keyboard can’t move into it, so a link inside can be seen but not used. When the note needs a link, use a popover instead. It stays open until people close it, so they can reach the link with a mouse, a finger or the Tab key.
                          

                          Try: point at or click the info icon, then try to click Learn more, or reach it with Tab.
                          Learn more sits inside a tooltip.
                          Learn more sits in a popover that stays open until you close it.
                          

                          4Don’t repeat the label
                          A tooltip that repeats a visible label tells people nothing new, but it still pops up over nearby content, such as the price next to the button, and screen readers read the same words twice. If the label already says it, leave the tooltip out.
                          

                          Try: point at Add to cart, or Tab to it.
                          A tooltip on Add to cart says “Add to cart”.
                          No tooltip, and a screen reader says the label once.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice that tooltips only add a name or a detail, and that on touch screens the name has to be visible instead.
                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Popover
                          

                          

                          A popover is a small box that opens next to the button people pressed. It holds a few related controls or details, such as view options, a guest count or a contact card. It stays open until people click outside it, press Esc or press the button again.
                          

                          Unlike a tooltip, it opens on a click and can hold buttons, fields and links. Unlike a dialog, it doesn’t block the page behind it.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
                          
          
                          Map options
                          
          
          
          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: open it, change a setting, then click outside or press Esc. The change stays.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          The common forms are options, a picker, a details card and a tip. Options and pickers change something on the page, a details card shows more about a person or a link, and a tip points at something new once.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep popovers useful.
                          

                          

                          1Keep it to a few controls
                          A popover has room for only a few controls, so with seven fields in it, people scroll inside the box to find a field, then scroll again to find Save. When a task needs more fields than that, use a side panel or a page, where the fields can be grouped and Save stays in view.
                          

                          Try: click Team lunch, change the place to Mercado, then save.
                          The whole event form is squeezed into a small popover that scrolls.
                          The form opens in a side panel, with room for every field and Save in view.
                          

                          2Don’t lose work when it closes
                          People close popovers by clicking outside them, often without thinking, so if that also throws away what they typed, their work is gone without a word. Save each change the moment it’s made, so nothing is lost however the popover closes. If people need to review changes before they count, use a dialog with Save and Cancel instead.
                          

                          Try: press Rename, type a new name, then click outside the box.
                          Clicking outside closes the popover and drops the new name.
                          The new name applies as you type, so clicking outside keeps it.
                          

                          3Don’t open popovers from popovers
                          Each popover that opens another adds a layer on top, so people lose track of where they are, and one choice can close every layer at once. The next change then starts again from the first button. Put related choices side by side in one popover or panel, and apply them as people click.
                          

                          Try: make the title orange and large. Watch the click count.
                          Color and Size each open a second popover, and every pick closes them all.
                          Color and size sit side by side in one popover, and each pick applies at once.
                          

                          4Keep the result in view
                          When a popover covers what it changes, people adjust blind: they close it to see the result, then open it again to adjust some more. Place it beside the thing being changed, or, if there isn’t room, use a side panel and leave the thing itself in full view.
                          

                          Try: press Brightness and drag the slider.
                          The Brightness popover covers the photo.
                          The Brightness slider opens beside the photo, which stays in view.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Menu
                          

                          

                          A menu is a short list of commands that opens from a button. It holds actions people need now and then, like Rename, Duplicate or Delete, so they don’t crowd the screen. Picking an item runs it and closes the menu.
                          

                          Where a select fills in a value, like a size or a country, and the field keeps showing that value, a menu runs a command, and then it’s gone.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
                          Road trip mixPlaylist · 24 songs
                          
        
                          
          
          
                          
            
            
            
            
                          
            
          
                          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: open the menu with a click, or Tab to it and press Enter. Use the arrow keys to move and Esc to close.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Most menus open from a button: a “More” button with three dots, or a button with a name like Sort, which may let people pick one setting. A context menu opens when people right-click or long-press an item, and a menu bar along the top of a window holds all of an app’s commands.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep menus useful.
                          

                          

                          1Keep it short
                          In a menu of more than about a dozen items, people have to read every item to find the one they want, and if it’s out of view at the bottom, they scroll past it or give up. Split the list into small groups with the common actions on top. Move rare actions out, or let people type a few letters to find them. Very large sets need a command palette.
                          

                          Twenty commands in one list, with Copy link near the bottom. Try: open the ⋯ menu and copy the file’s link.
                          The same commands in small groups with dividers, and typing filters the list. Try: open the ⋯ menu and copy the link. Then open it again and type “col”.
                          

                          2Keep the main action in view
                          Every trip into a menu costs a click and a search. That is fine for rare actions, but for the action people take most, like Reply in email, they pay it every time. Give the one or two most used actions their own buttons, and keep the menu for the rest.
                          

                          Try: reply to Lena. Watch the click count.
                          Reply is hidden in the ⋯ menu with six other actions.
                          Reply has its own button, and the menu keeps the rarer actions.
                          

                          3Put options to compare on the page
                          A menu shows names only, and only while it’s open, so to compare prices or dates, people open it again and again and keep the numbers in their head. When options differ in price, time or size, lay them out on the page with those details, for example as radio buttons or cards, so people can compare them in one look.
                          

                          Try: find the cheapest delivery that arrives by Wednesday.
                          Delivery options sit in a menu, and each one’s price and date show only after you pick it.
                          Every delivery option is on the page with its price and date.
                          

                          4Don’t nest submenus
                          Each submenu opens on hover and switches when the pointer slips onto a neighbor, so people retrace their steps or pick the wrong item without noticing. Keep a menu to one level, two at most. When a choice needs more steps, open a dialog that shows every option at once and has room to explain them.
                          

                          Try: open File and download the whole document as a Word file.
                          Download opens a submenu, which opens another.
                          Download… opens a dialog that shows every choice at once.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice that the most common actions stay in view, the rest wait in a short grouped list, and very large sets get a search.
                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

                          


                          
  
                          
    
                          Chapter 19
                          
    
                          Dialogs & panels
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          A dialog blocks the page until people answer. A side panel usually leaves the page usable, and only its modal form blocks it. Block the page only for a decision or task that has to come first.
                          
  
                          

  
                          
    
                          Dialog
                          

                          

                          A dialog is a box that opens over the page and asks the person something. The page behind it is dimmed and can’t be used until they answer. Use it for a decision they have to make before they go on, such as deleting something for good.
                          

                          A popover also opens over the page, but a click anywhere else closes it.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
        
                          
          
                          
            
                          Delete 3 notes?
                          
            
                          Grocery list, Book ideas and Gift list will be deleted. You can’t undo this.
                          
          
                          
          
                          
            
            
          
                          
        
                          
                                
      
                          Try it: press Delete 3 notes, then Archive 3 notes. Delete can’t be undone, so it asks first, says exactly what will go and labels the button with the action. Archive just happens and offers Undo.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Dialogs come in four common forms, set by what they ask for: a confirmation, a choice about unsaved work, a short form and a notice. They differ in how many buttons they have and which button gets focus first.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Five rules keep dialogs useful.
                          

                          

                          1Don’t use it for news
                          People open an app to do something, like read their mail, so a box with news or a tip stands in their way, and most close it without reading. Put the news where people can open it when they want, such as a “What’s new” entry or a short note they can close. They can read it now, later or never, and the mail works right away.
                          

                          Try: open the email from Sam.
                          A “What’s new” dialog opens over the inbox.
                          A short note above the inbox links to What’s new and can be closed.
                          

                          2Offer Undo instead of asking
                          If every action asks “Are you sure?”, people learn to press OK without reading, so the one time it matters, the dialog doesn’t protect them. Let actions that can be undone happen at once, and offer Undo. Keep the dialog for the rare action that can’t be undone, and say what will be lost.
                          

                          Archive and Delete both ask “Are you sure?” first. Try: archive two chats, then delete one. Count the clicks.
                          Archive happens at once and offers Undo. Delete still asks, says what will be lost and says “Delete chat” on the button. Try: archive two chats and press Undo once. Then delete one.
                          

                          3Give long tasks a page or a panel
                          A dialog is a small box that covers the page, so a long form inside it hides what people need to look at, like the chart behind it. To check a number they have to close the dialog, and they lose what they typed. A page or a side panel gives them room to scroll and look things up, and keeps what they entered.
                          

                          Try: press Edit report and set an alert just below the slowest day on the chart.
                          The report settings open in a dialog that covers the chart.
                          The report settings open in a side panel, and the chart stays in view.
                          

                          4Name the action on each button
                          “OK” and “Cancel” don’t say what will happen. When someone leaves a photo they were cropping, “Cancel” could mean cancel the crop or cancel leaving, so people have to read the whole question, and many guess wrong. When each button names its action, the buttons alone answer the question, and the one that throws work away stands out.
                          

                          Try: press ← Photos, then pick the button that keeps your crop. Read only the buttons.
                          The buttons say “OK” and “Cancel”, and OK has focus.
                          The buttons say “Keep editing” and “Discard crop”, and Keep editing has focus.
                          

                          5Don’t open it on load
                          A dialog that opens with the app stands between people and what they came for. They haven’t done anything yet, so they close it unread. Ask at the moment it matters, like after they press Download, when the question is about what they just asked for and they read it.
                          

                          Try: press Reset to open the app again, play Road trip, then press Download.
                          A “Rate us 5 stars” dialog opens as soon as the app does.
                          Nothing opens at start. Download asks about mobile data when you press it.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice which actions get a dialog at all, and that the buttons say what will happen.
                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Side panel
                          

                          

                          A side panel opens along the left or right edge of the screen. It holds a second task next to the main view, such as comments on a doc, the details of a photo or search filters. In most forms, people can keep using the main view while it’s open.
                          

                          Unlike a dialog, it shares the screen, so people can look at both and move between them.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
                          Meal plan
                          
        
                          Pasta bakeTacosLentil stew
                          
        
                          
          
          
                          
            
            
            
            
            
          
                          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: open Recipes and add a few meals while you watch the meal plan.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Side panels come in three forms, which differ in what happens to the page: a docked panel makes it narrower, an overlay panel covers its edge, and a modal panel dims it and blocks it.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep side panels useful.
                          

                          

                          1Give the main task the full width
                          A panel is narrow, which is fine for a side task. When the task in it becomes the main job, like writing a long reply, lines wrap every few words and the draft is hard to read back. Give that task a full page or a mode of its own, with a clear way back.
                          

                          Try: press Reply and keep writing the email.
                          The reply opens in a narrow panel beside the inbox.
                          The reply opens full width, with a way back to the inbox.
                          

                          2Use the whole screen on phones
                          On a phone, a side panel takes half the screen, so the page next to it shrinks to a sliver and neither half is big enough to use. Let the panel cover the whole screen while people choose, with a clear Close or Back. When they’re done, the page comes back at full size.
                          

                          Try: press Filters and pick size M.
                          On a phone, the filter panel squeezes the shoes into a sliver.
                          The filters cover the whole screen, with Close and Show results.
                          

                          3Keep one panel per side
                          Each panel takes another slice of the screen, so with three open, the document people are editing becomes a thin strip. Allow one panel on each side, and use tabs inside it for the rest. Switching tabs changes what’s in the panel, and the document keeps its room.
                          

                          Try: open Comments and History too.
                          Outline, Comments and History each open their own panel beside the doc.
                          Outline, Comments and History take turns in one panel.
                          

                          4Don’t dim a page people still use
                          A dimmed page tells people it’s off-limits, so they don’t think to click the photos behind the panel, and if they do, the click only closes it. If the page is meant to stay usable, keep it bright and clickable, so picking another photo updates the panel in place.
                          

                          Try: with Info open, pick another photo.
                          The Info panel dims the photos, and clicking one closes the panel.
                          The photos stay bright, and picking another updates the panel.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          Notice that the main view stays visible and usable while the panel is open, and what changes when space runs out.
                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

                          


                          
  
                          
    
                          Chapter 20
                          
    
                          Inputs
                          
  
                          
  
                          
    
                          Pick an input by the decision: does it apply right away or on Save, how many options are there, and does the exact value matter?
                          
  
                          

  
                          
    
                          Switch
                          

                          

                          A switch turns one setting on or off. The change takes effect the moment it’s flipped, with nothing to save, so people expect to see the result at once.
                          

                          That is what separates it from a checkbox, which marks a choice in a form and does nothing until people press Save or Submit.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: flip each switch and watch the preview.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Switches come in four common forms. Most sit in a settings list, one per row, and some add a line that explains the setting. One switch can also turn a whole group of settings on or off, and in a toolbar a switch changes how the page is shown.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep switches useful.
                          

                          

                          1Don’t use it in a form with Save
                          A switch slides to On at once, so the setting looks done. In a form that still needs Save, people leave without pressing it, and the change is lost. Use a checkbox there, because it reads as a choice that waits for Save.
                          

                          Switches sit in a form that still needs Save. Try: turn on Weekly summary, then press ← Inbox as if you’re done.
                          The same form uses checkboxes. Try: check Weekly summary, then press Save.
                          

                          2Name the setting and show its state
                          A label like “Turn off emails” reads as a command, and with the switch off it becomes a double negative. A vague label like “Notifications” doesn’t say which kind. Either way, people have to puzzle out what’s on, and many get it wrong. Name one setting per row, and write “On” or “Off” next to the switch, so the answer doesn’t depend on color.
                          

                          Try: answer the question using only the settings.
                          “Notifications” and “Turn off emails”, with no state in words.
                          Each row names one setting, like “Email me when someone comments”, and shows “On” or “Off”.
                          

                          3Show what really happened
                          Some changes take time or can fail, like turning on backup while the phone is offline. If the switch says On at once, people trust it and find out when a photo is lost. Show a small busy state while the change runs, and if it fails, flip the switch back and say why.
                          

                          Try: turn on Back up photos and wait a few seconds.
                          The switch says On at once, though the phone is offline.
                          The switch shows it’s busy, then flips back and says why.
                          

                          4Use it only for on and off
                          A switch has two positions. When a setting has three choices, “Off” could mean either of the others, and one of them can’t be reached at all, which people only find out by flipping it. Use a segmented control or a radio group, so every choice is in view with its name.
                          

                          Try: set streaming to use the least mobile data.
                          One “High quality” switch covers three choices, and Low can’t be reached.
                          Low, Normal and High each have a segment.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Checkbox
                          

                          

                          A checkbox marks a yes or no choice. In a group, people can check any number of boxes, from none to all, and nothing happens until they press a button such as Save or Place order.
                          

                          That separates it from a switch, which acts the moment it’s flipped, and from radio buttons, which allow only one choice in a group.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
                          Export your data
                          
        
        
        
        
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: check and clear single items, and watch “Select all” show a mixed state when only some are checked.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Checkboxes come in four common forms: a single box, a group, a card and a box on each row of a list. They differ in how many choices there are and which button acts on them.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep checkboxes useful.
                          

                          

                          1Use radio buttons for one choice
                          Square boxes say “pick any”, so when only one option is allowed, checking a second one leaves the first checked too, and people learn the rule only when the next step shows an error. Radio buttons say “pick one”, and choosing one clears the other by itself.
                          

                          Try: switch delivery to Express, then press Continue.
                          Delivery options are checkboxes, so two can be checked.
                          Delivery options are radio buttons.
                          

                          2Use a switch when it applies now
                          Checkboxes usually wait for a Save or Done button, so when a change happens at once with no button, people aren’t sure it worked. Use a switch there, with “On” next to it to confirm the change.
                          

                          Try: turn on Do not disturb. Is it on now, or is there a Save step?
                          Do not disturb is a checkbox that acts at once, with no Save button.
                          Do not disturb is a switch, with “On” or “Off” next to it.
                          

                          3Make checked mean yes
                          With a label like “Don’t send me updates”, people have to leave the box empty to say yes, so people who skim see “send me updates”, check it, and get the opposite. Write the label as the thing they can choose, like “Send me updates”, so checking the box gives them what they want.
                          

                          Try: you want updates by email. Set the box, then press Create account.
                          The box says “Don’t send me updates”.
                          The box says “Send me updates”.
                          

                          4Add search and Select all to long lists
                          In a long list, people have to scroll and read every name to find the ones they want, which is slow and makes it easy to miss one. A search box cuts the list down, and Select all checks what’s left in one click. When only some are checked, Select all shows a dash.
                          

                          30 names, with no search. Try: invite the four people named Alex.
                          A search box, and a Select all for the names that are left. Try: search for alex, then use Select all.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Radio group
                          

                          

                          A radio group is a short list of options where people pick exactly one. Every option is visible, so people can compare them before they choose, and picking one clears the one picked before.
                          

                          Its round buttons say “pick one”, where checkboxes allow any number.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
                          
          Save screenshots as
          
          
          
        
                          
      
                          
      
                          Try it: use the arrow keys inside the group, and read the short line under each format.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Most radio groups are a stacked list. Two or three short options can sit side by side on one line. When each option needs a price or a detail, the options become cards. Picking one option can also open a follow-up field, such as “Tell us more”.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Four rules keep radio groups useful.
                          

                          

                          1Keep it to a few options
                          Past about six options, the group becomes a long column: people read down it to find their country, and the Continue button ends up far below. A field that filters as people type, or a select, keeps the form short, and a few typed letters bring up the right answer.
                          

                          Every country is a radio button in one long column. Try: find Portugal, then press Continue.
                          The country field filters as you type. Try: type “por”, pick Portugal, then press Continue.
                          

                          2Preselect the safe choice
                          With nothing picked, people can’t tell if they have to answer. If they skip it, the app has to choose for them, and it may pick the least safe option, like sharing the file with anyone who has the link. Pick the safest common option up front, so skipping still gives a safe result, and if no option is safe, leave it empty and ask for an answer.
                          

                          Try: press Copy link without picking anything.
                          No option is picked.
                          Only me, the safest choice, is picked from the start.
                          

                          3Make long options easy to compare
                          When each option is a long sentence, the price, the billing and the rules run together, and people have to read every word to see how two plans differ. Turn each option into a card, with the name and the one fact people compare first, and the details on a short line below.
                          

                          Try: pick the plan that costs the least per month.
                          Each plan is one long sentence.
                          Each plan is a card with its name, its price a month and one short line.
                          

                          4Don’t use it to switch views
                          Radio buttons look like a form setting, so people expect to press Save before anything changes, and a calendar that jumps to Month the moment they click doesn’t match that. Stacked in a column, the buttons also push the calendar down. For a view that changes at once, use a segmented control in the toolbar, like other calendar apps.
                          

                          Try: switch the calendar to Month.
                          Day, Week and Month are radio buttons above the calendar.
                          Day, Week and Month are a segmented control in the toolbar.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Segmented control
                          

                          

                          A segmented control is a row of two to five buttons joined into one. Exactly one segment is on, and picking another changes the view or mode right away, with no Save button.
                          

                          That is what separates it from tabs, which move between different content, like Overview and Reviews. A segmented control shows the same content in another way, like a day, a week or a month of the same calendar.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          Showing 312 songs
                          
      
                          Try it: pick each segment and watch the line below it.
                          
    
                          
    

                          Forms
                          

                          Most segmented controls use short text labels, and well-known views can use icons instead. On a phone, the control often spans the full width under the page title. With exactly two options, it works like a switch that names both sides.
                          

                          
  
  
                          
    
    
    
    
  
                          
  
                          
  
                          
  

                          

                          Rules
                          

                          Three rules keep segmented controls useful.
                          

                          

                          1Keep it to a few short labels
                          Long labels or more than five options don’t fit on one line, so the control wraps into a block of buttons that is hard to scan and no longer looks like one switch. Use tabs for views like these, because they stay on one line and scroll sideways. For a value rather than a view, use a select.
                          

                          Try: open Connected apps.
                          Six long section names wrap into a block.
                          The six sections are tabs in one row that scrolls sideways.
                          

                          2Use it only for changes that apply at once
                          People expect a segmented control to take effect the moment they click it, so if the choice waits for a Save button, they leave and the change is lost. When a choice needs saving, use a radio group, which reads as part of a form.
                          

                          The segments set a value that needs Save. Try: pick Only me, then press Back.
                          The same choice as radio buttons, above Save. Try: pick Only me, press Save, then press Back.
                          

                          3Make the selected segment stand out
                          The selected segment is the only thing that tells people what they’re looking at. With a faint tint, they can’t tell if the chart shows a day, a week or a month, and on a dim screen or in bright light the tint disappears. Give the selected segment a solid fill and bold text, so it reads at a glance.
                          

                          Try: switch the range a few times. Which one is the chart showing?
                          The selected range has a faint tint.
                          The selected range has a solid fill and bold text.
                          


                          

                          In real products
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
      
                          
      
                          
      
                          
      
      
    
                          

                          

                          

  
                          
    
                          Select & combobox
                          

                          

                          A select shows the current choice in a closed field, and people open it to see the list and pick one option. A combobox adds a text field, so people can type to narrow a long list down.
                          

                          Where a radio group shows every option all the time, a select hides them until it’s opened, which saves space but costs a click and makes options hard to compare.
                          

                          
      
                          
        
        
        
        
                            
      
                            
      
                            No file selected
                            
      
                            Try it: type “por” to filter, use the arrow keys, and press Enter. Recent files come first, then folders.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            There are four common forms. A plain select opens a short list. A combobox adds typing to filter a long list. A multi-select lets people pick several. An autocomplete suggests answers but also accepts text that isn’t in the list.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep selects and comboboxes useful.
                            

                            

                            1Show short lists in full
                            With only a few options, a dropdown hides them for no reason, and every change takes two clicks. Show them as a segmented control or a radio group, so they’re all in view and a change takes one click.
                            

                            Try: set the priority to Urgent, then back to Normal.
                            Four priorities hide in a dropdown.
                            The four priorities sit in a segmented control.
                            

                            2Make long lists searchable
                            In a long list, people scroll through the whole alphabet to find one name, which is slow and makes it easy to scroll past the one they want. Let people type a few letters to filter. Put the items they use most at the top and group the rest, so common picks are one click away.
                            

                            Every font sits in one long list. Try: change the font to Roboto.
                            A search box, with recent fonts above all the others. Try: change the font to Roboto. Then try typing “mono”.
                            

                            3Show previews when looks matter
                            Some options differ in how they look, like themes or photo filters. A name like Atlas or Juno says nothing about that, so people open the list again and again to try each one. Use a gallery or a panel that shows a small preview of each option, so people can compare them side by side and pick once.
                            

                            Try: find the green theme.
                            Themes are listed by name only.
                            Each theme shows a small preview.
                            

                            4Let people pick several when they need to
                            A single-choice list replaces the old pick without saying so: someone adds a second person, the first one drops off, and they find out only when that person never gets the email. When people may pick several, use checkboxes, or a multi-select that keeps every pick in view.
                            

                            The To field holds one person at a time. Try: send the email to both Sam Lee and Priya Nair.
                            Each person becomes a chip with its own remove button. Try: add Sam Lee and Priya Nair, then remove one.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice how each product fits the control to the choice: a filter for long lists, previews when looks matter, chips for several picks, and an open list when people compare.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Slider + number field
                            

                            

                            A slider sets a value by dragging a handle along a track. The track shows the whole range, so people see where the value sits between the lowest and the highest. Dragging is quick, but it’s hard to land on one exact number.
                            

                            A number field is the opposite: exact, but it doesn’t show the range, and people can’t try values by feel. Many settings show both, side by side.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                            
        
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: set Minutes to exactly 37 with only the slider, then type it in the field. The two stay in sync.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Sliders differ in what they let people set. A plain slider moves smoothly. Adding a number field makes it exact. A range slider has two handles for a minimum and a maximum. A stepped slider snaps to a few fixed values.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep sliders useful.
                            

                            

                            1Let people type the exact value
                            When the range has more values than the track has pixels, one pixel covers several values, so landing on exactly 37 takes many tries, and with a finger it’s worse. Put a number field next to the slider, so people can drag to get close and type the exact value.
                            

                            Seats from 1 to 300 can only be set by dragging. Try: drag the slider to exactly 37 seats.
                            A number field sits next to the slider. Try: type 37, or drag close and fix it in the field.
                            

                            2Spread out a huge range
                            On a straight track from $1 to $10,000, all the small amounts share the first few pixels, so setting $50 by dragging is nearly impossible. Use a number field, or a slider where $1 to $10, $10 to $100 and so on each get the same room, with a field beside it for any exact amount.
                            

                            A straight track from $1 to $10,000. Try: set the alert to $50 by dragging.
                            $1, $10, $100, $1k and $10k sit evenly along the track, with a field beside it. Try: drag to $50, or type 50 in the field.
                            

                            3Make the handle easy to grab
                            A tiny handle is hard to hit with a mouse, and a finger covers it completely. If clicking the track does nothing and the keyboard can’t reach it, some people can’t set the value at all. Make the handle and its hit area bigger, let a click on the track move it there, and let arrow keys move it too, with Shift for bigger steps.
                            

                            Try: set the volume to about 80%. Then try clicking the track, and Tab with the arrow keys.
                            A tiny handle. Clicking the track or pressing keys does nothing.
                            A bigger handle. Clicking the track or pressing the arrow keys moves it, and Shift takes bigger steps.
                            

                            4Show what the value does
                            When only a number changes, people can’t tell if higher is stricter or looser, so they guess or leave it alone. Label both ends with what they mean, and show the effect while people drag, like which emails would go to Spam.
                            

                            Try: move the slider. Does a higher number catch more spam, or less?
