                            Only a number from 1 to 10 changes.
                            The ends say “Let more through” and “Catch more”, and five emails show where they’d go.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice how each product pairs dragging with something exact or something you can see: a typed number, a live result, or a preview of where you’ll land.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Text field
                            

                            

                            A text field is a box where people type their own words: a name, an address, a message, a search. A label above it says what goes in, and hints and errors appear below it.
                            

                            That is what separates it from a picker, which offers only valid values, like the days on a calendar. A text field accepts anything people type, so it has to say what it expects and help when the text doesn’t fit.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
        Shown in your photo library and on shared links.
        
        
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: leave the field as it is, press Tab and read the message. Then clear it and press Tab again.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Text fields come in four common forms, set by what people type. A single line holds a short value, like a name or an email. A multi-line box holds longer text, like a message. Search and password fields are single lines with a control of their own.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep text fields useful.
                            

                            

                            1Say back what you understood
                            Some values can be written in more than one way: “12/11” is 11 December in the US and 12 November in most other places. If the field guesses without saying so, people find out at the hotel desk. Use a picker for values like this, or read the typed text back in words and ask when it could mean two things.
                            

                            The field reads the date its own way and doesn’t say how. Try: type 12/11, meaning 11 December, then press Search hotels.
                            The field reads the date back in words, and asks when it could be two days. Try: type 12/11, pick the date you mean, then press Search hotels. Try 25/12 too.
                            

                            2Keep the label visible
                            A placeholder disappears as soon as there’s text in the field, and after that nothing on screen says what the field is for. People can’t check a filled form without clearing it, so a value in the wrong field gets through. Put the label above the field, where it stays while people type.
                            

                            Try: press Use saved address. Two values went into the wrong fields. Find and fix them.
                            Placeholders stand in for the labels.
                            Each field has its label above it.
                            

                            3Show long text in full
                            In a small fixed box, people only see a slice of what they wrote, so they can’t reread it before they post. If typing also stops at a hidden limit, the end of their text is lost. Use a box that grows as they write, and show a count when there is a limit.
                            

                            Try: click the review and add a sentence at the end. Then try to read the whole review.
                            The review sits in a one-line box with a hidden limit.
                            The box grows with the text and counts toward its 160-character limit.
                            

                            4Say how to fix it
                            “Invalid username” has the same problem as a bare “Invalid date”: people can’t tell whether it’s the dot, the length or a name someone else has, so they change things at random. Say what’s wrong in plain words and offer a value that works, one click away.
                            

                            The error says only “Invalid username.” Try: press Create account. Then try to work out what to change.
                            The error says “That username is taken. Try ‘maya.lee2’.” and offers a button to use it. Try: press Create account, then use the suggestion.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice how each field fits the text it holds: a label that stays, a box that grows, a count near the limit, and the value shown back the way it will be saved.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Structured picker
                            

                            

                            A structured picker lets people enter a value with a set format by pointing at it: a day on a calendar, a time from a list, a color from a row of swatches. Every value it offers is valid, so people can’t enter a date that doesn’t exist or a color the app can’t use.
                            

                            Where a text field takes any text and checks it afterwards, a picker shows the possible values up front, so people choose one instead of remembering the format.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                            
          
          
                            
          
                            
        
                            
        
                            
          
          
        
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: pick a color, click a swatch, or type a hex code, and watch the other two follow.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Pickers take the shape of the value they hold. A calendar picks one date, and a range calendar picks a start and an end. Times often come as a set of slots. Colors from a short list come as swatches.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Three rules keep pickers useful.
                            

                            

                            1Let people type too
                            A calendar is quick for a date next week, but slow for a date people know by heart, like a birthday: March 1988 is hundreds of clicks back. Put a text field next to the picker and accept the common ways of writing the value. The picker follows what people type, so they can still check it or click instead.
                            

                            The date of birth can only be clicked on a calendar. Try: set the date of birth to 14 March 1988. Count the clicks.
                            A text field above the calendar takes the date as typed. Try: type 14 Mar 1988 (or 1988-03-14) into the field.
                            

                            2Show every allowed value
                            Sometimes only a few values are allowed, like the 8 colors a calendar keeps for events. A free color strip suggests that any color will do, so people pick one, save, and get a different one with no reason given. Show the allowed values as swatches, chips or radio buttons, so what people pick is what they get.
                            

                            Try: pick a color, press Save, and compare the event with what you picked.
                            A free color strip, though only 8 colors can be saved.
                            The 8 allowed colors are swatches, with the picked one named.
                            

                            3Put the context in the picker
                            A bare calendar doesn’t say which day is today, so to pick “a week from now”, people have to work out today’s date and count squares. Mark today in the calendar, offer presets for the usual choices, like “In 7 days”, and spell out the result in words, so people can check it before they move on.
                            

                            Try: make the link expire one week from today.
                            A bare calendar, with today unmarked.
                            Today is marked, presets offer 1, 7 or 30 days, and the result shows in words.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice how each picker gives a fast path for the common case and a way to be exact: presets, context inside the calendar, or plain typing.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

                            


                            
  
                            
    
                            Chapter 21
                            
    
                            Actions
                            
  
                            
  
                            
    
                            The most prominent button should be the main thing to do on that screen, and there should be only one.
                            
  
                            

  
                            
    
                            Button hierarchy
                            

                            

                            A button starts an action: save, send, pay, delete. Its style shows how important that action is, so people can find the main step without reading every label.
                            

                            That is what separates it from a link, which takes people to another page or place. A button does something where they are.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
        
        
        
      
                            
      
                            
        
        vs
        
      
                            
      
                            Click a button to see its role
                            
      
                            Try it: the disabled Play can’t tell you why it’s disabled. The enabled one explains what’s missing when you press it.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Buttons come in three styles, set by how important the action is: primary, secondary and tertiary. A fourth, destructive style marks actions that delete or lose something.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep buttons useful.
                            

                            

                            1Keep one primary button
                            When two buttons are filled, neither one stands out, and people have to read both labels before they know which one takes them forward. Give each screen or dialog one filled button for the main step, and make the others secondary or tertiary, so they’re still there but quieter.
                            

                            Try: glance at the cart for one second. Which button finishes the order?
                            Continue shopping and Check out are both filled.
                            Only Check out is filled. Continue shopping is plain text.
                            

                            2Say what the button does
                            As with dialog buttons, OK, Yes and Cancel only make sense next to the question: during an upload, “Cancel” could mean stop the upload or close the question. Use a verb and an object, like “Stop upload”, so each button makes sense on its own.
                            

                            Try: press Upload 3 photos, then stop the upload.
                            The buttons say “Cancel”, then “Cancel” and “OK”.
                            The buttons say “Stop upload”, then “Keep uploading” and “Stop upload”.
                            

                            3Set the risky action apart
                            People press familiar buttons by habit, often by where they sit, so if Delete looks like Save and sits where Save usually goes, one quick click removes a folder and all its files. Make the destructive button red and move it away from the main button’s spot. Where you can, let people undo it instead of asking them to be careful.
                            

                            Delete folder is filled like Save, in the last spot. Try: rename the folder to “Q3 final” and save it. Go fast, the way you would at work.
                            Delete folder has a red outline, sits at the far left and offers Undo. Try: rename the folder and save it. Then press Delete folder and use Undo.
                            

                            4Explain why it won’t work
                            A grayed-out button shows that something is missing, but not what, and when every field looks filled in, people recheck the whole form or give up. Keep the button enabled, and when it’s pressed, say what’s missing and move the cursor there. Or show the reason next to the button before it’s pressed.
                            

                            Book table is grayed out, with no reason given. Try: press Book table. Then try to work out why it won’t go.
                            Book table stays enabled. Pressing it says the phone number needs 9 digits and puts the cursor there. Try: press Book table, then follow the message.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice how each screen has one strong action, and how the risky one is set apart and named for what it does.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Icon button
                            

                            

                            An icon button is a button that shows a small picture instead of a word: a magnifier for search, an × to close, a heart to like. It fits in tight spaces like toolbars and photo overlays, and suits actions people use again and again.
                            

                            That is what separates it from a button with a label. A word can be read the first time, but an icon has to be recognized, so it only works for actions people already know or quickly learn.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
        
        
      
                            
      
                            
        
      
                            
      
                            Try it: guess what each icon does, then hover the third one. Below the row, the same action has a label.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Icon buttons come in four common forms. Plain ones sit in a toolbar and do one thing each. Toggles stay on or off, like bold or mute. A floating button holds the main action on a phone screen, and a More button opens a list of the actions that don’t fit.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Three rules keep icon buttons useful.
                            

                            

                            1Label icons people don’t know
                            Only a few icons mean the same thing to everyone, like search, close, settings and home. Most others, like crop, could mean several things, so people click around to find out, and some never find the right one. Give those buttons a word, and keep bare icons for the few that everyone knows.
                            

                            Layers, Adjust and Crop are bare icons. Try: crop the photo. Count your tries.
                            Each tool has a word next to its icon. Try: crop the photo.
                            

                            2Keep the row short
                            In a row of ten look-alike icons, every action gets the same weight, so people hover them one by one to find the one they want. Group related icons, give the main action a word, and move rare actions into a More menu, so there is less to scan.
                            

                            Ten bare icons in one row. Try: save a copy of the file. Watch how many buttons you check first.
                            The zoom icons form a group, Save a copy has a word, and five rare actions wait in More. Try: save a copy of the file. Then open More to see the rare actions.
                            

                            3Make them big enough to hit
                            A 16 px button is smaller than a fingertip, and with no gap between buttons, one tap covers all three, so people hit Close when they meant Add. Make each button at least 24 px (the WCAG 2.2 minimum), ideally 40 to 44 px, with space between, and keep Close a little apart from the rest.
                            

                            Try: move the pointer over the player and press + to add the song. The circle is about the size of a fingertip.
                            Three 16 px buttons with no gap.
                            Three 40 px buttons, 8 px apart.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice which icons stand alone and which get help: a label, a tooltip with the shortcut, or a menu with words.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Link vs button
                            

                            

                            Links and buttons are both things people click, but they do different jobs. A link takes people to another page or place. A button does something where they are: it saves, sends, adds or deletes.
                            

                            The difference matters because browsers treat them differently: a link has an address, so people can open it in a new tab, bookmark it and come back with Back, and a button has none of that. So choose by what happens on click, not by how it should look.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                            Carry-on bags must fit in the overhead bin. Read the bag rules.
                            
        
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: press Add a bag, then click Read the bag rules, which takes you to the start of this book.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Each comes in a few forms. A link can sit inside a sentence or stand on its own, and a button can be a full button or a lighter text button. A link can also look like a button when it’s the main next step: the look follows how important it is, but whether it’s a link or a button still follows what it does.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Three rules keep links and buttons clear.
                            

                            

                            1Use a button when something changes
                            People open links in a new tab just to look, so if a link deletes or sends something, opening it is enough to do it, with no warning and no way back. A button tells people that pressing it does something, so they press it on purpose. Put Undo next to the result to cover a slip.
                            

                            Try: Ctrl-click (⌘-click on Mac) Edit to open it in a new tab. Then do the same with Delete.
                            Delete is a link, like Edit.
                            Delete is a button that offers Undo. Edit stays a link.
                            

                            2Use a link to go somewhere
                            People open pages in a new tab to keep their place, and use Back to return. A button that only swaps the view breaks both: the address doesn’t change, so there’s nothing to bookmark or share, and Back can’t return to the page they came from. A link keeps all of this working, the same as on every other site.
                            

                            Try: hover Open agenda, then Ctrl-click or middle-click it to read the agenda in a new tab. Or click it, then press Back.
                            Open agenda is a button that swaps the view.
                            Open agenda is a link with its own address.
                            

                            3Underline links in text
                            A link that differs from the words around it only by color is easy to miss, because people with color blindness or low vision, or anyone on a dim screen, see plain text. An underline marks it without relying on color, so it still shows in grayscale. Links that stand on their own, like “See all orders”, can do without it, because their place already says what they are.
                            

                            Try: find the two links in the text. Then turn on Grayscale.
                            The two links differ from the text by color only.
                            The two links are underlined.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice that in each product a link and a button sit side by side.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

                            


                            
  
                            
    
                            Chapter 22
                            
    
                            Containers
                            
  
                            
  
                            
    
                            Tabs, accordions and cards save space by hiding some content until people open it. Keep in view what people need every time or need to compare, and hide only the rest.
                            
  
                            

  
                            
    
                            Tabs
                            

                            

                            Tabs split one thing into a few parts and show one part at a time. A hotel page might have Overview, Rooms and Reviews. The tab names sit in a row with the selected one marked, and picking a tab swaps the panel below it while the rest of the page stays where it is.
                            

                            Each tab holds different content, where a segmented control changes how the same content is shown, such as a list or a grid.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                            
          
          
          
        
                            
        
                            Running shoes
                            Desk lamp
                            
        
                            Wool scarf
                            Phone case
                            
        
                            Rain jacket
                            Coffee grinder
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: click a tab, or focus one and use the left and right arrow keys.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Tabs come in three common forms, which differ in who decides what the tabs are and in what each tab remembers. Line tabs split one section of a page, a tab bar holds the main sections of a phone app, and document tabs are ones people open and close themselves, like browser tabs.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep tabs useful.
                            

                            

                            1Put things to compare side by side
                            Tabs show one panel at a time, so when people need to compare, such as rooms and their prices, they flip back and forth and keep the numbers in their head. That is slow and easy to get wrong. Put the options side by side, or in one table with a column per option, so the eye does the comparing and the answer takes one look.
                            

                            Try: Find the cheapest room that includes breakfast.
                            Each room sits on its own tab.
                            One table puts the three rooms side by side.
                            

                            2Keep to a few tabs
                            Only so many tabs fit in a row, so the rest hide past the edge, often behind a faint fade, and people miss them or scroll sideways to look. For more than about six sections, list them top to bottom in side navigation, where every section is visible and the list has room to grow. Or keep a few tabs and put the rarely used sections in a select.
                            

                            Try: Find the Language settings.
                            Nine settings tabs run past the edge behind a fade.
                            The nine sections are listed down the side.
                            

                            3Use a stepper for steps
                            Tabs tell people they can open them in any order, so when the parts have to happen in order, people jump ahead and only learn at the end that something earlier was needed. A stepper shows the order and where people are, and it checks each step before the next one, so nothing fails at the last moment.
                            

                            The checkout steps are tabs, so Payment opens before the address is in. Try: Jump to the Payment tab and press Pay.
                            A stepper moves on with Next and checks the street first. Try: Get to Payment with Next, and fill in the street when it asks.
                            

                            4Keep short content on one page
                            When each tab holds a field or two, checking them all costs a click per tab, and people never see the whole thing before they save. On one short page with headings, they check everything at a glance and save with one click.
                            

                            Try: Check the title, guests and reminder, then press Save. Watch the click count.
                            Each tab holds a single field.
                            The three fields sit on one page under headings.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice when products use tabs, and what they do instead when there are too many.
                            
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  
  

                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Accordion
                            

                            

                            An accordion is a stack of headers. Each header opens to show the content under it and closes to hide it again, which keeps a long page short when most people need only part of it, like the answers on a help page or the filters in a shop.
                            

                            Where tabs keep their names in a row and show one panel at a time, an accordion keeps its headers in a column, opens each section in place, and can show several at once.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                            More settings
                            Pages per sheet 1
                            Margins Default
                            Scale 100%
                            
        
                            Paper
                            Size A4
                            Tray Auto
                            
        
                            Color
                            Print in Black and white
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: open and close sections, and notice which one you’d open every single time.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Accordions differ in how their sections open and in what a closed header shows. In the most common form, each section opens on its own. In another, opening one section closes the others. In a filter panel, each closed header also shows what’s chosen inside it.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep accordions useful.
                            

                            

                            1Show what people come for
                            Most people open an order page to see when it arrives, so if that sits behind a closed header, every visit costs the same extra click. Show the part people come for as soon as the page loads, either open or above the accordion, and leave behind headers only what few people need.
                            

                            Try: Check when your order arrives. Then press Reload, as if you came back later, and check again.
                            Delivery status sits in a closed section.
                            The status sits above the accordion.
                            

                            2Don’t fold what people read in full
                            Some pages are read from top to bottom, like the details of a home before booking it. In an accordion, people open the sections one by one, and a closed header doesn’t show what’s inside. Put it all on one page instead, with headings to guide the eye and a few links at the top that jump to each part.
                            

                            Try: Find out about parking, pets and free cancellation.
                            The cabin’s details fold into four closed sections.
                            One page with headings, and links at the top to each part.
                            

                            3Keep it one level deep
                            Each level of nesting costs another click and pushes the content further in, so a setting three levels down is hard to find and people lose track of where they are. Open one level, and group what’s inside with small headings. If that is still too much, split it into separate pages.
                            

                            Try: Change the email digest to Daily.
                            The digest setting sits three levels down.
                            One level, with Email and Push as small headings inside.
                            

                            4Don’t hide what people must see
                            People read what’s open and skip what’s closed. If a problem sits in a closed section, such as an expired card, the page looks fine and people leave, and they find out later, when something stops working. Show the problem where people look first, with the fix next to it, and keep the accordion for extra detail.
                            

                            The expired-card warning sits inside Details. Try: Read the page. Is your plan OK? Then open Details.
                            The warning and Update card sit above Details. Try: Read the page, then press Update card.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice what stays open: the part people use most is shown, and the rest folds into headers that open in place.
                            
      
                            
        
        
        
        
      
                            
      
                            
      
                            
      
      
    
                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Card
                            

                            

                            A card is a box that holds one item: a photo album, a home to rent, a product. It shows just enough to tell items apart, such as a picture, a name and a detail or two, so people can scan a set of cards, compare them at a glance, and open one to see the rest.
                            

                            A row in a list lines up the same details in columns, which is better for comparing dates or prices. A card gives each item room for a picture instead, which helps when people know items by how they look.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                            Lemon pasta
                            Ready in 20 minutes
                            
        
                            Green curry
                            Serves 4, mildly spicy
                            
        
                            Banana bread
                            One bowl, about an hour
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: click anywhere on a card to open its recipe, then press the ⋯ in its corner.
                            
    
                            
    

                            Forms
                            

                            Cards come in a few forms, and the form decides what a click on the card does. A media card leads with a picture, and a horizontal card puts the picture beside the text, so it fits in a list. A summary card shows a few key figures, like an account balance. A choice card is picked instead of opened, like a plan.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep cards useful.
                            

                            

                            1Give each card one main action
                            Every button on a card takes space from the name and the picture, so a page of busy cards is hard to scan. Risky actions like Delete also end up next to everyday ones, one slip away. Let a click anywhere on the card open it, and put the rarer actions in one ⋯ menu.
                            

                            Try: Open Trip plan, then share Q3 budget.
                            Each card has five buttons, Delete among them.
                            A click on the card opens it, and the rest wait in one ⋯ menu.
                            

                            2Put the cards in order
                            With no order and no dates, every card is a guess, and people open them one by one to find the right one. Sort or group them the way people remember the items, such as newest first for albums, and show the date. For comparing details like photo counts, offer a list view, where the values line up in columns.
                            

                            Nine albums in no order, with no dates. Try: Find the newest album. Click one to check its date.
                            The albums are sorted newest first, with dates and a List view. Try: Find the newest album. Then switch to List to compare photo counts.
                            

                            3Make the whole card one target
                            When a card holds several click targets, one inside another, people can’t predict what a click will do: a shop name might open the shop, and a heart might save the item and open it too. Make the card one link that always opens the item, and keep the one extra action, like save, outside that link, so it does only its own job.
                            

                            The shop name and the reviews open their own pages inside a clickable card. Try: Click different parts of the card to open the shoe: the photo, the shop name, the ♡.
                            The whole card opens the shoe, and ♡ only saves it. Try: Click anywhere on the card. Then go back and press ♡.
                            

                            4Don’t put everything in a card
                            Cards are for separate items of the same kind, like albums or homes to rent. When every setting sits in its own box, the page fills with borders and shadows, nothing groups, and the boxes look clickable when they aren’t. Use plain rows under headings, and let the space between them do the grouping.
                            

                            Each setting sits in its own box. Try: Hover a box and click it. Then change Text size.
                            The settings are plain rows under two headings. Try: Change Text size.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice how little each card shows, and that none has more than one extra action.
                            
      
                            
        
        
        
        
      
                            
      
                            
      
                            
      
      
    
                            

                            

                            

                            


                            
  
                            
    
                            Chapter 23
                            
    
                            Navigation
                            
  
                            
  
                            
    
                            Navigation shows where you are and where you can go. It’s for places; actions belong on buttons.
                            
  
                            

  
                            
    
                            Side navigation
                            

                            

                            A side navigation is a list of an app’s main places, down the left edge: Home, Documents, Shared, Settings. People use it to move between those places, and it always marks the one they’re in. It stays in the same spot while the page beside it changes.
                            

                            Where tabs split one thing into parts, like the details and the reviews of a product, a side navigation moves between separate areas of the app, and it can hold more of them.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                            
          Today
          Workouts
          Plans
          
          Settings
        
                            
        
                            Today
                            
      
                            
      
                            Try it: move between areas, and watch the background on the current one and the page title.
                            
    
                            
        

                            Forms
                            

                            Side navigation comes in four common forms. A full sidebar shows an icon and a label for each place. A nested one lets places open to show their own pages. A rail is a narrow strip of icons with short labels, for pages that need the width. On phones, the list moves into a drawer that opens over the page.
                            

                            
  
  
                            
    
    
    
    
  
                            
  
                            
  
                            
  

                            

                            Rules
                            

                            Four rules keep side navigation useful.
                            

                            

                            1Keep it to places
                            People read every item in the sidebar as a place to go, so when one of them runs an action instead, like New folder, pressing it takes them away from the page they were on. The new folder then lands somewhere else, and they have to go looking for it. Put actions on buttons in the page, where they act on what people are looking at.
                            

                            New folder and Upload sit in the sidebar among the places. Try: you’re in Photos. Press New folder in the sidebar, then Create. Where did the folder go?
                            New folder and Upload are buttons at the top of the page. Try: you’re in Photos. Press New folder or Upload at the top of the page.
                            

                            2Group long lists
                            When every area sits in one long list, all of them look equally important, so people read the whole list each time, and daily work sits next to setup pages they open once a year. Group items under short headings so people can skip to the right group, fold away the groups people rarely need, and move setup pages into Settings.
                            

                            Eleven areas sit in one flat list. Try: find Discounts, then Taxes.
                            Two headings, a folded More, and setup pages moved into Settings. Try: find Discounts. Then open More and Settings to see where the rest went.
                            

                            3Show labels with icons
                            Most icons don’t say what they are, so with icons alone people point at one after another to read the tooltips, and next time they do it again. A short label with each icon lets them find a place at a glance and remember it. If space is tight, let the rail expand to show the labels. Icons alone can work in a tool people use all day, like VS Code, where there are few icons to learn and the open view’s name heads the panel beside them.
                            

                            Try: open Presets.
                            Five icons, with their names only in tooltips.
                            Each icon has a short label under it.
                            

                            4Mark the current place
                            If nothing in the sidebar is marked, people have to work out where they are from the page, and when the page title also uses different words from the item, they can’t match the two at all. Highlight the current item and give the page the same name, so people can tell where they are from either side of the screen.
                            

                            Try: say which sidebar item this page belongs to. Then open the others.
                            No item is marked, and titles like “Your music” use other words.
                            The current item is highlighted, and the page title matches it.
                            


                            

                            In real products
                            

                            Notice how each one marks the current place and makes room for more items.
                            
      
                            
        
        
        
        
      
                            
      
                            
      
                            
      
      
    
                            

                            

                            

  
                            
    
                            Breadcrumbs
                            

                            

                            Breadcrumbs are a short line of links above a page title, like My drive / Family / Holidays. They show where the page sits in a structure, from the top level down, and let people jump to any level above in one click.
                            

                            A Back link goes up one level at a time. Breadcrumbs show every level at once, so people can skip several in one go.
                            

                            
      
                            
        
                              
        
                              
        
                              
      
                              
      
                              Try it: open categories, then use the breadcrumb to jump back up several levels in one click.
                              
    
                              
        

                              Forms
                              

                              Most breadcrumbs show the full path, with a link for each level. Some add a small menu after each level, so people can move sideways to a neighbor as well as up. On phones, many show only the level above.
                              

                              
  
  
                              
    
    
    
  
                              
  
                              
  
                              
  

                              

                              Rules
                              

                              Three rules keep breadcrumbs useful.
                              

                              

                              1Skip them in flat structures
                              With only one or two levels, the trail mostly repeats the page title: one more line to read that doesn’t take people anywhere new. A clear title says where people are, and a Back link covers the one way up.
                              

                              Two levels of trips, with a trail above each title. Try: open a trip and read the line above each title.
                              Each trip has a clear title and a ← My trips link. Try: open a trip, then press ← My trips.
                              

                              2Show location, not history
                              A trail made of the pages people visited changes every time and says nothing about where the page belongs, so finding more things like it means starting again from the top. Leave the visited pages to the Back button, and make the trail show where the page sits in the structure, so its category is one click away however people got there.
                              

                              Try: find more running shoes using the trail.
                              The trail lists the pages you visited: Search, Sale, Wishlist.
                              The trail shows where the shoe sits in the shop: Shoes, then Running.
                              

                              3Shorten long paths
                              A deep path wraps onto a second line and pushes the page down, and people have to read every level to find the one they want. Keep the top level and the current one, and put the middle behind a “…” button, where the middle levels are still one click away.
                              

                              Try: jump up to Clients.
                              Seven levels, from Files down to March, fill the trail.
                              The trail reads “Files / … / March”.
                              


                              

                              In real products
                              

                              Notice that every level above the page is one click away, and that long paths get shortened in the middle.
                              
      
                              
        
        
        
        
      
                              
      
                              
      
                              
      
      
    
                              

                              

                              

  
                              
    
                              Stepper & wizard
                              

                              

                              A stepper, also called a wizard, splits a long task into a few steps in a fixed order, such as Delivery, Payment and Review. A row at the top names the steps, marks the current one and ticks off the ones that are done, so people answer a little at a time and can always see how much is left.
                              

                              Where tabs open in any order and are never finished, a stepper has an order, and each step is done before the next one starts.
                              

                              
      
                              
        
                                
          
                              1. 1Choose design
                                2. 
          
                              2. 2Write message
                                3. 
          
                              3. 3Send
                                4. 
        
                              
        
                              
          
        
                              
        
                              
          
        
                              
        
                              
          
                              
        
                              
        
                              
      
                              
      
                              Try it: change the message, go Back, then Next again, and check that your message is still there.
                              
    
                              
        

                              Forms
                              

                              Steppers come in three common forms. A horizontal stepper names each step in a row across the top. A vertical one stacks the steps and opens the current one in place. On phones, many show only a count and a progress bar.
                              

                              
  
  
                              
    
    
    
  
                              
  
                              
  
                              
  

                              

                              Rules
                              

                              Four rules keep steppers useful.
                              

                              

                              1Let people jump back
                              In a strict stepper, changing one answer means going back through every screen and forward again, which costs so many clicks that people stop checking their answers. Make finished steps clickable, and put an Edit link next to each answer on the review step. If people need to move around freely, use one page with sections instead.
                              

                              Try: ship to Work instead, then get back to Review. Watch the click count.
                              Finished steps can’t be clicked, and Review has no Edit links.
                              Finished steps can be clicked, and each answer on Review has an Edit link.
                              

                              2Give regulars a shortcut
                              A guided path helps the first time, but someone who sends the same invoice every month still has to sit through the welcome screen and every step. Offer templates or a one-page form next to the guided path, so newcomers keep the guide and regulars finish in a couple of clicks.
                              

                              Try: send Northwind its monthly invoice. Count the clicks.
                              Every invoice starts at the welcome screen and goes through each step.
                              The welcome screen offers saved templates next to the guided path.
                              

                              3Keep answers on Back
                              Losing answers on Back is the most common stepper bug. People have to choose everything again, and they may miss that a value was reset, like the number of copies going back to 1, and order the wrong number of prints. Hold on to every answer until people finish or cancel the whole task, so checking a step costs nothing and people check more.
                              

                              Try: pick a size, set Copies to 3, press Next, then Back.
                              Back clears the size and resets Copies to 1.
                              Back keeps the size and the copies.
                              

                              4Use as few steps as you can
                              Past about five steps, people lose count of how much is left, and some give up before they pay. Most of the extra screens only confirm an answer that was already picked. Cut steps, merge them, or fill them with smart defaults that people can change in one place. Three named steps fit on one line, so the end is always in sight.
                              

                              Try: press Next until you reach Pay.
                              Booking a flight takes nine screens.
                              Three named steps, with seat, bags and meal set by defaults you can Change.
                              


                              

                              In real products
                              

                              Notice how each one shows how far along you are and asks for a little at a time.
                              
      
                              
        
        
        
        
      
                              
      
                              
      
                              
      
      
    
                              

                              

                              

                              


                              
  
                              
    
                              Chapter 24
                              
    
                              States
                              
  
                              
  
                              
    
                              Every component spends time in states other than the default: loading, empty, error, disabled. Design each of them.
                              
  
                              

  
                              
    
                              Interaction states
                              

                              

                              Interaction states are the different looks one control takes as people use it: hover, focus, pressed, selected, disabled, loading, and the result after. Each state tells people something they need in that moment: that the control reacts, that it heard the click, that it’s working, or that it’s done.
                              

                              A state lives on the control itself, so people see it exactly where they acted. A message, like a toast or an inline message, is for anything that needs more words than a control can hold.
                              

                              
      
      
                              
      
                              
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
        
      
                              
    
                              
        

                              Forms
                              

                              States fall into four kinds, by what they report. Hover and pressed follow the pointer, focus shows where the keyboard is, selected shows what’s chosen, and disabled and loading say what the control can do right now.
                              

                              
  
                              
    
    
    
    
    
  
                              
  
                              
  
                              
  
  

                              

                              Rules
                              

                              Four rules keep interaction states useful.
                              

                              

                              1Design every state, not just the default
                              A button that looks the same while it sends, after it fails and when there’s nothing to send gives people no answer, so they press again or give up. Give each state its own look and words, such as “Sending…”, “Sent” and “Retry”. Before building, list every state (default, hover, focus, pressed, disabled, loading, error, success) and check each one in the browser.
                              

                              Try: press Send and watch the button. Then turn Wi‑Fi off, type a message and send it. Empty the box too.
                              Send looks the same while sending, after a failure and with nothing to send.
                              Send shows Sending…, Sent and Retry, and turns off when the box is empty.
                              

                              2Say why it’s off
                              A disabled control shows that people can’t act, but not why, so they check every field and guess. Put the reason right next to it, or keep it enabled and explain when it’s pressed, the same fix as for a disabled button.
                              

                              Try: work out why Publish is off, then publish the post.
                              Publish is off, with no reason given.
                              “Pick a topic to publish.” sits next to Publish.
                              

                              3Keep the focus ring
                              Without a focus ring, keyboard users can’t see which button they’re on, so they press Enter and hope. As in Keyboard and focus, restyle the ring to fit the design instead of removing it. :focus-visible shows it only when people use the keyboard, so it never shows on mouse clicks.
                              

                              The reply buttons have no focus ring. Try: click “Team lunch”, then press Tab, Tab, Enter. Which reply did you pick?
                              A restyled ring shows on Tab, but not on mouse clicks. Try: click “Team lunch”, then press Tab, Tab, Enter. Then click a button with the mouse.
                              

                              4Block the second click
                              If a button still works while it’s loading, a nervous double-click places two orders. Once it’s pressed, ignore repeat clicks and show that it’s working. Keep its width fixed too, because a button that grows to fit “Placing your order…” moves the buttons next to it, like content that loads late.
                              

                              Try: double-click Place order, or click it fast a few times.
                              Place order still takes clicks while it loads, and it grows.
                              Place order ignores repeat clicks and keeps its width.
                              


                              

                              In real products
                              

                              
      
                              
        
        
        
        
      
                              
      
                              
      
                              
      
      
    
                              

                              

                              

  
                              
    
                              Empty state
                              

                              

                              An empty state is what a screen shows when there’s nothing in it: no albums yet, no search results, no tasks left. Instead of a blank space, it says what belongs here and how to get the first one.
                              

                              Loading means content is on its way, and an error means something failed. Empty means everything worked, and there’s nothing to show.
                              

                              
      
                              
        
        
        
      
                              
      
                              Saved places
                              
      
                              Try it: compare Blank and Helpful. Then open No results and compare its message and button.
                              
    
                              
        

                              Forms
                              

                              Empty states come in three common kinds, set by why the screen is empty: first use, no results and all done. Each kind needs different words and a different action.
                              

                              
  
                              
    
    
    
  
                              
  
                              
  
                              
  
  

                              

                              Rules
                              

                              Three rules keep empty states useful.
                              

                              

                              1Say what goes here
                              “No items” doesn’t say what belongs on the screen or how to add it, so people have to find the small + in the corner on their own. Name what will show up here, and put the button for the first one inside the empty space, where it takes one press.
                              

                              Try: make your first album.
                              The Albums screen says only “No items”.
                              “No albums yet”, with a New album button in the empty space.
                              

                              2Offer one way to start
                              Five equal buttons make a new person stop and compare them, and none of them looks like the place to start. Give one main action, and at most one quieter one beside it, such as a link to templates for people who look for them.
                              

                              Try: you’re new here. Start your first document.
                              Five equal buttons: New, Upload, Templates, Import and Help.
                              New document leads, with a quieter Browse templates below it.
                              

                              3Match the message to the cause
                              If an empty search and an unstarted wishlist both say “No items”, people can’t tell which problem they have, and a search that’s too narrow needs a different fix than a list that’s new. For no results, name the filter and offer to clear it. For first use, explain how to add the first item.
                              

                              Search and Wishlist both say “No items”. Try: look at Search, then Wishlist. Can you tell why each one is empty?
                              Search names the size filter and offers to clear it. Wishlist explains how to save. Try: look at both tabs, then use the button on each.
                              


                              

                              In real products
                              

                              Notice that each empty screen says what belongs there and puts the first step inside the empty space.
                              
      
                              
        
        
        
        
      
                              
      
                              
      
                              
      
      
    
                              

                              

                              

  
                              
    
                              Error state
                              

                              

                              An error state is what a screen, or part of one, shows when something failed: a page didn’t load, a save didn’t go through, a link is broken. It says what went wrong in plain words and offers the next step.
                              

                              It sits where content would be, like an empty state, but it means the opposite: something failed, and people need to know what and what to do about it.
                              

                              
      
                              
        
        
      
                              
      
                              Music library
                              
      
                              Try it: switch between Vague and Helpful, and compare what each says failed and what you can do next.
                              
    
                              
        

                              Forms
                              

                              Error states come in four common kinds, set by what failed: content that didn’t load, an action that didn’t go through, a link to something that’s gone, and a page people aren’t allowed to open. Each kind needs a different next step.
                              

                              
  
                              
    
    
    
    
  
                              
  
                              
  
                              
  
  

                              

                              Rules
                              

                              Four rules keep error states useful.
                              

                              

                              1Say what failed
                              When every problem gets the same words, people can’t tell if they made a mistake, lost their connection or hit a bug, so they don’t know what to fix. Name the thing that failed, and say where the cause lies: in what they entered, in the connection, or on the product’s side. People then know whether to change their input, wait for the connection or try again later.
                              

                              Try: press Save event. Then change the end time or the Simulate setting and save again.
                              Every failure says “Something went wrong.”
                              Each message names its cause: the end time, no Wi‑Fi or the server.
                              

                              2Offer the next step
                              An error with only an OK button closes and leaves the problem where it was. Put the next step on buttons in the message, such as Try again or Get help, as in Error messages. Most failures go away on a second try, and help is there when they don’t.
                              

                              Try: get to your photos.
                              The error offers only OK.
                              The error offers Try again and Get help.
                              

                              3Keep people’s work
                              When an upload of 40 photos fails halfway and the error clears the selection, people have to pick all 40 again, and the 18 that already uploaded get sent a second time. Keep what people chose and what already finished, so Retry continues from where it stopped.
                              

                              Try: press Upload 40 photos and wait for the connection to drop. Then finish the upload.
                              The error clears the selection and the progress.
                              The photos stay selected, and Resume uploads the 22 that are left.
                              

                              4Don’t lead with the code
                              “Error 500” means nothing to most people, who can’t tell whose fault it is, or whether to retry or wait. Lead with plain words: say what didn’t load, that it isn’t their fault, and what to do. The code can stay below in small text, for when they contact support.
                              

                              Try: read it as someone who doesn’t build software. Whose problem is it? Should you retry or wait?
                              The screen shows only “Error 500”.
                              Plain words lead, and the code sits in small text below.
                              


                              

                              In real products
                              

                              Notice that each one names what failed, keeps the work, and offers the fix right there.
                              
      
                              
        
        
        
        
      
                              
      
                              
      
                              
      
      
    
                              

                              

                              

                              


                              
  
                              
    
                              Cheat sheet
                              
    
                              Before you pick one, ask three questions
                              
  
                              
  
                              
    
                              How urgent is it?
                              Sets how much it may interrupt: its step on the interruption ladder.
                              
    
                              How long must it stay?
                              Sets whether it fades, stays while true, or waits for an answer.
                              
    
                              What must people do?
                              Sets whether it holds words, buttons, or a whole form.
                              
  
                              
  
                              Quick reference
                              Start from what the person needs, then read across. Each component links to its entry.
                              
  
                              
    
                              
      
                              If people need to…UseAvoid
                              
      
        
                              Know an action workedToast, with Undo if reversibleA dialog
                              
        
                              Fix a problem with one field or itemInline messageA toast
                              
        
                              Know about a state that lastsBannerA toast
                              
        
                              Notice a count without interruptionBadgeA banner
                              
        
                              Wait a few secondsSpinner, delayed 400 msA full-screen loader
                              
        
                              Wait for long workProgress bar, in the backgroundA spinner
                              
        
                              Wait for a known layoutSkeletonA blank screen
                              
        
                              Learn what an icon doesTooltip, or a visible labelMust-know info in a tooltip
                              
        
                              Adjust a few settings in placePopoverA dialog
                              
        
                              Run a command on one itemMenuA row of many buttons
                              
        
                              Decide before going onDialogA banner
                              
        
                              Do a side task while seeing the main viewSide panelA modal dialog
                              
        
                              Turn something on right nowSwitchA checkbox
                              
        
                              Choose any of several, applied laterCheckboxA switch
                              
        
                              Choose one of a fewRadio group or segmented controlA select
                              
        
                              Choose one of manySelect or comboboxA long radio group
                              
        
                              Set a value in a rangeSlider + number fieldA slider alone
                              
        
                              Enter free textText fieldA placeholder as the label
                              
        
                              Enter a known formatStructured picker + typed inputFree text
                              
        
                              Do the main thing on a screenPrimary buttonTwo primaries
                              
        
                              Act in a tight spaceIcon button, if the icon is universalUnlabeled custom icons
                              
        
                              Go somewhereLinkA button
                              
        
                              See one part of something at a timeTabsTabs for things people compare
                              
        
                              Hide rarely needed detailAccordionTabs
                              
        
                              Scan items, then open oneCardsCards full of buttons
                              
        
                              Move between areasSide navigationNavigation for actions
                              
        
                              Get back up a hierarchyBreadcrumbsThe Back button only
                              
        
                              Follow a fixed sequenceStepperTabs
                              
        
                              See that a control heard themInteraction states on the controlOne look for every state
                              
        
                              Start when there’s nothing yetEmpty state, with one way to start“No items”
                              
        
                              Recover when something failsError state, with a next step“Something went wrong”
                              
                                    
    
                              
  
                              


                              


                              
  
                              Part 4
                              
  
                              Effective design
