                              Taking a problem to a shipped solution with agents and tools. You frame, decide and check; agents explore and build.
                              

                              


                              
  
                              
    
                              Before you start
                              
    
                              One problem runs through this part
                              
  
                              
  
                              
    
                              Most chapters use one problem in their Try-it demos: people lose unsaved work when they close a workflow tab. The worked example in the last chapter follows it through every stage.
                              
    
                              How each entry reads
                              
    
                              Each entry is one step of the work. It says what the step is for, with a demo that most often uses the problem above. Then the rules: each shows a common mistake and what to do instead, with a demo you can switch between the two. Last, how real teams and products do it.
                              
  
                              

                              


                              
  
                              Chapter 25
                              Work in a loop: frame, explore, decide, build, check
                              
  
                              Good work runs in a loop: frame the problem, explore options, decide, build, check, and learn for the next round. Agents can do much of the exploring and building, but the framing, deciding and checking stay yours.
                              

  
                              
    
                              The loop
                              

                              

                              Every change goes through the same loop. Problem and Brief frame the work, then come Explore, Decide, Build and Check, and what Learn finds starts the next round. Each stage takes something in and hands something on, so a skipped stage leaves the next one guessing.
                              

                              Agents make Build fast, so the stages around it matter more: framing the problem before, and checking the result after.

                                ↺ Learn feeds the next Problem

                                Each stage at a glance. What you own, what agents do shows how the split moves with the kind of work.
                                

                                StageTakes inHands onWho owns it
                                ProblemA signal: a support thread, a ticket, something you hit yourself.One sentence: who has the problem, and what stops them.You
                                BriefThe problem statement and what you know about it.A short brief: the goal, limits, what’s out of scope and how you’ll know it worked.You (agents can draft)
                                ExploreThe brief.Several real options, each with its trade-offs.Agents, you steer

                                LearnWhat the check found, and feedback after release.A note, and the next problem or a sharper brief.You
                                

                                Rules
                                

                                Five rules keep the loop useful.
                                

                                

                                1Frame the problem before you build
                                A ticket that names a fix sends the agent straight to Build, and it builds that fix quickly and well. If the fix doesn’t solve the real problem, people still have it and the fast build was wasted. Frame the problem and write a short brief first, so the agent explores answers to the right question.
                                

                                Try: press Send to agent, then Check with people.
                                The ticket names a fix: a red badge on the bell.
                                The ticket states the problem, the goal and how to check it.
                                

                                2Close the loop
                                A merged pull request means the change shipped, not that it worked. When shipping is the last step, nobody checks, and the problems it didn’t solve come back weeks later as support requests. Check the change against the brief and write down what you learned, because that note becomes the problem for the next round.
                                

                                The change ships, the ticket closes, and nobody checks it. Try: press Ship, then Two weeks later.
                                After shipping, the change is checked against the brief, and the lesson is written down. Try: press Ship. Then press Write down what we learned, and Start the next round.
                                

                                3Choose yourself, and write down why
                                Agents are quick to build the first idea that fits. If you merge it because it’s already built, the agent made the choice, and later nobody can say why it was done this way. Ask for several options, pick one yourself, and write the reason in the ticket or the PR.
                                

                                The agent’s first idea gets merged, with no reason written down. Try: press Merge, then Three weeks later.
                                The agent offers three options. You pick one and write why. Try: pick an option, write one line about why, then record it.
                                

                                4Try it in the real app
                                Tests an agent wrote check what the agent thought of, so they can all pass while the change fails people in a case nobody listed. Open the change in the real app and walk through the brief yourself. A problem found before the merge costs minutes, not a bug report.
                                

                                All 12 of the agent’s tests pass, and the change is merged untried. Try: press Merge.
                                Before the merge, you try it on a phone, as the brief asks. Try: press Try it on a phone, then tap the comment field.
                                

                                5Frame a hunch as a question
                                Some work starts from a hunch, with no evidence yet and a goal that’s still moving. Written as a spec, the hunch gets built as if it were known, and a whole round passes before anyone learns it was wrong. Write the brief as a question instead: what you want to find out, what you believe now and what would change your mind. Keep the rounds short, and let each Learn rewrite the brief.
                                

                                The hunch is written as a spec. Try: press Ship it.
                                The brief is a question, with what would change your mind. Try: press Finish round 1.
                                


                                

                                In real products
                                

                                Notice how long a round runs in each: a week, eight weeks, or as long as one test takes.
                                
      
                                
        
        
        
      
                                
      
                                
      
                                
      
      
      
                                

                                

                                

  
                                
    
                                What you own, what agents do
                                

                                

                                Agents are good at wide, repeatable work: searching a codebase, writing test scaffolds, making many variations. You keep the judgment: framing the problem, choosing between options and checking the result. Between agent steps, put a checkpoint where you read what came back before the next step starts.
                                

                                Where the loop names the stages of a change, this entry says who owns each one. Agent output often sounds sure, but confident wording isn’t evidence, so ask for the file, the test or the screenshot behind each claim before you build on it.
                                

                                
      
                                
        
                                
          
          
          
        
                                
        
                                
          
                                YouAgentsRough split, not a measurement
                                
          
                                  
        
                                  
        
                                  
          
          
        
                                  
        
                                  
      
                                  
      
                                  Try it: switch the kind of work and watch the split move. Decide stays yours in every case. Then tick the two mistakes to see what goes wrong.
                                  
    
                                  

                                  An agent can draft any part of a brief, and any option or check, as long as it says where each part came from, such as a support thread, a ticket or a file. Confirming who has the problem, the evidence and the problem itself stays with you, and so do the choice between options and every judgment call. The table shows the split from the demo for each kind of work.
                                  

                                  StageSmall fixNew featureOpen exploration
                                  ProblemReproduce it yourself. Is it really one line?You confirm people really lose work, and when.A hunch to test, not a spec.
                                  BriefExpected and actual, in one sentence.An agent can draft from the ticket; you cut and sharpen.What question should the prototypes answer?
                                  ExploreAn agent finds the cause. Usually one obvious option.Subagents sketch three options in parallel.Many quick prototypes as artifacts.
                                  DecideYou approve the fix, or notice it isn’t small after all.You pick one and write why.You choose what to learn more about, or stop.
                                  BuildThe agent writes the fix and a test that failed before.Claude Code builds in a worktree, plan first.Throwaway build; speed over code quality.
                                  CheckTests run; you check the real app once.Agents run tests; you close real tabs.You watch people try it. That part is yours.
                                  LearnIs it a pattern? Note it, or close it.You decide what becomes the next problem.Write down what you now believe.
                                  

                                  Rules
                                  

                                  Four rules keep the split between you and agents useful.
                                  

                                  

                                  1Ask for trade-offs, not a verdict
                                  When you ask an agent to pick the best design, it picks one and sounds sure about it, so you get a choice with nothing to check and can’t explain it later. Ask for the options and what each one is good at and costs, then make the choice yourself. If you already lean one way, write it down first, so the agent’s confident answer doesn’t become yours, as Hear their read first explains.
                                  

                                  Asked for the best design, the agent answers “Option B is the best.” Try: read the answer, then press Use B.
                                  The agent lists three options, each with what it’s good at and what it costs. Try: compare the three options and pick one.
                                  

                                  2Hand over the wide, repetitive work
                                  Some tasks are long only because there is a lot of the same thing: every use of a color token, every form to update, ten variations of a layout. Doing them by hand takes hours that framing and checking needed. Agents can do that work, several at once, and you spend the time you get back reading what they found.
                                  

                                  You open 48 files by hand, looking for the old color token. Try: press Open the next file a few times.
                                  Three agents search all 48 files at once, and you read the list. Try: press Send to 3 agents.
                                  

                                  3Stop after each agent step
                                  If exploring flows straight into planning and building, an early misreading carries all the way through, and you find out at the end, when many files have changed. Stop after each step and read what came back. Claude Code’s plan mode, where the agent proposes a plan and changes no files until you approve it, is one built-in checkpoint.
                                  

                                  The agent explores, plans and builds in one go. Try: press Start.
                                  The agent stops after exploring and again after planning. Try: press Start, read what the agent found, then correct it.
                                  

                                  4Review the plan before the build
                                  A wrong approach takes a minute to fix in a short plan, but in a finished diff (the changed lines of code) it runs through many files, and fixing it means building again. Read the plan before the agent builds, as Plan, then take small steps explains.
                                  

                                  You review only the finished PR, with 14 files changed. Try: press Review the PR.
                                  You review the four-step plan before anything is built. Try: press Review the plan.
                                  


                                  

                                  In real products
                                  

                                  Notice where each tool stops and hands over to a person: before the merge, at the sliders, before Send.
                                  
      
                                  
        
        
        
      
                                  
      
                                  
      
                                  
      
      
      
                                  

                                  

                                  

  

  

                                  


                                  
  
                                  Chapter 26
                                  Write the brief agents build from
                                  
  
                                  An agent builds what you write down, not what you meant. A good brief names the problem, the context to use and how you’ll check the result.
                                  

  
                                  
    
                                  Write the problem brief
                                  

                                  

                                  A problem brief is a short note written before anyone builds. It says who has the problem, what should change, what’s off limits and how you’ll know it worked, so an agent can explore answers without guessing what you meant.
                                  

                                  Where a ticket often names a fix, a brief names the problem, so better fixes can still turn up. Its neighbors do other jobs: a context pack holds the materials the agent works with, and a definition of done lists the checks the change must pass. Keep a brief to one page. A longer one likely covers more than one problem, so split it. Say where each part came from, and leave what you don’t know empty.
                                  

                                  
      
                                  
        
        
      
                                  
      
                                  
        
                                  
          
                                  
          
                                  
          
                                  
          
                                  
          
                                  
          
                                  
        
                                  
        
                                  
          
                                  Brief check
                                  
          
                                  
          
                                    
        
                                    
        
                                    
          
                                    Ready-to-paste brief
                                    
          
                                    
          
                                    
        
                                    
      
                                    
      
                                    Try it: switch to Rough ticket and read the check. Then fix each flag: describe what goes wrong instead of the dialog, replace “better”, and add non-goals and success criteria. Copy the result when the check is clear.
                                    
    
                                    

                                    The brief check in the demo flags four things. Passing it doesn’t make a brief clear, but each flag is worth fixing.
                                    

                                    FlagShows whenFix
                                    MissingA field is empty: who, problem, goal, constraints, non-goals or success criteria.Fill it in. Without non-goals, an agent may widen the scope, and without success criteria, nobody can say when it’s done.
                                    VagueA field uses a word from the vague-word table, such as “better” or “intuitive”.Say what you’d see happen.
                                    Too broadWho is only “users”, “user”, “everyone”, “everybody”, “people”, “all users” or “anyone”.Name the people and the moment, like “people editing in several tabs”.
                                    SolutionThe problem names a control: dialog, modal, popup, pop-up, button, toggle, banner, toast, checkbox or menu.Describe what goes wrong instead.
                                    

                                    Rules
                                    

                                    Four rules keep a brief useful.
                                    

                                    

                                    1Describe the problem, not the fix
                                    An agent builds the fix a brief names, and nothing else, so a simpler answer never comes up. Frame the problem instead: state the problem and the goal, and list any fix you have in mind as one option.
                                    

                                    Try: press Send to agent.
                                    The brief names a fix.
                                    The brief states the problem and the goal, and lists the fix as one option.
                                    

                                    2Say what’s out of scope
                                    An agent that sees nearby problems tends to fix them too. The change grows, you review work you didn’t ask for, and some of it may undo choices made on purpose. List the non-goals, such as the page layout or the button wording, so the change stays the size you meant.
                                    

                                    Try: press Send to agent and read the PR.
                                    The brief has no non-goals.
                                    The brief lists what’s out of scope.
                                    

                                    3Say how you’ll know it worked
                                    Without success criteria, “done” means whatever the agent or the reviewer feels, so the review turns into opinions and gaps slip through. Write criteria you can check in the app, such as a time, a step count or a key that must work, and turn them into the definition of done.
                                    

                                    The brief has no success criteria. Try: press Is it done?
                                    The brief lists criteria you can check in the app. Try: press Check against the brief.
                                    

                                    4Replace vague words with what you’d see
                                    Words like “better”, “cleaner” and “intuitive” mean something different to every reader, so each agent fills them in its own way, and none of the results is wrong by the brief. Replace each vague word with something you could watch happen, such as “people pay in three steps or fewer”.
                                    

                                    Try: press Ask 3 agents.
                                    The brief asks for “cleaner and more intuitive”.
                                    The brief names what you’d see happen.
                                    


                                    

                                    In real products
                                    

                                    Notice that each format makes the writer state the problem and the limits before anyone builds.
                                    
      
                                    
        
        
        
      
                                    
      
                                    
      
                                    
      
      
      
                                    

                                    

                                    

  
                                    
    
                                    Pack the context
                                    

                                    

                                    A context pack is what a new teammate would need on their first day: design tokens, components to reuse, copy rules, examples of good screens, repo conventions and the design frames. An agent that doesn’t get these makes up its own, and the result may work but doesn’t look or read like the rest of the product.
                                    

                                    Where the problem brief says what to solve, the context pack says how things are done here. Include the accessibility rules too: focus order, labels, and which color tokens pass contrast. An agent may skip rules that aren’t in the pack, and the gap only shows up in review.
                                    

                                    
      
                                    
        
        
      
                                    
      
                                    
        
                                    Same request: “Warn people before they close a tab with unsaved changes.”
                                    
        
                                    
          
                                    
            
                                    Context pack
                                    
            
            
            
            
            
            
          
                                    
          
                                    
            
                                    What the agent made
                                    
            
                                    
            
                                    
          
                                    
        
                                    
        
                                    
          
                                    
          
                                      
        
                                      
      
                                      
      
                                      Try it: compare No context with the full pack. Then tick items one at a time and watch which guess each one removes.
                                      
    
                                      

                                      Rules
                                      

                                      Four rules keep a context pack useful.
                                      

                                      

                                      1Point to the design system by path
                                      An agent doesn’t know your design system unless you show it where it lives, so it writes a new button with its own color, shape and focus style. Each one is small, but they add up to a product that looks patched together. Give the path to the token file and the components to reuse, and name the ones it must not rebuild.
                                      

                                      Try: compare the new button with Sign out. Then press Tab to move between them.
                                      With no path to the design system, the agent writes its own button, with no focus ring.
                                      The request names the token file and Button.vue, and the new button matches Sign out.
                                      

                                      2Pick what this task touches
                                      Pasting the whole repo or every design page seems thorough, but the agent then has to guess which parts matter, and it may copy an old screen instead of the current one. The brief itself can get lost in the pile. Pick what this task touches: one or two similar screens, the frames for this flow, the rules that apply.
                                      

                                      Try: press Send to agent.
                                      The whole repo and the team wiki are attached, and they fill the context.
                                      Two similar screens, the flow’s frames and the copy rules are attached.
                                      

                                      3Show the look, don’t only describe it
                                      Words leave room for guessing: “a small image on the left” can mean many sizes and positions, and the agent picks one. Link the design frame instead, or attach a screenshot of a similar screen. Claude Code can read Figma frames through the Figma MCP connector (MCP is a standard way to plug tools into an agent).
                                      

                                      Try: compare the design with what the agent made.
                                      The card is described in words, and the agent’s version differs in four places.
                                      The Figma frame is linked, and the agent’s card matches it.
                                      

                                      4Keep the stable parts in one file
                                      Tokens, copy rules and conventions rarely change between tasks. Pasting them into every request takes time, and sooner or later one part gets left out, so that task breaks a rule the others followed. Keep the stable parts in a file the agent reads every session, such as CLAUDE.md, the project notes file Claude Code loads on its own. Add only the task-specific parts to each brief.
                                      

                                      Try: press Next task until all three are done.
                                      The rules are pasted into each request, and task 3 misses the copy rules.
                                      The stable rules live in CLAUDE.md, and all three tasks follow them.
                                      


                                      

                                      In real products
                                      

                                      
      
                                      
        
        
        
      
                                      
      
                                      
      
                                      
      
      
      
                                      

                                      

                                      

  
                                      
    
                                      Define done so both of you can check it
                                      

                                      

                                      A definition of done is the list of checks a change must pass before you call it finished. Write each one as something you could see or run, such as a behavior, a state or a test that passes, and mark who checks it. An agent can prove many of them with a test run or a screenshot, but some need your judgment, such as whether the wording reads well.
                                      

                                      Where Define “good” before building decides what a good result is, this entry turns it into checks for one change, so you and the agent agree on when it’s finished.
                                      

                                      
      
                                      
        
                                      Goal: closing a tab never loses work unless the person chooses to.
                                      
        
                                      
          
          
          
                                      
            
            
            
          
                                      
        
                                      
        
                                        
        
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        Try it: press Make checkable on a vague line to see the check it becomes and who can verify it. Then filter to You verify: those are the parts you can’t hand off.
                                        
    
                                        

                                        Rules
                                        

                                        Four rules keep a definition of done useful.
                                        

                                        

                                        1Ask for proof, not a report
                                        An agent says a change is done when it believes it is, and that message doesn’t tell you whether any check passed. If you approve on its word, the bugs reach people first. Ask for the test run and the screenshots in the pull request, and look at them before you approve.
                                        

                                        The pull request only says it’s done and tested. Try: read the pull request, then press Approve.
                                        The pull request shows the test run and a screenshot for each check. Try: open the test run, then press Approve.
                                        

                                        2Name what you’d see
                                        “It feels intuitive” can’t pass or fail, so it gets marked done without a check. Write what you’d see instead, as in the problem brief, such as which result shows first. Keep the calls that need judgment, labeled as yours, and look yourself: a screenshot proves a state exists, not that it reads well.
                                        

                                        Try: press Check on each line.
                                        The criteria read “Search feels intuitive” and “It works well”.
                                        Each criterion names what you’d see, and the one judgment call is marked as yours.
                                        

                                        3Cover the other states
                                        Criteria often describe only the path where everything works, so nobody checks what happens when a save fails or several tabs are unsaved, which is where people lose work. List the other states too: several unsaved tabs, a failed save, keyboard only, a narrow window.
                                        

                                        Try: pick each state and see what happens.
                                        The criteria cover only one unsaved tab.
                                        The criteria list all five states, and each one is checked.
                                        

                                        4Put the tests in the brief
                                        Tests planned for later rarely get written, so the next change can break this one without anyone noticing, and people find out first. Name the tests in the brief, such as a Playwright spec (a test that clicks through the app in a real browser) for the new behavior, so they ship in the same pull request.
                                        

                                        Try: press Ship, then Two weeks later.
                                        The brief says “We’ll add tests later.”
                                        The brief names the spec to add: duplicate-workflow.spec.ts.

                                        Chapter 27
                                        Explore wide before you narrow
                                        
  
                                        Look at several different solutions before you pick one. Agents make each direction cheap to sketch, so spend that on range, not on polish.
                                        

  
                                        
    
                                        Get many directions cheaply
                                        

                                        

                                        Before you build one answer, ask for several different ones. Give each direction its own short brief and its own subagent (a helper agent that works alongside the others), then lay the results side by side and choose. With agents a rough direction costs minutes, so the first idea doesn’t have to be the one you build.
                                        

                                        How the directions should differ, so that each one teaches you something, is the subject of Vary along named axes.
                                        

                                        
      
                                        
        How many directions
        
                                        
          
          
          
        
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        Problem: people lose unsaved work when they close a workflow tab.
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        Try it: start at 1, then switch to 3 and 6. Each card is what one subagent made from one short brief. Keep the two or three worth taking further.
                                        
    
                                        

                                        Rules
                                        

                                        Four rules keep exploring wide useful.
                                        

                                        

                                        1Ask for several at once
                                        If you ask one agent for one answer, you get the obvious idea, and every round of polish after that makes the same idea neater, not better. Ask for several directions at the same time instead: one subagent per direction, or one git worktree (a separate working copy of the code) each when a direction needs real code.
                                        

                                        One agent returns a recent list, and each polish only adds icons, dates or sorting. Try: press Polish a few times.
                                        Three subagents return three different ideas at once. Try: press Ask for three.
                                        

                                        2Give each one its own bet
                                        Agents given the same prompt tend to land on the same answer, so you get three versions of one idea, differing only in wording or layout, and think you’ve explored. Write each brief around a different bet about what people need, such as “never interrupt” or “make it fixable in one step”. If two results still differ only in layout, rewrite one brief with a different bet.
                                        

                                        Try: press Run all three and compare the cards.
                                        Three agents share one brief and return three red toasts.
                                        Each brief carries its own bet, and the three results differ.
                                        

                                        3Keep them equally rough
                                        When one direction looks finished and the others are sketches, the finished one wins, and you end up choosing the polish, not the idea. Ask for every direction at the same level of detail, so the only difference left is the idea.
                                        

                                        Try: pick the direction you’d take further.
                                        One direction is finished and the others are sketches.
                                        All three directions are equally rough.
                                        

                                        4Set the number first
                                        Asking for “a few more” has no natural end. The pile grows, each new card adds less, and nothing gets chosen. Decide before you start how many directions to ask for, say three to six, then keep two or three and drop the rest.
                                        

                                        With no set number, the pile keeps growing. Try: press One more a few times.
                                        The number is set before you start: ask for four, keep two. Try: press Keep on the two you like best.
                                        


                                        

                                        In real products
                                        

                                        
  
                                        
    
    
    
    
  
                                        
  
                                        
  
                                        
  
  

                                        

                                        

                                        

  
                                        
    
                                        Vary along named axes
                                        

                                        

                                        When you ask for options, name what should change between them. An axis is one dimension with two ends, such as how loud a message is, from silent to blocking. Lay two axes out as a grid, one across and one down, and each cell becomes a direction. The options then differ in ways you chose, so each difference tells you something.
                                        

                                        Where Get many directions cheaply asks for many directions, this entry decides how they should differ.
                                        

                                        
      
                                        
        
        
      
                                        

      
                                        
        
                                        
        
                                        All three ask the same question at the same moment. The only choice left is wording.
                                        
      
                                        

      
                                        
        
                                        
          
                                        
            
                                        
          
                                        
            
                                        
        
                                        
        
                                        
        
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        Try it: look at the three versions, then switch to Named axes. Pick a cell to read the direction, then change the axes and watch the whole grid change. Look at the odd corners too.
                                        
    
                                        

                                        Rules
                                        

                                        Four rules keep axes useful.
                                        

                                        

                                        1Name the axis and its ends
                                        “Make three versions” gives no direction, so you get the same idea three times with small changes. Name the dimension and its two ends instead, such as “how loud, from silent to blocking”, and ask for one direction per point along it.
                                        

                                        Try: press Send and compare the versions.
                                        “Make three versions” returns three toasts that differ only in wording.
                                        The request names the axis, silent to blocking, and gets four directions, each a step louder.
                                        

                                        2Vary what people notice or do
                                        Color, label and corner radius are easy to vary, but people using the app barely notice them, so options that differ only there can’t teach you anything about the experience. Vary how loud it is, where it shows up and when it happens. If both ends of an axis would look the same to someone using the app, pick another axis.
                                        

                                        The axes are color and corner shape. Try: pick two cells. What would someone using the app notice?
                                        The axes are where it shows up and when it happens. Try: pick two cells and compare them.
                                        

                                        3Change two things at a time
                                        When every option differs in every way, a test shows a winner but not the reason. Vary two axes at a time and hold the rest fixed. Then two options that differ on only one axis, such as neighbors in the same row or column, show what that axis does.
                                        

                                        Try: press Show the test results.
                                        Three options differ in all four ways at once.
                                        Four options vary loudness and timing, and the place and wording stay fixed.
                                        

                                        4Look at the odd cells
                                        Some cells look wrong at first, such as a blocking dialog after the fact, and it’s tempting to drop them unread. Look at each one before you drop it, because a strange corner often shows why its neighbor works.
                                        

                                        The odd cells are dropped without a look. Try: open the dropped cells.
                                        Every cell gets a look before it’s dropped. Try: open Blocking, after.
                                        


                                        

                                        In real products
                                        

                                        
  
                                        
    
    
    
  
                                        
  
                                        
  
                                        
  
  

                                        

                                        

                                        

  
                                        
    
                                        Prototype in the real material
                                        

                                        

                                        A prototype answers a question about a design. Build it in code, at the fidelity the question needs and no higher. A clickable artifact page answers questions about feel and timing, and a branch in the app answers questions about real storage, real data and real speed.
                                        

                                        Code also lets you try the prototype with a keyboard and a screen reader, which a static mock can’t. Do that before you pick a direction, not after it ships.
                                        

                                        
      
                                        
        What do you need to find out?
      
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        
      
                                        Try it: pick a question. The rung that fits is marked. Lower rungs can’t answer it; higher rungs answer it too, but cost more.
                                        
    
                                        

                                        Rules
                                        

                                        Four rules keep prototypes useful.
                                        

                                        

                                        1Make timing questions clickable
                                        Some questions are about time: is a toast up long enough, does a reply feel slow. A static mock can show a toast, but not how long it stays. Make a clickable page with a real timer and real keyboard behavior, and try it yourself.
                                        

                                        A static mock of the toast, with a note that it fades after 4 seconds. Try: find out whether 4 seconds is enough to press Undo.
                                        A clickable page with a real 4-second timer. Try: press Remove, then try to press Undo in time.
                                        

                                        2Sketch before you branch
                                        A branch in the app takes days and is slow to throw away, so if you build one per direction just to compare them, most of that work goes in the bin. Compare directions as sketches first, and build in the app once the question is about the real thing.
                                        

                                        Each of three directions gets a full branch, just to compare them. Try: build all three, then pick one.
                                        The three directions are sketched, and only the chosen one gets a branch. Try: sketch all three, pick one, then build it.
                                        

                                        3Write the question at the top
                                        A prototype without a question has no point where it’s finished, so it keeps growing and nobody can say what it showed. Write the question at the top of the prototype, add only what helps answer it, and stop when it’s answered.
                                        

                                        The prototype has no question at the top. Try: press Add something a few times.
                                        The question sits at the top, and work that doesn’t answer it is skipped. Try: press Add dark mode, then Watch three people.
                                        

                                        4Decide what happens to the branch
                                        A prototype branch is built to answer a question fast, so it skips tests and takes shortcuts. If it ships as it is, those shortcuts reach people. Decide on purpose: rewrite it with tests, or keep it only after it passes the same review as any other change.
                                        

                                        The prototype branch, with a hack and no tests, is merged as it is. Try: press Merge as it is.
                                        The branch is rewritten with tests, or kept only after a full review. Try: pick one of the two ways.
                                        


                                        

                                        In real products
                                        

                                        Notice how far each one goes: one page, one component, a real branch, real people.
                                        
  
                                        
    
    
    
    
  
                                        
  
                                        
  
                                        
  
  

                                        

                                        

                                        

  

  

                                        


                                        
  
                                        Chapter 28
                                        Decide with judgment, not by polish
                                        
  
                                        
    
                                        Agents can make every direction look finished, so polish no longer tells you which one is right. Score directions against the brief, check each one hard, and keep only the parts that hold up.
                                        
  
                                        

  
                                        
    
                                        Score directions against the brief
                                        

                                        

                                        A decision matrix scores each direction from 1 to 5 against each criterion in the brief. Each criterion gets a weight, so the things the problem is about count more. The weighted total starts the decision, but it doesn’t make it.
                                        

                                        A score of 4 against a 3 is a judgment, not a measurement. Write one line of why next to each score, so a reviewer can argue with the reason instead of the number.
                                        

                                        
      
                                        
        
                                        
          
                                        Weights from the brief
                                        
          
                                        ×3
                                        
          
                                        ×2
                                        
          
                                        ×1
                                        
          
                                        ×2
                                        
          
                                        Scores 1–5, higher is better.
                                        
        
                                        
        
                                          
        
                                          
      
                                          
      
                                          Try it: with the brief’s weights, Keep drafts leads. Raise Low effort to 3 and watch the winner change, then set No interruption to 0.
                                          
    
                                          

                                          Rules
                                          

                                          Four rules keep a decision matrix useful.
                                          

                                          

                                          1Score against the brief, not the polish
                                          Agents make every direction look finished, and the most polished one draws the eye, but polish says little about whether it solves the problem. Score every direction against the brief’s criteria before you pick.
                                          

                                          A polished progress ring sits next to two plain sketches. Try: pick the direction you’d build.
                                          Each direction gets a score against the brief, with a reason for each score. Try: press Score against the brief, then pick.
                                          

                                          2Set the weights before you score
                                          Once you’ve seen the scores, it’s easy to nudge the weights until your favorite wins, and the matrix only confirms what you already wanted. Write the weights down from the brief first, then score on your own before you read anyone else’s scores, an agent’s included, so their read doesn’t become yours.
                                          

                                          The weights are set after the scores are visible. Try: move the weights until Undo toast wins.
                                          The weights come from the brief and are locked before the scores show. Try: press Lock weights and show scores.
                                          

                                          3Use the total to start the decision
                                          A total of 24 against 23 looks like an answer, but the numbers are judgments. If one small change to a weight flips the winner, the directions are close, so decide on the risk you care about most and say which one it is.
                                          

                                          A to Z leads by one point, and the total is treated as the answer. Try: press Ship the winner.
                                          One step on one weight flips the winner to Recently used. Try: press Predictable ×1 and watch the winner.
                                          

                                          4Keep three to five criteria
                                          With many criteria all weighted the same, the one the problem is about counts as little as “looks modern”, so a direction can win while failing the problem. Keep three to five criteria from the brief, and weight the ones the problem is about higher.
                                          

                                          Twelve criteria, all weighted the same. Try: find the row the problem is about, then compare the totals.
                                          Four criteria from the brief, with the problem’s own criterion weighted highest. Try: compare the totals.
                                          


                                          

                                          In real products
                                          

                                          
  
                                          
    
    
    
  
                                          
  
                                          
  
                                          
  
  

                                          

                                          

                                          

  
                                          
    
                                          Check output that looks finished
                                          

                                          

                                          Agent-made screens often look finished and still have problems: vague copy, a broken keyboard path, a missing state, or a color a little off the design tokens. A screenshot hides all of these, so you find them by using the screen the way people will.
                                          

                                          In Let agents prove their work the agent runs checks and shows you the results; here you use the result yourself and catch what no check covered.
                                          

                                          
      
                                          
        
                                          0 of 6 found
                                          
        
                                          
      
                                          
      
                                          
        
                                          
          
          Inpaint test
        
                                          
        
                                          
          
          
                                          
            
                                          
              
              
            
                                          
            
            
            
                                          
              
              
            
                                          
          
                                          
        
                                          
      
                                          
      
                                          
      
                                            
      
                                            Try it: an agent built this restore dialog for the tab-close problem. Six things are wrong with it, and two parts are fine. Click or Tab to a part and press Enter to inspect it. Stuck? Reveal all.
                                            
    
                                            

                                            Rules
                                            

                                            Four rules keep this check useful.
                                            

                                            

                                            1Use it, don’t just look at it
                                            A screenshot shows how a screen looks, not how it works: it can’t show that Tab skips a button, that an empty name gets saved, or that text is too faint to read. If you approve from the picture, people find these problems after release. Open the real thing: Tab through it, trigger the errors and read the copy out loud.
                                            

                                            The agent’s screenshot of the rename dialog looks right. Try: press Approve.
                                            The rename dialog is live, so you can Tab through it and try an empty name. Try: Tab through the dialog. Then clear the name and press Save.
                                            

                                            2Look at every state
                                            Agents build the state they were shown, usually the one with data, but people also see the screen empty, loading and failing. A blank panel on a first visit looks broken, and a spinner that never stops leaves people stuck. Ask for each state and look at each one before you approve.
                                            

                                            The agent shows only the state with data. Try: press Approve.
                                            The empty, loading and error states can be opened too. Try: open each state and see what people get.
                                            

                                            3Check values against the tokens
                                            A padding of 15 instead of 16, or a color that’s almost the brand color, looks fine by eye. Each one is small, but the next change copies it, and the product slowly stops matching itself. Check spacing, corners and color against the design tokens. Ask the agent for token names, not raw values.
                                            

                                            The agent’s Save button looks like the existing one. Try: compare the two buttons, then press Approve.
                                            Each of the button’s values is compared with its design token. Try: press Check against tokens, then Use the tokens.
                                            

                                            4Collect problems, then send one list
                                            Sending problems to the agent one at a time takes many rounds, and a fix for one can bring back an earlier one, so you end up checking the same thing again. Collect everything you found in one list first, and send it back with the checks the agent should run, such as a Playwright test for the keyboard path and screenshots in both themes.
                                            

                                            Four problems go to the agent one at a time. Try: press Send next problem until none are left.
                                            The four problems go in one list, with two checks to run. Try: press Send the list.
                                            


                                            

                                            In real products
                                            

                                            
  
                                            
    
    
    
    
  
                                            
  
                                            
  
                                            
  
  

                                            

                                            

                                            

  
                                            
    
                                            Combine the best parts, cut the rest
                                            

                                            

                                            When you have several design directions, the best answer is often none of them whole: it takes the strongest part of each and cuts the rest. Then you check that the parts you kept still work together as one design.
                                            

                                            Agents make it cheap to get many directions, so the work that’s left is choosing which parts solve the problem and which only add to it. In the demo, each direction has three parts: the trigger (what starts it), the surface (what people see) and the recovery (how they get their work back).
                                            

                                            
      
                                            
        
                                            AAsk on closeBKeep draftsCUndo the close
                                            
        
                                            
          Trigger: what starts it
          
          
          
        
                                            
        
                                            
          Surface: what people see
          
          
          
        
                                            
        
                                            
          Recovery: how they get it back
          
          
          
        
                                            
        
                                            
          
                                            Combined design
                                            
          
                                              
          
                                              Clashes to resolve
                                                
          
                                                Trade-offs you accept
                                                  
          
                                                  Cut
                                                  
        
                                                  
        
                                                  
      
                                                  
      
                                                  Try it: you start with all of direction A. Swap one part at a time and watch for clashes. Then try B’s trigger with C’s surface and recovery: nothing blocks closing, and the draft keeps Undo working after a restart.
                                                  
    
                                                  

                                                  Rules
                                                  

                                                  Four rules keep this choice useful.
                                                  

                                                  

                                                  1Take directions apart
                                                  Each direction is usually strong in one place and weak in others, so if you pick one whole, you keep its weak parts too. Split every direction into the same parts, such as trigger, surface and recovery, and pick the best version of each part.
                                                  

                                                  One direction gets picked whole, weak parts included. Try: pick each direction in turn and count the strong parts.
                                                  Each direction is split into how people start, browse and choose. Try: pick the strongest option in each row.
                                                  

                                                  2Cut what the problem doesn’t need
                                                  Good ideas pile up fast, and each one sounds worth keeping, but every part is something to build, test and explain, and people have to work out what each control does. Write the problem down and keep only the parts that solve it. The rest can wait until people ask for it.
                                                  

                                                  All six ideas stay in. Try: look at the cost and at the panel people get.
                                                  Only the parts that help with mentions stay. Try: untick the parts the problem doesn’t need.
                                                  

                                                  3Read the result as one story
                                                  Parts from different directions can contradict each other. A design can keep both a confirm dialog and an Undo toast: each makes sense alone, but together they ask people to decide twice. Describe the combined design in one sentence, from trigger to surface to recovery. If the sentence needs an “or”, cut one side.
                                                  

                                                  Try: delete a photo and read the story.
                                                  The design keeps both a confirm dialog and an Undo toast.
                                                  One way back: the photo goes at once, and a toast offers Undo.
                                                  

                                                  4Write down why parts were cut
                                                  A few weeks later, nobody remembers why a part was cut, so someone suggests it again and the team repeats the discussion or adds it back. Write one line per cut part in the ticket or the pull request, so it comes back only with new evidence.
                                                  

                                                  Try: press Two weeks later.
                                                  The pull request doesn’t say why regex patterns were cut.
                                                  The pull request says why each part was cut.
