                                                  Chapter 29
                                                  Build in small, reviewable steps
                                                  
  
                                                  Plan before any code, then build in small steps that each end with a check. Agents can run most of the checks, but the calls on what people will see stay yours.
                                                  

  
                                                  
    
                                                  Plan, then take small steps
                                                  

                                                  

                                                  Before an agent writes code, agree on a plan with it, for example in Claude Code’s plan mode. Then build one small change at a time, and check each change before the next one starts.
                                                  

                                                  Small steps keep mistakes cheap: when a step fails review, only that step goes back. In one big change, a problem in one part sends the whole change back, and it’s harder to find.
                                                  

                                                  
      
                                                  
        
        
      
                                                  
      
                                                  
        
                                                  Plan · agreed before any code
                                                  
        
                                                    
      
                                                    
      
                                                    
        
                                                    
        
                                                    
        
                                                    
      
                                                    
      
                                                    Try it: step 3 fails review. Compare how much work goes back in each approach. Then tick other steps, or none, and compare again.
                                                    
    
                                                    

                                                    Rules
                                                    

                                                    Four rules keep small steps useful.
                                                    

                                                    

                                                    1Plan before code
                                                    If you ask an agent to build a whole feature from one prompt, it makes every decision on its own, and you find the wrong ones in review, after the code is written. Ask for a plan first and read it, because changing a step in the plan takes a sentence, and changing it in code can take a day.
                                                    

                                                    The agent builds the whole feature from one prompt. Try: press Build it, then Review.
                                                    The agent writes a plan first, and its wrong step is fixed before any code exists. Try: press Ask for a plan, fix the wrong step, then approve.
                                                    

                                                    2Slice so each step works
                                                    Steps sliced by layer, such as database, then server, then screen, leave nothing to try until the last step lands. Problems then show up all at once, and nobody knows which step caused them. Slice so each step leaves the app working and gives you something to try. If a step can’t stand on its own, merge it behind a feature flag, a switch that keeps new code turned off for people, until the step that completes it lands.
                                                    

                                                    Try: press Land next step four times.
                                                    Settings search is sliced by layer, from the index to the search box.
                                                    Each step adds one part of search that you can try.
                                                    

                                                    3Give every step a check
                                                    Without a check, a step is “done” when the agent stops typing, so a broken step looks the same as a working one, and the next step builds on it. Write the check into the plan next to each step: a unit test, an end-to-end spec, a screenshot or you trying it. A step is done when its check passes.
                                                    

                                                    The plan has no checks, and the agent calls each step done. Try: run all four steps, then press Try it yourself.
                                                    Each step in the plan has its own check. Try: run all four steps.
                                                    

                                                    4Finish one step before the next
                                                    Open questions about a step don’t go away when the next step starts. Later steps build on the answer, so a late answer can undo several steps of work. Finish the review of one step, open questions included, before the next one starts.
                                                    

                                                    Step 2 can start while a question on step 1 is still open. Try: start steps 2 and 3, then answer the question.
                                                    Step 2 waits until the question on step 1 is answered. Try: answer the question, then start steps 2 and 3.
                                                    


                                                    

                                                    In real products
                                                    

                                                    Notice that each step is small, leaves things working, and gets checked before the next one builds on it.
                                                    
        
                                                    
          
          
          
          
        
                                                    
        
                                                    
        
                                                    
        
        
      
                                                    

                                                    

                                                    

  
                                                    
    
                                                    Let agents prove their work
                                                    

                                                    

                                                    When an agent says it’s done, ask it to show the proof: which unit tests ran, the end-to-end specs for the screens it changed, screenshots before and after, and a clean type check. Then you can see what was checked and what wasn’t.
                                                    

                                                    Proof isn’t the same as trying the change. Checks cover only what someone thought to test, so the proof tells you where the agent looked. Trying the change yourself, as in Check output that looks finished, covers the rest.
                                                    

                                                    
      
                                                    
        
                                                    
          
                                                    The change
                                                    
          
                                                      
            
                                                    • Workflow store: track unsaved changes per tab
                                                      • 
            
                                                    • Tab bar: a dot on tabs with unsaved changes
                                                      • 
            
                                                    • Close dialog: Save, Don’t save, Cancel
                                                      • 
            
                                                    • Shortcut: close tab goes through the dialog
                                                      • 
          
                                                    
        
                                                    
        
                                                    
          Checks the agent runs
          
          
          
          
        
                                                    
      
                                                    
      
                                                    
        
                                                    Bugs hiding in this change
                                                    
        
                                                      
        
                                                      
      
                                                      
      
                                                      Try it: only unit tests run at first. Tick more checks and watch which bugs get caught before review. Tick all four and see which one still slips through.
                                                      
    
                                                      

                                                      Rules
                                                      

                                                      Four rules keep this proof useful.
                                                      

                                                      

                                                      1Ask what ran, and see the output
                                                      “All tests pass” is also true when no tests ran. A new test file can be empty, or the agent can run a folder that doesn’t touch the change. Ask which tests ran and have the agent paste the output. Also read the test diff: an agent can make a failing test pass by changing what the test expects.
                                                      

                                                      The agent reports that all tests pass. Try: press Approve.
                                                      You ask to see the test output first. Try: press Show the test output.
                                                      

                                                      2Run the end-to-end specs for visible changes
                                                      Unit tests check logic, not screens, so a change can pass every unit test and still move a button people rely on, or break a flow another screen depends on. For anything people see, run the end-to-end specs that touch the changed screens, and compare screenshots from before and after.
                                                      

                                                      Only unit tests run for a toolbar change. Try: press Approve.
                                                      The end-to-end spec runs too, with screenshots from before and after. Try: switch between Before and After, then press Fix and rerun.
                                                      

                                                      3Get screenshots for each theme, width and state
                                                      A screenshot in one theme at one width shows only the case that was easiest to check. Ask for light and dark, wide and narrow, and the states that matter, such as empty, error and long names. Each one catches different problems, as Let an agent run design QA shows.
                                                      

                                                      One screenshot: light theme, wide window. Try: look for a problem in the screenshot, then press Approve.
                                                      Four screenshots: light, dark, narrow and a long name. Try: open each screenshot and count the problems.
                                                      

                                                      4Try it yourself anyway
                                                      Green checks only mean that nothing tested broke, so a case nobody thought of still gets through. Before you approve, try it in the real app for a few minutes, the way people will.
                                                      

                                                      All checks are green, and the change is approved untried. Try: press Approve.
                                                      The same green checks, and you try the change before approving. Try: delete two photos, then press Undo twice.
                                                      


                                                      

                                                      In real products
                                                      

                                                      Notice that “done” comes with proof anyone can open: a list of checks, a link, a picture.
                                                      
        
                                                      
          
          
          
          
        
                                                      
        
                                                      
        
                                                      
        
        
      
                                                      

                                                      

                                                      

  
                                                      
    
                                                      Call out what people will see
                                                      

                                                      

                                                      Every change people will see is a design decision: the wording, the spacing, which kind of dialog appears. An agent makes these choices for you if you let it, so treat each one as a proposal: decide on it, then name it in the pull request.
                                                      

                                                      This keeps the decisions with the people who own them. When the pull request describes each visible change, reviewers can judge it, but a change it doesn’t mention gets approved without anyone deciding on it.
                                                      

                                                      
      
                                                      
        
                                                      Agent’s change summary
                                                      
        
                                                        
      
                                                        
      
                                                        
        
                                                        Pull request description
                                                        
        
                                                        Ask before closing a tab with unsaved changes
                                                        
        
                                                        
        
                                                        
      
                                                        
      
                                                        Try it: approve or reject each line marked “People will see this”. The PR description puts what you approved first. One line is something the agent changed on the side; decide if it belongs here.
                                                        
    
                                                        

                                                        Rules
                                                        

                                                        Four rules keep these calls visible.
                                                        

                                                        

                                                        1Decide on each visible choice
                                                        An agent fills every gap with a default: generic wording, the nearest dialog, a button that says OK. Each default looks reasonable on its own, so it ships without anyone choosing it. List the choices people will see and decide on each one: keep it, change it or drop it.
                                                        

                                                        The agent’s wording and button labels ship as they are. Try: press Remove next to Ana and read the dialog.
                                                        Each visible choice is listed as a proposal to decide on. Try: decide on each choice, then press Remove next to Ana.
                                                        

                                                        2Keep side changes out
                                                        Agents often change things on the way: a font size, a color, a label in another screen. Buried in a bigger pull request, these changes ship without review, because the description doesn’t mention them. Drop them, or move them into their own pull request with their own note.
                                                        

                                                        A “while I was there” change is buried in the pull request. Try: press Approve, then look at the app.
                                                        The side change can move to its own pull request, or be dropped. Try: press Move to its own pull request.
                                                        

                                                        3Lead with what people will notice
                                                        Reviewers and teammates read the first lines of a description. If those lines list files and functions, they have to work out from the code what changes for people. Start with what people will notice, in their words, and put the code notes under it.
                                                        

                                                        Try: read the first three lines. What will people notice?
                                                        The description starts with files and functions.
                                                        The description starts with what people will notice.
                                                        

                                                        4Check before saying “no visible change”
                                                        Refactors and shared components often change how things look by a few pixels or a color, and saying “no visible change” without checking hides that from reviewers. Compare screenshots from before and after, and skim the diff for new strings, styles and components. If anything differs, describe it as a visible change.
                                                        

                                                        The pull request says “no visible change” without checking. Try: press Approve.
                                                        The screenshots are compared before anyone approves. Try: switch between Before and After.
                                                        


                                                        

                                                        In real products
                                                        

                                                        Notice that each change people will see is shown on its own, in plain words, where someone can decide on it.
                                                        
        
                                                        
          
          
          
        
                                                        
        
                                                        
        
                                                        
        
        
      
                                                        

                                                        

                                                        

  
  

                                                        


                                                        
  
                                                        Chapter 30
                                                        Check it with evidence
                                                        
  
                                                        A change is done when you can show it solves the problem, not when it merges. Pick the evidence that fits the change: people using it, a number from the brief, or a design QA pass.
                                                        

  
                                                        
    
                                                        Watch a few people use it
                                                        

                                                        

                                                        Watching people use a design is the quickest way to see where it fails. Give a few real people a task, stay quiet while they try it, and note where they stall. Five people usually show the problems that matter, because the big ones come up again and again.
                                                        

                                                        Analytics are different: they show where many people drop off, but not why. A session shows the why, one person at a time. An agent’s review can’t stand in for one: it predicts what people might do, and a session shows what they do.
                                                        

                                                        
      
                                                        
        
                                                        
          
                                                        Session plan
                                                        
          
                                                        
            Task to give
            
            
            
            
                                                        
          
                                                        
          
                                                        
            Watch for
            
            
            
          
                                                        
          
                                                        
            Questions to ask after
            
            
            
            
            
                                                        
          
                                                        
        
                                                        
        
                                                        
          
                                                        
            
                                                        Problems across sessions
                                                        
            Sample notes
          
                                                        
          
                                                        
          
                                                          
          
                                                          No sessions yet.
                                                          
          
                                                          
            
            
          
                                                          
        
                                                          
      
                                                          
      
                                                          Try it: pick each task wording and read why it helps or hurts. Tick the questions you’d ask. Then log all five sessions and see which problems repeat.
                                                          
    
                                                          

                                                          Rules
                                                          

                                                          Four rules keep these sessions useful.
                                                          

                                                          

                                                          1Watch what people do
                                                          Ask people whether they’d use something, and most will say yes, because they want to be kind and can’t know what they’ll do later. What they do with a real task is better evidence, so give them the task and watch where they go.
                                                          

                                                          You ask “Would you use this?” and count the yeses. Try: press Ask all five, then See what happened after release.
                                                          You give a task and watch what each person does. Try: press Watch five sessions and read what each person did.
                                                          

                                                          2Describe the goal, not the feature
                                                          If the task names the feature, people look for that word on screen and find it, so you learn that they can read, not that they’d find their way. Describe what they want to get done, in their own words, and you see where they look first.
                                                          

                                                          Try: press Give the task and watch where they look.
                                                          The task names the Memories tab.
                                                          The task describes the goal: find last summer’s beach photos.
                                                          

                                                          3Stay quiet when they get stuck
                                                          Silence feels awkward, so you’ll want to help as soon as someone stalls. But the stall is the finding, and if you help, you never learn why it happened. Note where it happened and wait. Ask “What did you expect?” at the end, and only step in if they want to give up.
                                                          

                                                          Try: press Play session and read the notes at the end.
                                                          You help as soon as they stall.
                                                          You stay quiet, note the stall and ask what they expected.
                                                          

                                                          4Fix what repeats
                                                          One person’s trouble may be theirs alone. If you change the design after each session, every person sees a different version, and you can’t tell which problems repeat. Run all the sessions on the same version and tally what went wrong, then fix what more than one person hit.
                                                          

                                                          Try: press Log session five times.
                                                          The design changes after every session.
                                                          All five sessions use one version, and you keep a tally.
                                                          


                                                          

                                                          In real products
                                                          

                                                          Notice that each one watches what people do, not what they say, and looks for problems that repeat.
                                                          
      
                                                          
        
        
        
        
      
                                                          
      
                                                          
      
                                                          
      
      
    
                                                          

                                                          

                                                          

  
                                                          
    
                                                          Measure against the brief
                                                          

                                                          

                                                          Measuring against the brief means choosing, before you build, the numbers that will show whether the brief’s goal was met. Each success criterion gets one number that moves only if people got what they needed. You add one number that must not get worse, and read both next to what people say.
                                                          

                                                          Without this, teams count what is easy to count, and a banner can be seen a million times and still help nobody.
                                                          

                                                          
      
                                                          
        
                                                          
          
          
          
        
                                                          
        
                                                          
          
                                                          From the brief
                                                          
          
                                                          
          
                                                          
            Which number answers it?
            
                                                          
          
                                                          
          
                                                          
        
                                                          
        
                                                          
          
                                                          Measurement plan
                                                          
          
                                                            
        
                                                            
      
                                                            
      
                                                            Try it: for each criterion, try all three numbers. Only one of each three really answers it. Fill the plan with those.
                                                            
    
                                                            

                                                            Rules
                                                            

                                                            Four rules keep these numbers useful.
                                                            

                                                            

                                                            1Count the outcome, not the activity
                                                            Views and clicks are easy to count, so they end up on the dashboard, but they rise with traffic whether or not anyone got what they came for. Count the outcome instead, as a share of the people who could have reached it, such as finished reorders out of everyone who opened a past order. Then more visitors alone can’t move the number.
                                                            

                                                            Try: switch to Sale week and read the number.
                                                            It counts clicks on Reorder.
                                                            It counts finished reorders as a share of the people who opened a past order.
                                                            

                                                            2Add a number that must not get worse
                                                            A change can raise one number by hurting something else, so if you only watch the number you want to raise, you’ll pick the version that does the most harm. Add a guardrail: one number that must not get worse, with a limit you set before looking. In an A/B test, where each group of people gets a different version, a version that crosses the limit is out, however good the main number looks.
                                                            

                                                            Try: pick the version you’d ship.
                                                            An autoplay test tracks only listening time.
                                                            A guardrail: people who turn autoplay off must stay under 5%.
                                                            

                                                            3Pick the numbers before you build
                                                            If you choose the number after release, the event you need is often missing, so you can only look at what happens to be logged, and that rarely answers the brief. Write the numbers in the brief and add their events in the same pull request. An event only needs to record that something happened, such as a suggestion being picked, so never log what people typed or made.
                                                            

                                                            Try: press Two weeks later.
                                                            Nobody named a number before release.
                                                            The brief names the number, and the pull request adds its event.
                                                            

                                                            4Read the number with what people say
                                                            A number tells you that something changed, not why. A drop can mean people stopped wanting a feature, or that they can’t find it anymore. Read it next to support threads and a few watched sessions, which usually explain the change.
                                                            

                                                            Price alerts dropped, and the team reads only the number. Try: press Decide.
                                                            Support threads and sessions sit next to the number. Try: open the threads and sessions, then press Decide.
                                                            


                                                            

                                                            In real products
                                                            

                                                            Notice that each team counts a number that moves only when people get what they came for, and some add one that must not get worse.
                                                            
      
                                                            
        
        
        
        
      
                                                            
      
                                                            
      
                                                            
      
      
    
                                                            

                                                            

                                                            

  
                                                            
    
                                                            Let an agent run design QA
                                                            

                                                            

                                                            Design QA means checking a change everywhere people will see it before it ships: in light and dark, on narrow and wide screens, and in every state it can be in. An agent can render all of those and list what looks wrong much faster than you can. You still read the list, open the important findings yourself and decide what to fix.
                                                            

                                                            The agent does the looking, which is slow and easy to skip, and you keep the judgment that tools lack: what matters to people, and what is a false alarm.
                                                            

                                                            
      
                                                            
        
                                                            
          
                                                            
            
                                                            Preview
                                                            
            
                                                            
              
              
            
                                                            
          
                                                            
          
                                                            
        
                                                            
        
                                                            
          
                                                            
            
                                                            Design QA · restore banner
                                                            
            
                                                            
          
                                                            
          
                                                            Not run yet.
                                                            
          
                                                              
        
                                                              
      
                                                              
      
                                                              Try it: run the checks. Markers show where each problem is in the preview. Switch the preview to 360px, apply the fixes one by one, then run the checks again.
                                                              
    
                                                              

                                                              Rules
                                                              

                                                              Four rules keep design QA useful.
                                                              

                                                              

                                                              1Check every theme and width
                                                              You build in your own theme on your own screen, so that’s where the change looks right. Other people use dark mode and phones, and that’s where text goes faint and buttons get cut off. Have the agent take screenshots in light and dark, at 360px and at a desktop width, every time. It takes the agent seconds.
                                                              

                                                              Try: press Run checks and read the report.
                                                              The agent checked one screenshot: light, at desktop width.
                                                              It checked light and dark, at desktop width and 360px.
                                                              

                                                              2Render every state
                                                              The state you designed is usually the one that works. Problems hide in the others: while it loads, when it fails, when a name is long. List every state the change can be in, and have the agent render each one with real, messy data, because it is longer than the sample.
                                                              

                                                              Only the finished upload was checked, with a short sample name. Try: press Run checks, then Use a real file name.
                                                              All four states were rendered with real file names. Try: press Run checks, then Fix the long name.
                                                              

                                                              3Open the findings yourself
                                                              An agent can misread a screenshot, or flag something that is meant to look that way. If you apply every finding without looking, you can break what was right. Open at least two findings yourself and check them against the brief. Dismiss the wrong ones and say why.
                                                              

                                                              All three findings are applied without looking. Try: press Fix all, then read what happened to the Pay button.
                                                              Each finding is opened and checked before anything changes. Try: open each finding and keep or dismiss it.
                                                              

                                                              4Test with the keyboard yourself
                                                              An automated scan checks things like contrast and missing labels, but it can’t tell whether the focus moves in a sensible order, or whether a screen reader reads the page in a useful way. Tab through the change once and try a screen reader once. Only then call it accessible.
                                                              

                                                              Try: click Name and press Tab a few times.
                                                              The scan found no issues, and the form was called accessible.
                                                              Someone tabbed through it, found the order wrong and fixed it.
                                                              


                                                              

                                                              In real products
                                                              

                                                              Notice that the tool renders every state, theme or size and points at what changed or failed, but a person makes the call.
                                                              
      
                                                              
        
        
        
        
      
                                                              
      
                                                              
      
                                                              
      
      
    
                                                              

                                                              

                                                              

  
  

                                                              


                                                              
  
                                                              Chapter 31
                                                              One problem, start to finish
                                                              
  
                                                              Here the running example goes through every stage, with the small artifact each stage leaves behind. Then a map shows which tool fits which job.
                                                              

  
                                                              
    
                                                              Follow one problem through
                                                              

                                                              

                                                              This entry follows one problem from brief to release: people lose unsaved work when they close a workflow tab. Each stage ends with one small thing someone else can read: a brief, a context pack, directions, a decision, a plan, checks and a note on what you learned. The stages follow the loop, with Problem folded into the brief and the context pack as a step of its own.
                                                              

                                                              With those artifacts, anyone can pick up the problem at any stage and see why it went the way it did, including you a month later. The rule demos below use smaller problems of their own.

                                                              Sample brief · Linear ticket
                                                              
              
                                                              People lose unsaved work when they close a workflow tab.
                                                              
              
                                                              
                
                                                              Who
                                                              People with several workflows open, tidying their tabs.
                                                              
                
                                                              Trying to
                                                              Close what they don’t need without thinking about it.
                                                              
                
                                                              In the way
                                                              A tab with changes can close before they meant to keep them.
                                                              
                
                                                              Evidence
                                                              Three support threads this month, and you lost work the same way in your own runs. To check: how often it happens.
                                                              
                
                                                              Done when
                                                              Closing a tab never throws away changes without a choice the person made.

                                                              You
                                                              
            
                                                              Agents
                                                              
          
                                                              
        
                                                              
        
                                                              
          
          
        
                                                              
      
                                                              
      
                                                              Try it: step through the seven stages with Next, the numbers, or the arrow keys on a number. At Decide, count “never loses work” twice and watch the winner change.
                                                              
    
                                                              

                                                              Rules
                                                              

                                                              Four rules keep the stages useful.
                                                              

                                                              

                                                              1Explore directions before you build
                                                              An agent builds fast, so it’s tempting to go from the brief straight to code. Then the first idea is the only idea, and a better one turns up in review, after the work is done. Spend that speed on directions instead: ask for three different ones, and pick one before anything is built for real.
                                                              

                                                              Try: press Next step until the work is done, and watch the days.
                                                              The agent builds the first idea it gets.
                                                              Three directions are sketched and one is picked before building.
                                                              

                                                              2Leave one artifact per stage
                                                              If each stage lives in your head or in a long chat, nobody else can follow it: when someone asks why you chose this design, the answer is somewhere in hundreds of messages. Leave one small artifact per stage: the brief in the ticket, the directions on a page, the decision and checks in the pull request.
                                                              

                                                              Try: find out why the default reminder is 10 minutes.
                                                              The work lives in one long chat with the agent.
                                                              Each stage left a small artifact, linked from the ticket.
                                                              

                                                              3Scale the stages to the problem
                                                              Agents make every stage cheap, so it’s tempting to run all of them at full size. For a typo, three directions and a scoring table waste a day and bury a one-word change. Ask what each stage is for, and if its artifact wouldn’t change a decision, keep it to a line.
                                                              

                                                              Try: read the work list and how long it took.
                                                              All seven stages run at full size for a typo.
                                                              The typo gets a one-line brief and one check.
                                                              

                                                              4Check the result after release
                                                              Merged isn’t done: the evaluation plan only helps if someone reads it after release. Go back to it once people have used the change, check each line, and write down one thing you learned.
                                                              

                                                              Try: press One month later.
                                                              The ticket closes when the pull request merges.
                                                              The evaluation plan is checked a month after release.
                                                              


                                                              

                                                              In real products
                                                              

                                                              Notice that each story moves through clear stages, and each stage leaves something others can read or try.
                                                              
      
                                                              
        
        
        
        
      
                                                              
      
                                                              
      
                                                              
      
      
    
                                                              

                                                              

                                                              

  
                                                              
    
                                                              Pick the tool for the job
                                                              

                                                              

                                                              Design work has separate jobs: frame the problem, gather context, explore, decide, build, check and share. Each job has a tool that fits it, and splitting the work by job keeps each step small enough to check, with a result the next step can use.
                                                              

                                                              One long chat can do all of it, but then the decisions are buried and nobody can check them. Whatever the agents make, the brief, the decision and the pull request’s list of behaviors should read as yours, because you’re the one answering for them.

                                                              Try it: pick a job. The tools it needs light up, with one line on how to use them and what that looked like for the tab-close problem.
                                                              
    
                                                              

                                                              Rules
                                                              

                                                              Four rules keep the tools working for you.
                                                              

                                                              

                                                              1Split the work by job
                                                              One chat asked to explore, decide and build does all three at once: it builds the first idea, and the choice between directions is never made in the open. Explore with parallel subagents, decide on a shared page, then build in a worktree with tests, so each step leaves something you can check.
                                                              

                                                              Try: read what each step left behind.
                                                              One chat explores, picks and builds a date picker in one go.
                                                              Each job goes to its own tool.
                                                              

                                                              2Read the real design values
                                                              A screenshot shows how a design looks, not the values behind it. An agent that rebuilds from one guesses the colors, spacing and corner radius, and each guess is a little off. Read the frames and tokens through the Figma connector instead, so the build uses the same values as the design.
                                                              

                                                              Try: turn on Overlay the design.
                                                              The button was rebuilt from a screenshot.
                                                              The values were read from the Figma file through the connector.
                                                              

                                                              3Ask for a test that fails first
                                                              An agent says “done” when the code runs, not when the behavior works, so if you take that on trust, the bug turns up when someone uses it. Ask for a test that fails before the change and passes after, then run the Playwright specs that touch the changed screens.
                                                              

                                                              The agent says it’s done, and you take its word. Try: add an item, then sign in.
                                                              A test fails before the change and passes after. Try: press Run the test, then add an item and sign in.
                                                              

                                                              4Share a link people can click
                                                              A screen recording shows one path, at the pace of whoever made it. People can’t try the other buttons, so their questions stay open. Publish the prototype as an artifact link people can click through, and link it from the ticket so it’s still there next week.
                                                              

                                                              The prototype is shared as a screen recording in chat. Try: try to press Skip in the recording.
                                                              It’s shared as a link people can click through, and linked from the ticket. Try: open the link and press Skip.
                                                              


                                                              

                                                              In real products
                                                              

                                                              Notice that each tool does one job well and hands its result to the next, instead of one tool doing everything.
